en: Preface to the *Record of the Layman’s Divided Lamp*:

Originally, the patriarchs transmitted one to another, and lamp after lamp continued in succession. Thus, the illuminating power was equally fused within the torch of wisdom, and its numinous light shone everywhere upon the dark alleys of the world.
Therefore, those ancient worthies and eminent monastics who sought the Way beyond the mundane extinguished the shadows of karma born of ignorance.
There were also those with innate faculties and sharp capacities who, through diligent study of the Buddha’s teachings, emerged from the fiery wheel of birth and death.

The patriarchs of this lineage, having received the weighty mandate of past transformations, frequently attained wondrous realization of the sacred understanding and reached a silent accord with the Chan school.
In all, there were seventy-two such individuals. Over the course of several thousand years, who has ever selected, compiled, and evaluated them? It was none other than my friend, Zhu Wozhen.

This gentleman’s learning encompassed both Chinese and Sanskrit classics; his emotions were extinguished and his intellect transcended the mundane. His mind served as a lamp of *prajñā*, and he was worthy to occupy the seat of Yunqi.
He delved deeply into the Buddhist scriptures with the great vow to deliver all beings, asserting that the body of a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) is fundamentally no different from that of a Buddha.

Seeing the nature of the Tathāgata, he encountered conditions without obstruction, realizing the unborn. Like Dingfan, who abandoned official office to seek the Way, or Zhang Hui, who renounced secular life.
As a monk, you pledged to reach the Ten Stages with Feng Liang; your insight into the Three Emptinesses was commended by Zhi Lin.
You composed the "White Ox" at Puan and discussed the "Yellow Bear" with Zi Yue. Having studied the Way while living as a layman, you have frequently encountered eminent worthies.

If you can suddenly shatter the mundane barriers and exert effort to eliminate the net of views, so that you may renounce all worldly things within the inner chambers, only then will you attain the field of liberation free from leakage.
A single step forward is itself Bodhi. One must cause the blade of wisdom to fly with its radiance and the pearl of the mind to burst forth;

its light shall divide and illuminate, extinguishing embers and rekindling them. This is sufficient to initiate the transmission of the torch for future generations and to raise the fading flames of the ancestral wind.
I have recorded these notes from my own hand and titled them "The Division of the Lamp. Is not the intent of this very thing? Is it not the intent of this very thing? I, [Name], [End of Text]

Having received [the texts], I collated them; opening and comparing them, I was filled with joy. They are almost identical to my previously composed *Liaoyi Lianzong* (The Lotus School of Definitive Meaning), both serving as precious rafts for those lost at the crossroads.
Recently, I have further compiled the *Fozu Gangmu* (Outline of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), tracing back even further to the profound source of the Dharma-ocean.
For over thirty years, I have satiated myself with the flavor of the Way; truly, I have become a contributing official to enlightenment, following in the footsteps of the seventy-two patriarchs.
Accepting directly beneath [the transmission]. Continued by the Layman Fenzhu (Fendeng).
Recorded by the Layman Guangxiu, Wang Yuanrui.
Preface to the Record of the Layman’s Transmission of the Lamp.
True Suchness is eternally quiescent yet eternally illuminating; Prajñā is without division yet without non-division. When it is divided, there is the essence of union:
ten thousand lamps originally converge in a single lamp. When it is united, there is the function of division: a single lamp suddenly disperses into ten thousand lamps.
This is certainly not something that can be constrained by physical forms, nor can it be fathomed by the intellect. My friend, your mind is empty.
From the essence of its nature, it plants the banner of radiant light; within the True Dharma, it kindles the lamp of inexhaustibility.
Lamenting that the distant past leaves no trace, yet deeming the transmitted accounts reliable, forty-one fascicles analyze and categorize every detail, thereby encompassing the essential framework;
seventy-two individuals exalt the Great Matter, further illuminating the transmission of the lamp. Thus, the Gate of Non-duality opens.
The Buddha of Golden Grain; Old Master Pang drank the West River dry. His pair of hands, free from affairs, never once performed a formal bow.
Suddenly, the scent of osmanthus fills the courtyard; without cause, it pierces through the nostrils. At the fifth watch, the chamber pot is kicked over, squeezing out the ancients' final word.
A clap of thunder at the crown of the head awakens that which was one's own from before. The frogs croak.
Beneath the moon, one suddenly shatters heaven and earth. As the sun rises from the surging waves, one seeks only the effort of marriage.
An eight-cornered millstone in the void; hidden within the Big Dipper in the heart. To lay hands upon it is to pass judgment. An iron man practicing Zen:
a dung ball of a dung beetle is not exchanged for ten thousand taels of gold. Mountain colors and stream sounds are entirely but a single spring dream. There is a Master.

I have inherited nothing from a teacher; yet the descendants of Master Wang are still here. Whether one is of the lineage of the immortals or not, the corpse-guarding ghosts merely regret their mistaken application of the mind.
Do not doubt the tongues of the old monks of the world; they have scrutinized and penetrated the seventeen hundred public cases.
When there is light, there is darkness within it; when there is darkness, there is light within it. True Suchness pervades the entire realm and has never been hidden. Ordinary...
If it were perfectly penetrating and unimpeded, it would be like the paper lamp extinguished by a gust of wind at Longtan, or Yun’gai not holding a torch to light his way.
Tell me, is this a lamp or not? To differentiate it is one thing; not to differentiate it is another. Heh!
A single expanse of empty mind—a heart of compassion—expresses its breath right here.
Thus, the layman Zhang Yi-zhen inscribed this preface for the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*.
The Treasury of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma-Eye was first transmitted to Mahākāśyapa, and so on through twenty-eight transmissions until Bodhidharma.
Moyan observed from afar that China possessed the karmic capacity for the Mahāyāna; he subsequently crossed the sea to come there. Moyan transmitted the Dharma to Huìkě;
Huìkě transmitted it to Sēngcàn; Sēngcàn transmitted it to Dàoxìn; Dàoxìn transmitted it to Hóngrěn; Hóngrěn transmitted it to Huínéng. Huínéng transmitted it to Huìràng and Xíngsī.
The descendants of these two lineages have caused the Five Lamps to shine with mutual brilliance—such as Linjì, Yúnmén, Wèiyáng, and Cáoxi.

The Cavern. Whether it be the Dharma-eye, or building a thatched hut atop a solitary peak, or untying the sack at the crossroads—when the bright mirror stands before the stand, Hu and Han appear of themselves;
when the precious sword is held in hand, killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion.

The "Qingzhou Shirt" and the "dry dung pellet"—to harbor doubts about these is to deviate from the truth. The spark struck from flint, the flash of lightning—once the eye turns, they are lost. It is ultimate!

It has reached its end; there is nothing further to be attained above this. Nevertheless, when examining the period when the Way of the Dharma flourished, wherever there was a master of transformation, there were necessarily those who propagated that transformation.
The masters of transformation are as described above and are fully recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).

As for those who propagated the transformation, there were such figures as Vimalakīrti, Pang Daoxuan, Zhang Wujin, and Song Jinglan. They concealed the great while manifesting the small, carrying the [teachings] across the waters.
"Dragging through the mud": to discuss the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) without destroying conventional designations (*prajñapti*). This, too, is a vast and expansive compassionate vow.

Having already established the long-standing path for harmonizing with the world to benefit sentient beings, I have therefore briefly excerpted from the Buddhist scriptures to compile the *Fourty-one Volumes of the Ancestral Canon*.

I have further compiled a record of seventy-two individuals among the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) who possessed a verifiable lineage of masters and were manifestations of those who had returned from transformation.

This work, titled *Fendeng Lu* (Record of Dividing the Lamp), consists of two fascicles. As for "dividing the lamp," this was the designation revealed to me in a dream during my compilation by the Venerable Śāriputra.
If one were to say that this book is not the "Inexhaustible Lamp," yet it is also not the case that it is not the "Inexhaustible Lamp," and if one wishes to...
Is it to be revealed by light to illuminate what comes hereafter? Xuedou said, "Thirty-three people entered the tiger’s den.
I also say, "Seventy-two people emerged from the dragon’s lair. This very book is right here before you; do you recognize the dragon?
A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net—do not say it is stuck in the water. Where the moonlight of non-existence is clear, waves arise even without wind. Study this!

Preface to the Annotated Compilation for Assisting the Teaching.
Song Lian:
Heaven bestowed upon us two sages—one from East Lu and one from West Zhuzi—to transform and guide the masses.
Although their established teachings differ, in making people incline toward the path of goodness, they are one and the same. Those who study the teachings of East Lu say: "I preserve my mind."
It is the cultivation of one's nature. Those who study in Western India say, "We clarify the mind and perceive its nature.
To investigate the reality of this, although it may seem slightly different from worldly principles, how could it ever transcend the single mind? As the transmission says:
A sage appeared in the Eastern Sea; his mind was the same as [the other sages], and his principle was the same. A sage appeared in the Western Sea;
his mind was the same, and his principle was the same. Sages appeared in the Southern and Northern Seas; their minds were the same.
The principle is the same. Thus, the mind is the source of all principles; it encompasses the great without exception and includes the minute without exception.
If one can fulfill its potential, one becomes a worthy and wise person; if one turns away from it, one becomes foolish and unworthy. If one awakens to it, one becomes one of the four sages.

Conversely, there are the six classes of ordinary beings. People of the world see only that the cultivation of ritual, music, law, and governance serves as the means for regulating society, while the maintenance of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom constitutes the essential path for entering the Way; thus they distinguish between the mundane and the supramundane.

There are things as opposite as ice and fire, or day and night; yet one does not realize that the extension of spring and summer causes all species to flourish with joy, while the contraction of autumn and winter causes all things to store and rest. All these emerge from the circulation of the single primordial qi (*yuanqi*);
beyond this qi, no other entity is ever perceived. The person of great realization possesses a comprehensive vision, seeing clearly through the eight directions.

It is vast and without the boundaries of fences, and has no demarcations of doors or thresholds; therefore, its utterances and discourses do not concern themselves with external forms or traces, but proceed entirely toward the Great Sameness (*Mahāsāmānya*).
How could petty men of shallow understanding—whose livers and gallbladders are as far apart as Hu and Yue—be sufficient to participate in this?
In the Song dynasty, there was a great being named Chan Master Xingshan Tanzong of Tanting; he was truly the Dongsan Conggong.

As a dharma heir of these [traditions], fearing that the defects of the later streams of the two schools might lead to mutual discord, he synthesized various texts and brought them into harmony, producing the *Yuanjiao* (Origins of the Teachings), the *Guangyuanjiao* (Extended Origins of the Teachings), the *Quanshu* (Exhortations), and the *Xiaolun* (Treatise on Filial Piety), with the *Platform Sutra Praise* appended thereto.
Furthermore, lest others not fully grasp his intent, he provided his own commentaries upon them, titling the collection the *Fujiao bian* (Compendium for Assisting the Teachings). As for Chan...
The Master may truly be called one who integrates the myriad principles within a single mind. I am originally of the same lineage as Zhang Fang;
I have studied and read extensively from the books of the Four Treasuries, and upon reaching my prime, I further applied myself deeply to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures).
Often observing their explanations to be vast, profound, and superior, I finally believe that what Liu Zongyuan said regarding their harmony with the *Yi* and the *Lunyu* is no mere falsehood.

It is delusory; therefore, many become excessively attached to the words and phrases [of this work]. Those who do not understand me may come to revile me with bared fists, yet I remain silent and do not respond, offering only a smile.
Now, because Master Guobai has re-carved this compilation, his contribution to students of the Way is truly great;
thus, I have taken up my pen to speak of it. Alas! Who can summon Chan Master [Wuzhu] for me?

Within the eternally quiescent light, we discourse together upon the single thread that unifies Confucianism and Buddhism. Gazing alone toward the heights of heaven with a sense of tranquil detachment, I have long contemplated these matters from afar.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Fahufa lun* (Treatise on Protecting the Dharma), by Song Lian.
The *Fahulun* (Treatise on Protecting the Dharma) was composed by Zhang Tianjue, the Grand University Scholar of the Song dynasty.
Chan Master Duwen re-carved it for publication and requested that I write a preface for its opening pages. The preface states: "Alas! The wondrous, luminous true nature is like the vast sky;
it is not confined by spatial location and originally possesses no form or substance. It is profound, tranquil, and serene; it is vast, desolate, and pure. It transcends..."
One does not know where it ends; one enters it and does not know where it reaches its limit. It is boundless with all things, perfectly wondrous and pervasive.
At such a time, there are no names of "Buddha" or "sentient beings," nor are there appearances of self or other. All things are encompassed within all things without obstruction;
how could even a single dharma be spoken of? Alas, now that the Great Simplicity has dispersed, people have abandoned the supreme truth.

Dissolute! Busily pursuing external objects, one follows only the inclinations of karmic consciousness and worldly attachments. This is just like a lost person whose body has fallen into a vast marsh where mist and smoke shroud all in darkness;

snakes and tigers roam in every direction, vying with one another to pursue and inflict harm upon the person. With disheveled hair, he flees in a frantic run, unable to distinguish the four cardinal directions.
Out of compassion, the Great Sage of the West [bestows] the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings... [not provided in source].
It need not be further explained; this is how this Dharma was established. When sentient beings hear this Dharma, they follow and practice it.
It is like encountering the light of the sun and meeting a virtuous and superior friend, who drives away all evils and leads one onto the broad highway;
one immediately leaves behind fear and attains peace and security. What blessing could exceed this? Yet, instead of deeply honoring its virtue, [people] conversely...
To revile and reject them is like brandishing a sharp sword to wound oneself; how could it possibly harm the Great Dharma? Alas!
When the Three Sovereigns governed the world, they skillfully utilized the times; the Five Emperors then shifted to benevolence and trustworthiness;
and the Three Kings further employed wisdom and valor. This is because the social climate shifts with each age; thus, those who govern must also guide according to the times.
Things changed. From the time of the Eastern Zhou dynasty onward, ignorance, perversity, depravity, and heterodoxy arose in great numbers;

fetters and manacles were insufficient to restrain prisoners, and the axe and the halberd were insufficient to instill awe. The Sage of the West extensively expounded the doctrine of cause and effect and the cycle of rebirth.

If the violent and powerful were to hear of this, their necks would turn crimson and sweat would break out on their backs; they would hesitate, shrink back, and even ants would not dare to tread upon it.
Would this not be of great benefit for supplementing what is lacking in governance and transformation? This is precisely what Liu Zongyuan meant by "providing secret support to the royal ordinances.
This describes merely its coarse manifestations. As for its higher level, one gazes inward with brilliant clarity—neither approaching nor departing. It may be...
Having escaped the base and turbid to reach the ultimate sublime and brilliant, and having transcended the three realms to ascend to wondrous enlightenment—this is truly not to be doubted.
How can one revile it? How can one reject it? Those in the world who observe this discourse may well be struck with awe and contemplate it;
they may be moved to alarm and reflect upon themselves. Nevertheless, I have a certain point to make, which I shall set forth as an admonition to the followers of the Śākya school.
When a building is solid, wind and rain cannot cause it to sway; when the vital energies (rō-ei) are full, disease cannot invade.
Should not those in black robes likewise reflect upon their own fundamental nature? I privately marvel at those who recite the words and deeds of the Buddha yet act as followers of external paths;
this is to destroy the Dharma themselves. To fail to observe the Vinaya and its rules is to abandon it oneself. This is... [self-abandonment].
This is to destroy the Dharma. For those who increase ignorance and whose anger does not cease, this is to destroy their own Dharma.
As the saying goes: "A family must first destroy itself before others can destroy it. Who then is to be blamed?

Now, in response to the Chan Master’s request, I have earnestly spoken these words for the sake of both the monastic and the lay communities. Whether they understand me or condemn me, I cannot avoid either.

Master Dàhuì’s Letter to the Practitioner Zhēnrú:
When will the dust and toil of this burning house ever come to an end? To obtain even a single day of peace and joy is the very model for ten million days.
Within that single day, if the mind does not run after things, does not engage in false imaginings, and does not cling to external objects, one is then identical with the three periods of time.
The Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas are in mutual accord; without attachment, they harmonize and naturally become one whole.
It was precisely for this reason that the World-Honored One spoke the Parable of the Burning House. As the Sūtra says: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small."
"The children are young and have no understanding; they are attached to their playthings and might fall down and be burned by the fire.

I shall speak to them of things to be feared," as is fully detailed in the sūtra. "This house has but one door and it is moreover narrow and small"—this refers to the inferiority of the faculty of faith.
Within this burning house, they lack wisdom and remain attached to the dust and toil of worldly existence."
They take worldly affairs as their pleasure because they do not believe there is a pure and wondrous bliss in leaving the burning house to sit in the open air.
If, while within it, one attains faith, recognizes the truth, and breaks through delusion— not clinging to the place of childish play, with a mind that does not wander in pursuit,
nor engage in false imaginings or conditions with external objects— then the very dust and toil of the burning house becomes liberation, and one exits the three realms.
...the place [of non-duality]. Why is this? Does not the Buddha say that regarding all objects, there is no dependence, no dwelling, and no conceptual differentiation?
One clearly perceives the vast establishment of the *dharmadhātu* and realizes that all worlds and all phenomena are equal and non-dual.
Therefore, by the power of the wisdom of their own practice, Bodhisattvas on the Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*) transcend all duality.
Riding upon this vehicle, although they have attained the treasury of the Buddha-realm, they manifest as dwelling within the realm of Māra;
although they have transcended the path of Māra, they manifest the practice of Māra’s arts; although they manifest conduct identical to that of non-Buddhists, they do not abandon the Buddha-dharma;
although they manifest compliance with all worldly ways, they constantly practice all supramundane dharmas. This is the true [practice] amidst the dust and toil of the burning house.
This is skillful means (*upāya*). Those who study Prajñāpāramitā yet abandon these skillful means to follow after worldly defilements (*kleśa*) will certainly be seized and controlled by Māra.
Furthermore, while following after such objects of perception, they insistently propound their own logic, claiming that afflictions are themselves bodhi and ignorance is itself great wisdom.

Step by step they walk within existence, yet mouth after mouth they discourse on emptiness. They do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma, and furthermore, they teach others...
There are those who deny cause and effect, claiming that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct bodhi, and that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder prajñā.
Such individuals allow demonic influences and evil poisons to enter their very hearts and bellies, yet remain entirely unaware of it.

Their desire to escape the toils of worldly existence is like pouring oil onto a fire to extinguish it—how lamentable! It is precisely these very toils of worldly existence that constitute the seed of the Tathāgata.
The teachings contain a clear exposition: for example, lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land; they grow only in low, moist, muddy swamps.

Likewise, those who emerge and submerge within the dust and toil of the burning house, undergoing immeasurable suffering, may suddenly develop weariness and detachment amidst that suffering and first give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi. This host of dust and toil constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata.
This refers precisely to this point. The way a layperson studies the Way is fundamentally different from that of one who has left the household life.
From childhood, the renunciant remains far removed from worldly toil; parents do not provide them with delicacies, and their six kin are certainly abandoned and separated.

Their body dwells in a pure monastery, and their eyes behold the serene countenances and sacred features of the Sages. Moment by moment they remain focused on the Way, and thought after thought proceeds without interruption. As for what they observe:

There are no writings that are not the Buddha’s writings; there are no actions performed that are not the Buddha’s work. One does not look upon objects of desire; one receives the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha.
Only that which is praised by the Buddha does one dare to rely upon and practice; that which is censured by the Buddha one does not dare to violate.
There are enlightened masters whom one may seek out and visit; there are virtuous friends and good companions with whom one may consult for resolution. Even if there are [habits]...
Those who have not yet eliminated the outflows (*āsrava*) may temporarily violate the Buddha’s discipline and have already been expelled by the community;

compared to them, the worldly person does not even come close—falling short by ten thousandfold. While the worldly person dwells within the burning house, throughout the four modes of deportment, they take greed, hatred, and delusion as their companions;
whatever they do, whatever they hear, and whatever they see is nothing but unwholesome karma. Nevertheless, if one can...
In this regard, those who have attained thorough penetration possess a power that surpasses that of us monastics by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Only after such thorough penetration can one say that afflictions are themselves bodhi and ignorance is itself great wisdom.
Within the originally vast, quiescent, and wondrous mind, which is pure and perfectly luminous, all is swept away so that not a single thing exists to act as an obstacle—just like the great void.

Emptiness is generally so; even the single word "Buddha" is but an external object. How much more so, then, could there be any room for worldly toil, afflictions, or the bonds of affection to act as opposites?

If one can strike through to the bottom while within the burning house, there is no need to seek to leave the household life by creating strange anomalies, feigning deformities, or ruining one's attire—thereby extinguishing human nature, severing ancestral sacrifices, and becoming a sinner within the system of names and teachings. The Buddha did not teach this.
It is the same for human beings. It is simply said that those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body, to them he manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma;
those who are to be saved by the body of a minister, to them he manifests the body of a minister and preaches the Dharma;
and so on, even manifesting the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās for those who are to be saved by such forms.
And he preaches the Dharma for them. Furthermore, it is said that worldly occupations and industries all accord with correct principle and do not contradict the true nature (*dharmatā*).

One need only rely on one’s own station and act according to what one has realized, transforming those of a similar kind so that they likewise enter this gate; this is precisely how one repays the profound kindness of the Buddha.
One must simply ensure that mindfulness does not cease from moment to moment; do not concern yourself with whether you succeed or fail—this is [the practice of] past merit.
One lacks affinity with Prajñā. If one has not yet attained thorough penetration in this life, one will not be dragged away by evil karma at the time of death;
nor will one be entangled by worldly toil during the twelve periods of daily life. When emerging in a future life, one will likewise enjoy immediate realization.
There is no other method for studying the Way than taking awakening as the standard. If in this life...

This is the ultimate realization. One must persevere until the end of the future, constantly maintaining this mind. Although one has not yet awakened in this present life, one has nonetheless planted the seeds of *prajñā* upon the ground of one's nature;
thus, from generation to generation, one shall not fall into the evil realms, and in birth after birth, one shall never lose the human form.
One will not be born into a family of false views, nor enter the ranks of Mara’s army; how much less could one fail when the flower of the mind suddenly bursts forth in illumination?
At such a time, the Buddhas of the three periods of time bear witness to one’s potential, and the great patriarchs have no place to lodge [their authority].
This is not a matter of forced contrivance; it is because the Dharma is thus. Those who follow the Way of True Suchness (Tathatā) and wish to study this path need only rely upon this to practice.
Indeed, after a long time, one will naturally encounter it. What has been explained above is merely a case of administering medicine according to the illness for a particular occasion.
If you take this as a substantial reality, you are again mistaken. An ancient said: "When you see the moon, cease looking at the finger; when returning home, do not ask the way.
Having written this much, my inspiration has not yet run dry, but the paper is exhausted. For now, I shall cut off the entanglements.
Xinkong said: "Mahāmati, this book is clearly a single fascicle of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
If lay practitioners do not rely upon it for cultivation, they will surely find themselves flustered and frantic on the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month."
Master Lianchi’s Dharma Discourse:
"The Avatamsaka Sutra is Not as Good as the Gen Hexagram.
A Song dynasty Confucian once said, "Reading an entire volume of the Avatamsaka Sutra is not as good as contemplating a single Gen hexagram. This statement is truly profound and insightful.

Those who know their own errors may be excused; however, the mediocre and inferior believe this without doubt. They open the gate of false views and block the path of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng).
One must be cautious in what one says. Even if one were to recite and study an entire volume of the *Book of Changes* (*Yi jing*), it would not be as good as looking at a single hexagram, the Gen.
Yet even this is not permissible; how much less so the Buddha-dharma? How much less so the Avataṃsaka-sūtra of the Buddha-dharma?
The Avataṃsaka possesses immeasurable gateways; other Mahāyāna sūtras are but a single gateway among the immeasurable gateways of the Avataṃsaka.
The Avataṃsaka is the Heavenly King; the various Mahāyāna sūtras are the feudal domains; the various Hīnayāna sūtras are the vassal states of those domains. As for the rest...
This can be understood.

Regarding the sages of the two teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism, each established its own transformation according to its particular domain; it is certainly unnecessary to bifurcate them into two distinct entities.

Nor is it necessary to force them into agreement. Why? Confucianism governs the world, while Buddhism transcends the world. To govern the world, it is sufficient to follow the principles of the *Great Learning*:
investigation of things, extension of knowledge, sincerity, rectification, cultivation, regulation of the family, governance of the state, and bringing peace to all under heaven.

If one goes beyond this to what is excessively lofty and profound, the fundamental relationships and social ethics will not be established. To establish the transcendence of the world, however, one must indeed exhaustively explore the heights and depths to achieve success.

Though one may attain liberation, it is natural that one cannot remain entirely indifferent toward family, state, and the world; this is the inevitable course of principle and circumstance, and there is no cause for wonder.

If you insist that Confucianism is identical to Buddhism, then since the Six Classics, the *Lunyu*, and the *Mengzi* are already brilliantly complete, why wait for the birth of Śākyamuni or the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West?
If you insist that Buddhism is identical to Confucianism, then why not [use] the *Lengyan*...

To govern the world according to the principles of the *Lotus Sūtra* necessarily requires the founders such as Fuxi, Shennong, Yao, and Shun to establish the institutions above, and the sages such as Confucius and Mencius to clarify the Way below.
Thus, whether one separates these two or unites them, the resulting flaw is the same.

Nevertheless, it must also be understood that for those of perfect spiritual capacity, it is equally acceptable to separate them or to unite them; in either case, there is no flaw. This is something that cannot be left unknown.
The *Buddhadhātu-sūtra* states that all sentient beings, down to the crawling insects, possess Buddha-nature. When Mencius refuted Gaozi, he asked:

"If that were so, would the nature of a dog be the same as the nature of an ox, and the nature of an ox be the same as the nature of a human? There are those who cling to the words of this scripture...
This is not the view of Mencius. I consider it otherwise. That "all possess Buddha-nature" is a statement concerning the ultimate principle of transcending the world;
that "humans and animals are different" is a discourse concerning the present state of worldly existence. These two do not obstruct one another.

Therefore, when reaching the ultimate root and source, even ants and midges are directly equal and non-dual with the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Yet, according to their present manifestation...
Thus, while humans comprehend ten thousand transformations, animals possess but a single kind of knowledge; how could they be viewed as equals? Not only do humans and animals differ:

a dog watches for the night and barks when there is an alarm, yet an ox will open a lock, bore a hole through a wall, or break through a gate while remaining as calm as if it had neither heard nor seen anything.
The natures of dogs and oxen are indeed not the same—how much more so, then, is this the case for humans?
Ten thousand types of timber are of one and the same wood, yet the paulownia, the catalpa, the thorn-apple, and the bramble each differ.

The myriad rivers are one and the same water, yet the Yangtze, the Huai, the ditches, and the canals are each distinct. This is to be the same while never not being different, and to be different while never not being the same.
If one clings to this without understanding it, then when the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment, he universally saw all sentient beings as...
Perfectly Awakened One. Why are there still sentient beings today?
Wang Jiefu, Jiefu, in his imitation of Hanshan’s poetry, said: "I once was an ox or a horse; seeing grass and beans, I rejoiced. Furthermore, he once...

When a woman joyfully sees a man, if I were truly "I," it would be fitting for me to always remain thus. Amidst these trivial and shifting transformations, do not mistake external things for yourself. These words of Ouyang Xiu (Jiefu) are indeed insightful; yet why does he not say: "I am not the body, nor am I the mind. The body is subject to birth and death, while the mind undergoes change and transformation. If I were truly 'I,' I should never be separated from this body. But since I can leave the body and go elsewhere, I know that I am not the body. If I were truly 'I,' I should always possess consciousness. Yet at times I am without thought, and at times I am without sensation. Since I can exist without thought or sensation, I know that I am not the mind. The mind is but a guest; the body is but a lodging. How could I take what is temporary and regard it as myself? This is what one should say. It is because he did not speak thus that people still harbor doubts. Furthermore, if one asks: "If you are not the body, then who is it that experiences hunger and thirst? If you are not the mind, then who is it that perceives forms and sounds? The answer is: "Hunger and thirst are the functions of the physical organs; perception is the function of the sensory faculties. Both are merely instruments for the self to employ. If one were to claim that these are the self, then when the eyes are blind or the ears are deaf, the self would likewise be blind or deaf. When the hands are broken or the feet are lame, the self would likewise be broken or lame. Since this is clearly not so, how can one claim that the organs or faculties are the self? Therefore, one must know that the self is distinct from both body and mind. If one understands this, one will no longer mistake external objects for oneself. Thus, although Jiefu’s words are excellent, they are nonetheless incomplete. If one relies solely on his words, one will inevitably fall into error. This is why I have elaborated upon them here. I hope those who read this will understand. If you do not understand, then you have not yet grasped the meaning of these words. If you do understand, then you have attained the Way. I have heard flattering words; upon entering my ears, I was filled with joy. Yet I have also heard candid advice; my joy vanished and anger arose.
If I were truly a self, I ought to remain forever as I am. Amidst these trivial fluctuations, do not mistake external things for yourself.
Yet, you instead delight in flattery and loathe upright counsel; do you still regard external things as yourself?
Thus we know that for one of great intelligence, it is not difficult to speak of Chan, but it is difficult to attain Chan.
Regarding the "Verses on the Explanation of Chan" composed by Lord Wen Gong: this is a mirror for those who would truly study Buddhism without clarifying its principles.

However, his identification of conduct and speech worthy of emulation as the "indestructible body" and the non-deficiency of benevolence and righteousness as the "treasury of radiance" was merely a temporary expedient.

These words concerning illness are no superficial discourse. Indeed, being careful in speech and conduct and cultivating benevolence and righteousness are truly worthy of high esteem within the mundane world.
Yet, how could these be the indestructible diamond body? How easy it is to speak of the treasury of great spiritual radiance!
Furthermore, you take the "broad and untroubled" state of the gentleman as heaven, and the "constant anxiety" of the petty man as hell.

The principle is indeed sound; yet there is still the fallacy of clinging to the principle while losing sight of the facts. How could one say that stupidity is identical to oxen and sheep, or that ferocity is identical to tigers and leopards?
Beyond this, would there be no real oxen and sheep with their coats and horns, nor real tigers and leopards with their sharp fangs and saw-like claws?
I fear that when people see the refined and wondrous phrasing of Master Wen Gong, they will surely greatly [misunderstand].

They find joy and develop deep faith. However, the corruption of this trend leads to the repudiation of cause and effect, such that people become content with worldly virtues alone and no longer recognize the existence of anything superior.
Thus, this verse, originally intended to awaken people, instead ends up misleading them; it must not fail to be heard.
Fan Jingren said of himself, "For twenty years, I have never once given rise to a single thought. That Fan Jingren was a man of worth is indeed true;
yet, to not give rise to a single thought for a duration of twenty years may not be something easily achieved. Even Yanzi [Yan Hui]—still...
If one does not deviate for only three months, then beyond those three months, it is possible that thoughts may still arise.

Even Zhaozhou required forty years before he could achieve "one piece"; thus, while that "one piece" was not yet achieved, it is possible that thoughts arose. Would this not also apply to someone like Jingren?
Although coarse thoughts may be absent, do not subtle reflections secretly proliferate and arise without one's own awareness? It is not that I hold Jingren in low esteem;
rather, fearing that he might consider a small attainment sufficient, I offer this as a pre-emptive warning to himself.
Master Huì'ān criticized Buddhism for wearing silk and eating meat; Kōnggǔ has exerted great effort in refuting his views.

Nevertheless, one must not fail to recognize that Master Huì'ān also had points that assisted in the propagation of the Buddha's teachings. In his commentary on the *Mencius*, he states: "At fifty, one cannot be warm without silk."
Those under fifty years of age must not wear [silk]. Those over seventy do not feel satisfied without meat; those under seventy must not eat it.
The Buddha’s regulation is that animal fur and the silk from silkworm mouths harm living beings and violate compassion; therefore, one must wait until fifty to wear silk.
Then those who wear silk would be rare. To eat meat is to sever the seed of great compassion;
this is the Buddha’s prohibition. Only at seventy years of age may one eat meat; thus, those who eat meat would be rare.

Yet now, even infants already wear heavy furs and pure cotton to protect their bodies, and they are fed with roasted fat and sliced fresh meat to satisfy their mouths—long before they reach adulthood, let alone old age. If one were to...
If the teachings of Huì'ān were to prevail, would they not provide some assistance to the Buddha-dharma? Those who blame Huì'ān fail to perceive this;
therefore, I shall elucidate it for them. This is to protect the Dharma.
People know that the external protection of the Buddha-dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers, yet they do not realize that it is the Sangha who ought to provide that protection;
therefore, one must not fail to be cautious. There are three ways to protect the Dharma: first, to promote and honor Buddhist monasteries (*brahmacarya-sthāna*);

second, to circulate the Great Teaching; and third, to encourage and support the monastic community. Why speak of caution? Regarding the protection of monasteries: if a monastery truly belongs to [the Sangha], [then...]

Powerful and influential families have seized temple properties; it is only right that these be confiscated and restored. However, if one examines historical records and documents, the distinctions may not be clear.

Over the long course of time, names and titles have been interchanged and confused. Is it appropriate to seize such property by force? Land given through pious donation is called "auspicious ground" (*kṣetra*);
to give it away when one lacks the power to do so is termed a "thicket of grievous karma. If the monks merely offer exhortations...
The powerful layman Huà acted as the great patron (*mahādānapati*) for the restoration of the old monastery.

Yet he did not realize that the Buddha regards all sentient beings with equal compassion, just as he does Rāhula. The temple built by this man of calamity was vast, exceeding a thousand *qǐng* in area, and its height soared to the nine heavens.
With sandalwood for its timber and pearls and jade for its adornments, it was something the Buddha would pity rather than rejoice over; it was excessive.
To have no merit is not to be careful; this is the first point. As for those who protect the Teaching:
if their writings truly accord with the Buddha’s mind from afar and capture the essential meaning of the scriptures from near at hand, it is only right that they be praised and propagated.

But would it be appropriate to offer excessive praise to the rambling talk of outsiders, which stems from mere personal whims and biased views? If the monk [Wen]wei simply requests famous gentlemen to compose prefaces and postscripts, [that is another matter].
Second, one must not harbor doubts or cause confusion that misleads future students; to do so is a fault without merit, and one must therefore be cautious. Regarding the protection of the Sangha:
it is the principle that those who have truly practiced and truly awakened, possessing great wisdom and insight, should be honored and venerated;

and those whose practice is genuine and whose conduct is steadfast and sincere should be trusted and approached. As for those who are merely pretentious Chan practitioners, they are base and inferior.

As for commoners, may they also honor and trust them? If the Sangha only seeks to attach itself to noble families, hoping for their protection while wrapping sores in cotton, silk, and brocade, it will only increase their venom;
there will be fault rather than merit. One must be cautious of this, for it is the third [point].
In such a case, while the king and his ministers protect the Dharma, the Sangha destroys the Dharma. How tragic!
In response to Layman Sun Wugao’s extensive inquiry, [I reply:

Lately, your observance of the precepts has been quite rigorous. Although your minor virtues have not yet reached full brilliance, you have already committed no transgressions regarding major virtues.
Furthermore, are there not one or two words that may serve as an inscription for one's entire life?

Formerly, when Zigong asked about a single word for a lifetime, the Master answered with "reciprocity" (*shu*). Today, this single word of admonition is to be inscribed for a lifetime, leaving nothing unexhausted.
Why is this so? It is because the gathering of the mind is itself precept (*śīla*). Therefore, if one turns toward the Dharma of the Mind-ground...
If you can realize this within the gateway [of practice], then everything will be complete; what further need is there to discuss whether or not one maintains the precepts?

If it is otherwise, you must follow the teachings one by one and put them into practice. As the Sūtra says: "To restrain the mind is the precept; from the precept arises concentration; from concentration issues forth wisdom.
Concentration and wisdom constitute the full fruit of Buddhahood. When concentration is itself wisdom, one is tranquil yet constantly illumined.

Thus, when wisdom is conjoined with concentration, there is illumination while remaining eternally quiescent; this state of eternal quiescence and eternal illumination is called the Light of Eternal Quiescence (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*).

Furthermore, it takes its foundation from the precepts (*śīla*). How great indeed is the significance of the precepts! There are many kinds of precepts: the five precepts of the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the ten precepts of the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), the two hundred and fifty precepts of the fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*), the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Bodhisattva, and so forth, even unto the three...

Although there are a thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices, if one summarizes them by their great outline, the five precepts constitute the foundation. Confucianism also occasionally speaks of "precepts" (*jie*);
though these are not yet fully comprehensive, they are implicitly in accord with the Buddhist regulations. The Master said: "The gentleman has three things to which he must be cautious."

To refrain from lust is subsumed under the precept against sexual misconduct; to refrain from fighting is subsumed under the precept against killing; to refrain from coveting gain is subsumed under the precept against stealing.
These three—lust, killing, and stealing—are the most essential among the precepts; therefore, by citing these essentials, the remainder are encompassed.

To speak of being loyal and trustworthy to the point of not falling into disorder serves to include the prohibitions against alcohol and falsehood, which is likewise a means of pre-emptively cultivating these precepts so as not to...

As for their laxity: the Confucian precepts are sparse, while the Buddhist precepts are meticulous. The Buddha’s prohibition against killing extends even to the smallest crawling insects, whereas the Confucians merely state that one should not "unjustly" kill oxen, sheep, dogs, pigs, and the like;
they do not say "do not kill. They merely state that one should not fish with nets or use spears overnight;
they do not say "do not fish" or "do not use spears. To take it to its extreme, [the Confucian] would kill as soon as a moment of anger or envy arises.
The precepts are impure. When the eye grasps forms and the ear grasps sounds, the precept against stealing is impure;

when one hears the sound of hairpins and bracelets through a wall, the precept against sexual misconduct is impure. Reaching this point, both body and mind are severed, and both phenomena and principle are exhausted.

Today, while residing within the domestic quarters, one’s duties involve the administration of public affairs; as one is about to be entrusted with the altars of state and the people, how could one possibly maintain the precepts?

If one evaluates each case according to the standards for those who have shaved their heads and donned the dyed robes, then being unable to maintain every minute precept does not constitute a violation of the precepts.
What is valued is exerting effort in the primary essence of mental cultivation; once one attains a sudden, transcendent awakening, [all is resolved].
Then, even coughing, spitting, or swinging one's arms will all be nothing other than the pure Vinaya.

However, one must not claim to have attained what has not been attained and thereby give rise to "mad enlightenment," asserting that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi, or that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder Prajñā;
such views lead only to falling into the realm of Māra. If you can truly reflect back upon yourself from time to time and maintain constant mindfulness at every moment, [you will remain secure].

If you apply yourself to the practice of the *huatou* (critical phrase) of "Mindfulness of the Buddha" directed toward the Original Inquiry, not only will there be an awakening in the future, but you will immediately gain efficacy in the present.
You will have a sovereign mastery in daily life and will not be turned by external objects.
Even if you dwell in a field of sound, form, fame, and profit, or are surrounded day and night by wife and kin, you will be able to move with the world without being hindered.
Blending with the mundane and harmonizing with the light, one naturally emerges from the mud unstained. This is called the Great Gate of Liberation within the dust of the world.
By means of this, one benefits oneself; by means of this, one benefits others. Where could one go that would not be good? (The Dharma Words of Master Lianchi concludes.

Vimalakīrti (a Dharma Prince under the assembly of Śākyamuni).
In the city of Vaiśālī in Central India, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti.
Having already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, he had deeply planted the roots of goodness and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Possessing unimpeded eloquence and sporting with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he dwelt in Vaiśālī through skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of liberating sentient beings. By means of such skillful means, he manifested himself as being ill, and extensively [for their benefit...]
He preached the Dharma. The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and great disciples, entered Vaiśālī.
By means of his supernatural powers, Vimalakīrti had made the interior of his room empty; he removed all furnishings and attendants, leaving only a single couch upon which he lay as if ill.
When Mañjuśrī had entered his house, Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You have come without the characteristic of coming;
you have seen without the characteristic of seeing. Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, householder. If one has already come, there is no further coming;
if one has already gone, there is no further going. Why is this? That which comes comes from nowhere; that which goes—"

That which has gone has nowhere to go; that which was visible can no longer be seen. Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying, "O worthy ones, how does a bodhisattva enter the gate of non-duality?
After each of the thirty-two bodhisattvas had spoken, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "Worthy one, you should speak: what is this entry of a bodhisattva into [the gate of non-duality]?"
Regarding the Dharma-door of Non-duality, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Excellent! To be without even words or letters—this is the true Dharma-door of non-duality.

When he had finished speaking this Dharma, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, "We should go together to see the Buddha. Thereupon, by means of his supernatural power, he took all the great assembly along with him.
He placed the lion throne upon his right palm and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, he set it down on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood to one side with palms joined in single-minded devotion.
Śāriputra asked, "From where did you pass away to be born here? Vimalakīrti replied, "In the Dharma you have realized, is there any passing away or being born? Śāriputra said, "No."

There is no passing away or arising. If all phenomena possess neither the characteristic of passing away nor the characteristic of arising, why do you ask, "From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
Śāriputra, "passing away" is a deceptive phenomenon, a characteristic of decay and destruction. "Arising" is a deceptive phenomenon, a characteristic of continuity.
Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness; although they arise, they do not increase any evils. At that time...
The Buddha told Śāriputra, “There is a land named Abhirati; its Buddha is named Akṣobhya.
This Vimalakīrti has passed away from that land and come to be born here. Śāriputra said, “It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!
How can this man abandon a pure land and come to delight in this place of much anger and harm? Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, “In...”
"What do you think? When the sunlight appears, does it join with the darkness? He replied, "No. When the sunlight appears, there is no longer any darkness.
Vimalakīrti said, "For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa? He replied, "It is because he wishes to illuminate it and thereby dispel the darkness.
Vimalakīrti said, "In this same way, although a bodhisattva is born in an impure buddha-field, for..."
He transforms sentient beings, never associating with ignorance and darkness; he merely extinguishes the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with longing and yearned to behold the world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and his community of śrāvakas.
The Buddha said to Vimalakīrti, "Good son, for the sake of this assembly, manifest the Land of Bliss, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
the entire assembly desires to see them. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and manifested his supernormal powers.
With his right hand, he severed and took up the world-system of Sukhāvatī, placing it here in this very place. At that time—
Having completed the matters for the benefit of beings in this land of the World of Wondrous Joy, he returned once more to his original place.
[The author] comments: "In my view, Vimalakīrti was merely an elderly layman of Vaiśālī; yet, within the assembly of Śākyamuni..."
As for Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra and the others even said, "I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness.
They said, "That superior man is difficult to respond to; how is it that his gate and courtyard have become so exceedingly lofty and steep?
Huangbo said: "Vimalakīrti means 'Pure Name. 'Pure' refers to nature (xing); 'Name' refers to characteristics (xiang). Nature and characteristics are not different."
Therefore, he is titled "Vimalakīrti" (Pure Name). That which is represented by all the great Bodhisattvas exists within every person; it is not separate from the one mind.
To awaken to it is precisely it—seemingly without even the need to snap one's fingers, it is right here and now, Vimalakīrti himself.

Thus, as recorded in the *Lamp of Transmission*, the descendants of Bodhidharma fill the world, yet among them, those who were true practitioners and attained genuine realization as laymen numbered only several dozen.
There is nothing heard from without. How, then, can this be explained? Baizhang Yuan said:
"One, two, hundreds, thousands, tens of millions—counting on one's fingers and searching through texts, the numbers cannot be reckoned. Leave them for a moment before the dark window;
tomorrow I shall calculate them for you again. *Du!* Vimalakīrti has arrived!"

The Master said, "How narrow are these eyes? How comfortable is this body? Yunxia did not look back. The scholar said, "Speak one more turn, and this talk will be complete. Yunxia still did not look back.
The scholar said, "Among all of this, there is this one phrase that no one can speak. One day, the scholar visited Yunxia;
he stood before Yunxia with his hands folded in greeting, and after a short while, he departed. Yunxia did not look back. The scholar then returned.
"Come and sit. Xuexia, however, withdrew to stand before the Master with his hands joined. After a short while, he entered the abbot’s quarters.
The Master said, "You enter and I exit; there is still business to be attended to. Xuexia replied, "This old fellow, coming out and going in—when will it ever come to an end? The Master said:
[The Master] said, "There is not even a trace of compassion. Xiang said, "This fellow has led you to such a state. [The Master] asked, "By what means did he lead you?
Xiang picked up his scholar's head-dress (*fuhou*) and said, "He looks exactly like an old master monk.
The scholar took the head-dress and placed it on Xiang’s head, saying, "He looks exactly like a young layman. Xiang responded with three "Yes"es. The scholar said, "There is still that former..."
At that time, Xiqi was there. Xia threw down his *fuhou* (head-wrap) and said, "It looks very much like a black silk cap (*wusha jin*).
The Master also responded with three nods. Xia said, "How could one ever forget the breath of the past? The Master snapped his fingers three times and said, "Moving heaven, moving earth.
On another day, while the Master and Xia were walking together, they saw a pool of water. Pointing at it, Xia said, "Is it like this?"
The Master could not discern it. Yunxia said, "Truly, you cannot discern it. The Master scooped up water with his hand and splashed it over Yunxia three times.
Yunxia said, "Do not do that! Do not do that! The Master said, "It must be so! It must be so!
Yunxia also scooped up water and splashed it at the Master, saying, "At this very moment, what can be made of it? The Master said, "There is nothing outside. Yunxia said, "Attained."

"Those who hit upon the opportune moment are few. The Master asked, "Who is it that misses the opportune moment? One day, when Yunxia saw the Master approaching, she immediately made a gesture of running away.
The Master said, "That was still a gesture of casting off the body; what about a gesture of wincing in pain? Yunxia then sat down.
The Master drew the character for "seven" on the ground with his staff; Yunxia drew the character for "one" beneath it. The Master said, "Because of seven, one is seen."
First, upon seeing one [case], he forgot seven. Xiang then rose and departed. The Master said, "Sit for a short while longer;
there is still a second phrase remaining. Xiang asked, "Can one apply words here? The Master then wept and went out. One day, he arrived at Yangshan.

A questioner asked, "For a long time I have admired Yangshan; why is it that upon your arrival you instead conceal [the truth]? Yangshan held up his whisk. The questioner said, "Exactly so. Yangshan said, "Yes. 'Is' is the same as 'conceal.
The questioner struck a pillar and said, "Even though there is no one here, I still require the pillar to bear witness.
Yangshan threw down his whisk and said, "If you go to other places, feel free to cite this example. One day, while selling a colander, he descended [from the mountain].
Qiao Chi-pu was lying down by the side of his body. Zhao said, "What are you doing?
Zhao replied, "I saw my father fall to the ground, so I came specifically to help him up. Qiao said, "Fortunately, no one saw it.
While sitting, Qiao asked Zhao, "The ancients said, 'Clearly at the tip of every blade of grass, clearly is the meaning of the Patriarch. What does this mean? Zhao replied, "Old man, old man!"
"Great! Speak a word. The Layman asked, "How would you do it? Zhao said, "Clearly at the tips of the hundred grasses;
clearly the meaning of the Patriarch. The Layman then laughed. One day, while sitting alone in his hermitage, he suddenly exclaimed, "Difficult!
Difficult! Difficult! Ten piculs of sesame oil spread over a tree! Lady Pang, catching the sound, replied, "Easy! Easy! Easy! Like stepping down onto the foot of one's bed."
Zhao said, "It is neither difficult nor easy; it is the meaning of the Patriarchs atop a hundred peaks.

At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, when the Master was staying at a mountain cave in Xiangyang, the provincial governor Yu Di obtained the Layman’s writings and felt a deep sense of admiration for his extraordinary character.
He then sought an opportunity to pay him a visit, treating him as a long-acquainted friend, and they came and went without interval. As the Master was about to enter nirvana, he addressed Zhao:
He said, "Illusions have no reality; they follow whatever you perceive. You may go out and observe whether the sun has risen early or late, and report back at noon.
Zhao went out the door and quickly reported, "The sun has already risen, yet it is being eclipsed. You may try to observe it for a moment. The scholar asked, "Is it so? He replied, "It is.
The scholar left his seat and leaned over the window. Zhao immediately ascended to his father’s seat, joined his palms, and sat there until he passed away. The scholar [was struck with wonder].
Upon returning, he saw [the Master] smiling and said, "My daughter is swift and nimble. He then gathered firewood to prepare for his final affairs. Thus, seven more days were extended.
When Wang Rti went to inquire after his health, the Master rested his hand upon Wang's knee and gazed at him for a long while, saying, "I only wish that you would empty all that exists;
be careful not to fill what does not exist. Dwell well in this world; everything is like a shadow or an echo. He then spoke a verse:
He said, "Empty flowers fall as shadows; a mirage turns into waves. Having finished speaking, a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He sat upright as if in deep contemplation.
Pangti hurriedly called out to him, but he had already passed away. Pangti then performed the cremation according to the Dharma and immediately dispatched a messenger to inform his wife and children.
Pangmo said, "This foolish woman and this witless old man have departed without giving notice—is this truly bearable?"
He went to inform his son, who saw him clearing a slash-and-burn field and said, "Master Pang and Lingzhao have departed.
The son dropped his hoe and replied, "Aha! After a long while, he too stood up and passed away. His mother said, "How extreme is the folly and delusion of this ignorant son!

She then had him cremated as well. The people all marveled at this. Not long after, Master Pang’s wife traveled throughout the villages and neighborhoods to bid farewell before returning to seclusion. Thereafter, she remained hidden...
Their traces have vanished; no one knows where they have gone.
Zhan said: "The colt with four hooves trampled the world to death; Old Pang swallowed the Western River in a single gulp.
These two old fellows have squandered without remainder the household goods transmitted since the Buddhas and Patriarchs, leaving nothing for their descendants of later generations."
His grandson was so impoverished that he was as bare as if washed clean; how could it have been merely the abandonment of family treasures and sinking into the Xiang and Han rivers?
Furthermore, the eulogy says: Dongshan Shoujia said, "Greed, anger, and ignorance—how utterly ignorant they are! Truly, today we have caught them."
When walking, he strikes; when sitting, he beats. Entrust this to the Mind-King and examine it carefully. For immeasurable eons, one has not attained liberation. I ask you three: do you know or not?
*Tut!* Dongshan’s slip was no small matter. Shending Yinyi said: "Greed, anger, and ignorance are truly without knowledge.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, let them be as they may. When walking, he stays; when sitting, he follows. Entrust this to the Mind."
The King has nothing further to do; for immeasurable kalpas he has been fundamentally liberated. Why need one ask again whether he knows or not? *Du!* Even Shending has not failed to let slip a word.
Old Pang said: "Seek not the Buddha, seek not man; simply within your own mind, do not harbor greed or anger.
When the maladies of greed, anger, and delusion are suddenly exhausted, you are the very kin of the Tathāgata. *Du!* — Master Pang.
This is quite a slip of the tongue. Xinkong says: "The person is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the person. Originally, where could there be greed or anger?
The fierce lion roars repeatedly; who cares whether the Tathāgata is near or far? *Du!* Xinkong, too, has quite a slip of the tongue.
The Buddhas of the three periods appearing in the world and the patriarchs of successive generations transmitting the mind have done nothing other than for this one great causal matter.
Because this great matter is not yet clarified, beings continue to emerge and submerge in the cycle of birth and death through dust-like kalpas without end;
this is truly because the poisonous vapor has penetrated deeply and the life-root remains unsevered. Pang Laizi was indeed Śākyamuni...
The Buddha’s response-body as the one destined for succession has, throughout his entire collection of recorded teachings, been solely and earnestly exhorting people to uproot the three poisons.
As he said: "If you are unwilling to abandon greed and anger, your labor in reading and explaining the sutras is in vain. And again: "When the diseases of greed, anger, and delusion are exhausted..."
"He is indeed the Son of the World-Honored One. It is further said: "Seize the arrows of the three poisons and snap them all at once into emptiness.
Such exhortations are too numerous to mention. Why is this? When the three poisons are exhausted, the life-faculty is severed.
Once the life-faculty is severed, one wanders together with the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations within the ocean of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Master Yuanwu Keqin’s “General Verses on the Three Poisons” states: “Delusive thoughts are entirely due to these three fellows, Dragging one through the six realms and four modes of birth.
When suddenly tamed through effortlessness, One directly merges with the nature-sea of Vairocana.”
The layman further said:
"The most supreme matter in the world Is none other than the power of cultivating the Way. If one awakens to the principle of non-arising, the three realms naturally vanish;
When the aggregates are empty, wondrous virtue manifests— Non-thought is the state of cool clarity."
This is precisely the Land of Amitābha; where else could one seek the Western Paradise?
Evil thoughts fill the three realms, yet the mouth recites the name of Amitābha. Mind and mouth act in opposition; the bandits multiply ever more.
A single speck of dust gives rise to ten thousand objects; in an instant, they pervade the Sahā world.
Seeking the Buddha-way through forms and sounds, yet bringing all resulting fruits to the end as demons;
knowing that consciousness does not receive sensory dust, the mind likewise does not become deranged.
With wondrous wisdom acting as the master of the mind, one is named the King who Destroys Existence. In a mere moment, one realizes the six perfections and employs the five kinds of incense.
This is the true Sukhāvatī; It is also the true Western Quarter. Śākyamuni and Amitāyus dwell together in this site of enlightenment.
With a sense of shame and a virtuous faculty of intention, there is neither self nor other, and no personal body or defilement.

No other dust can be added; one always dwells in the ground of purity. Knowing that existence cannot surpass the former evil associates, one sees everywhere Amitābha throughout the ten directions as entirely equal.
This is the Temple of True Suchness, within which dwells the One of Immeasurable Life.
Originally there are no names; ordinary people do not enter into the principle.
Their minds are preoccupied with worldly affairs—begging for money to buy tiles and timber to roof over empty space for others.
Thus they are driven by the six thieves and turn their backs on true suchness-wisdom; throughout the day they undergo hardship, using deluded thoughts to pursue fame and profit.
For a practitioner who trains in this way, though kalpas may pass, they will ultimately not fail;
the four natures shall share one dwelling, and the three bodies shall share one chamber;
all evil associates shall see Amitābha Buddha.
Though one may preach of matters that fill the world, Upon entering the principle, there is truly nothing much to say. Constantly bound by conditioned phenomena, on what day shall we see Amitābha?
When the single thought-moment is pure, Lotus flowers bloom everywhere; Each flower is a pure land.
Yit'u Yirulai Xin Kong said:
"Among the scholar-officials who are brilliant and exceptionally gifted, some delight in discussing Chan while disparaging the Pure Land.
They fail to realize that Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land, and the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan. — Master Pang.
His lightning-fast wit strikes awe and trepidation in all quarters; yet when he utters it in verse, he repeatedly and earnestly reveals the essential meaning of the self-nature Amitābha.
Alas! This is truly something worth contemplating.
Han Yu, whose courtesy name was Tui-zhi, served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.

When Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty dispatched an envoy to welcome Buddhist relics into the imperial palace, the princes, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to prostrate themselves in worship, thronging the roads. Han Yu submitted a memorial offering a vehement remonstrance.
The Emperor was greatly incensed and intended to sentence him to death. Pei Du and Cui Qun petitioned for a slight reprieve, and he was instead demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou.
Upon arriving in Chao, he submitted a memorial urging the Emperor to perform the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tai; however, no response arrived for a long time.

Feeling depressed and unhappy, he heard that the Chan Master Dadian possessed great virtue and a high reputation, so he sent three letters inviting him to come, until the Master finally arrived and remained there.

For several days, or sometimes after entering meditative absorption for several days before arising, he became increasingly respectful. Later, Yu again went to visit Master Dian at his hut to inquire about the Way.
One day he asked, "How many years of age are you, Master? Dian held up his prayer beads and said, "Do you understand? Yu replied, "I do not understand.
Dian said, "One hundred and eight [beads] for day and night. Yu did not comprehend this. He returned the following day.
Upon arriving at the gate, he saw the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera). He recounted the previous conversation and asked, "What was the meaning of that? The Head Seat tapped his teeth three times.

When he saw Mazu Daoyi, he posed the same question. Mazu also tapped his teeth three times. Han Yu said, "So it turns out that the Buddha-dharma is not of two kinds. Mazu asked, "What is the reasoning behind this?
Han Yu replied, "Just now, when I questioned the Head Seat, it was exactly the same. Mazu said, "That is so."
He then summoned the Head Seat and asked, "Is it you who answered thus? The Head Seat replied, "It was Dadian. Thereupon, he beat him and expelled him from the monastery.
On another day, Han Yu said to Dadian, "I am burdened with the many affairs of the prefecture; I beg the Master for a single word on the essential points of the Buddha-dharma.
After a long silence, Dadian said nothing, and Han Yu was left at a loss. At that time, Sanping was serving as the attendant; he struck the meditation seat three times.
Huangbo said, "What? Baizhang replied, "First move with concentration; afterwards extract with wisdom. Huangbo remarked, "The Master’s teaching style is lofty and steep;
it was from the attendant that I gained an entrance. He subsequently served as the Prefect of Yuanzhou, leaving behind two sets of robes before departing.
In a letter to Minister Meng Jian, he wrote: "Huangbo is quite intelligent and understands the principles of the Way."
Truly able to transcend the physical body and prevail through principle, he was not disturbed or confused by external affairs.
Although I did not fully understand his words, there was certainly no obstruction within my own breast; I considered this difficult to attain, and so I began to associate with him.
Xinkong said, "Withdraw, with-draw! Although you do not fully understand, after all, who understands?
Who does not understand? Cui Qun (a Dharma heir of Chan Master Faqin of Mount Jing). Cui Qun was a native of Wucheng.
Before reaching the age of twenty, he passed the jinshi examination and held successive posts, eventually serving as Hanlin Academician. He attended upon Chan Master Faqin of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Qin was asked: "I, your disciple, wish to leave the household life; may I do so? Qin replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Upon these words, Qun attained realization. During the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty, he was appointed as the Inspector of Huguang.
As soon as he took office, he went to visit Chan Master Ruhui and asked, "By what means did you attain [enlightenment]?"
Hui said, "It is attained through seeing one's nature. At that time, Hui was suffering from eye disease. Yuanqun asked, "Since you say it is 'seeing one's nature,' what can be done about the eyes?

Hui replied, "Seeing one's nature is not the eyes; how could an ailment of the eyes cause any harm? Yuanqun bowed his head in gratitude. During the reign of Emperor Muzong, Hui was promoted to Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Lishubu Shangshu) and enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhao.
The commentary says: Let us set aside the matter of Duke Cui Zhao for a moment. What is the matter of a great man leaving the household life?
Rest! Rest! Great peace was originally brought about by the general; yet he is not permitted to witness that great peace.
Ganqi (the Lay Practitioner Ganqi of Chizhou, Dharma heir of Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan).
One day, he entered Nanquan’s hall to provide a vegetarian feast. Huangbo Xiyun was serving as the head seat (*shouzuo*). Ganqi requested that funds be distributed for the offering.
Huangbo said, “The two kinds of giving—of wealth and of the Dharma—are equal and without distinction. Ganqi asked, “If you speak thus, how can one be worthy of such a gift?”
[Daowu] said, "I have received it. The donor then took the offering outside. After a short while, he re-entered and said, "Please accept this gift of wealth.

Daoyun said, "The two gifts of wealth and Dharma are equal and without distinction. The donor then proceeded to give the offering. On another day, he entered the temple to provide gruel and invited Nanquan to recite the scriptures.
Nanquan then struck the gavel and said, "I request the assembly to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the sake of the cat and the white ox."
If [Master] Zhi was at the *pāramitā* hall, he would simply wave his sleeves and depart. Later, after the morning gruel, Master Quan asked the kitchen steward, "Where is Zhi?
The steward replied, "He left right then and there. Quan then smashed the cooking pot. Zhi used to receive guests who came and went.
Once, a monk asked him, "It is no easy matter for an attendant to receive guests. Zhi said, "It is like feeding a donkey or feeding a horse. The monk then withdrew. There was another [incident].
A monk living in a hermitage was soliciting alms for household goods. Zhi said, "I have a question; if you can answer it, I shall give you something.
He then wrote the character for "mind" (心) and asked, "What kind of character is this? The monk replied, "It is the character for 'mind'. Zhi then asked his wife, "What kind of character is this?

His wife replied, "It is the character for 'mind'. Zhi said, "In that case, my mountain wife ought to live in the hermitage as well. The monk was speechless, and Zhi gave him nothing. He then questioned another monk.
"Where have you come from? he asked. "I have come from Mount Gui," [the monk] replied. Zhizhe said, "A while back, a monk asked Mount Gui, 'What is the meaning of the West?
Mount Gui raised his whisk. How do you understand Mount Gui's meaning? "It is to clarify the mind by means of phenomena and to manifest the principle through objects," the monk replied.
Zhizhe said, "In that case, it would be best for you to return to Mount Gui. At that time, Yantou was staying at Zhizhe’s home.

Putting on his clothes, he intended to go out to offer his apologies to his wife. His wife then asked, "What did my father-in-law do? Zhi replied, "It must not be told.
His wife said, "What could it be? Everyone ought to know. Zhi recounted the previous incident. His wife said, "From now on, thirty years hence, you must..."

Contemplation (*guan*), called awakening (*jue*), called concentration (*ding*), called wisdom (*hui*), called clarity (*ming*), called penetration (*tong*), called salvation (*ji*), and called relinquishment (*she*).

He expanded these causes into eight verses on gradual cultivation. The verses say: (1) Contemplation: With the eye of the mind, contemplate the external forms outside the mind. From what do they arise? To what do they perish?

If truth and falsehood are distinguished, awakening arises from within them; without departing from the existence of the false, one attains true emptiness.

(3. Samādhi) If truth is not extinguished, the false does not arise; the source of the six sense organs becomes as still as water—this is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), by which one is liberated from birth and death.
(4. Prajñā) To focus through concentration, yet concentration still involves attachment; to be rescued by wisdom, for wisdom is without obstruction.

Clarity is not ignorance; when clarity reaches its ultimate, it becomes penetration. Penetration is unimpeded. What is this unimpededness?

It is the mastery of transformation. (7. Ji) The power of penetration is not permanent; it changes in response to thought. These manifested forms do not truly exist; they appear according to what is sought.

He spoke in verse: "Do not mistake the foremost pivot before the wind; Where in the vast void can thought be lodged?
If this mountain monk wishes to convey the message, It is when the moon rises over ten thousand miles of cloudless sky. Pu said: "This too is merely playing with the spirit."
