Fan Zhongyan (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huijue of Langya).
Fan Zhongyan, courtesy name Xiwen, was a native of Wu Commandery. During the reign of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty, he served successively as a Grand Councilor and Acting Prime Minister.
While serving as the regional governor of Wu, Chan Master Huijue of Langya came to visit him. After staying for several days, Zhongyan attained realization beneath the master’s words.

Upon his departure, he presented Jue with a verse of parting, which said: "Throughout consecutive days we conversed together, unraveling the knots of doubt; Who would have thought that in this ephemeral life there would be half a day of leisure?
I truly wish to remain in leisure with you, Master, until old age, Fully gathering our cognitive nature to enter the Mysterious Barrier.

While staying overnight at the post station of Baode while serving as the Pacification Commissioner of Hedong, he obtained an ancient scripture in one fascicle titled *The Verses on the Causes and Effects of the Sixteen Arhats*. It was not included in the Tripiṭaka.
Not yet recorded. Yan composed a preface for it, saying: "These verses are by one Venerable; all seven stanzas are words on awakening to the source and becoming a Buddha.
As I read them, each verse brings a new realization, and only then did I come to know that within the human world there exists boundless sacred Dharma.
Since these texts were omitted from the Great Canon, I have therefore entrusted them to the Śramaṇa Hui-zhe, so that they may circulate in the world. —Yin [Ji], Attendant Councillor.
Shu had once studied under Fayan and attained enlightenment; he and Yan were inseparable friends. On the day of his death, Shu first wrote a letter of parting for Yan.
When Yan arrived in haste, he wept aloud in grief. Shu opened his eyes and said, "I have already bid you farewell; why have you come back?"
"Furthermore, birth and death are the constant law of nature; how could Xiwen not understand this? Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
When Yan was young, while reading among the Changbai Mountains, he discovered a cache of gold in a temple one day. He covered it up and did not take it, even after he had attained high status.

He instructed his disciples to donate gold for the restoration of the temple. His lifelong conduct and achievements were brilliantly recorded in the historical annals; upon his death, he was posthumously titled Wenzheng and enfeoffed as the Duke of Chu.

The assembly said, "We only knew how to hasten our journey, unaware that we had lost our way. Lingtuo opened his arms and said, "A hundred years are but a single dream;

it is only today that I have finally awakened. He then offered this verse: "At thirty-eight years of age, I was muddled and ignorant. When I finally attained understanding, how is it different from ignorance?
The waters of the Bian River flow on and on; The embankments of Sui stretch far and wide. Master, you shall return home; The arrow-like waves rush eastward."
The eulogy says: "To know or not to know—the wooden horse neighs at night.

Zhao Bian (the Dharma heir of Chan Master Fohui Faquan), Zhao Bian, styled Yue Dao, called himself Zhi Fei Zi (The Son Who Knows His Faults). Whatever he did during the day, he would invariably burn incense and address Heaven at night.

During the Zhihe era of the Song dynasty, he served as a Court Censor (*shiyu*). In his official duties, he prosecuted wrongdoers without sparing even the high-ranking relatives of the imperial family.

In his private life, he was always accompanied by only a zither and a crane. A monk once offered him this poem: "One must walk upon the crown of Vimalakīrti’s head. Thereafter, he cast aside all worldly sounds and colors.
He bound his mind to the teachings of the school and sought the Way from Chan Master Chongyuan at Tiantianbasi.

Later, when Fohui Faquan resided at Nanchan in Quzhou, Huai went daily to visit and question him; however, Faquan never permitted him to utter a single word. Afterwards, while serving as the governor of Qingzhou, he often sat in meditation amidst his official duties.
Suddenly, a great thunderclap struck, and he immediately attained realization, composing a verse that begins: "Sitting in silence in the public hall..."

Xu leaned back against his armrest; the source of his mind was unmoving, as still as water. With a single clap of thunder, the crown of his head opened, awakening him to that which belongs to himself from the very beginning.
He looked up at the azure heavens, joyful beyond measure; in every moment and every speck of dust, there is nothing that is not so.
Those of middling or inferior capacity cannot hear this—it is merely the wondrous function of spiritual power. When Quan heard this, he laughed and said, "Zhao Yuedao has struck [the bell]."
Cai Erfu and Zheng Gongbi initially had no direction regarding the Chan school. Baoan exhorted them, writing in a letter:
"I, Baoan, consider that the Dharma of the Western Sage’s 'separate transmission outside the teachings' was not established for those of inferior or middling capacities.
Those of superior wisdom enter through sudden awakening; having attained it once, they possess it forever. The foolish, however, remain deluded and do not return."
The differences are myriad. Only the Buddhas and Patriarchs have transmitted mind-to-mind;

yet, when compelled to benefit living beings and engage with others, they employed various expedient means such as blows and shouts, fists and pointing fingers, raising eyebrows and blinking eyes, striking the mallet and brandishing the whisk, as well as speech, writing, and all manner of other methods.
As the distance from the Sages grew ever greater, the disciples of various quarters forgot the root and pursued the branches, abandoned the source to follow the waves, until the tide overflowed.
All are thus submerged; these are truly what may be called pitiable. Your servant, Bai, is unworthy. Last autumn, while first stationed in Qingzhou, I was moved by certain realizations.
Having come to know somewhat that one's original nature is neither deficient nor redundant, I believe the ancients were not mistaken when they called it the "Dharma-gate of Peace and Joy.
Recently, I have been honored by the Grand Preceptor and the Palace Attendant, who commanded me to seek out the records of Chan. Your servant has long been favored by their grace.
Upon hearing this, I was filled with joy and delight; unconsciously, I began to dance with my hands and tread with my feet.

I humbly reflect that your honors possess such ultimate wealth and nobility, such flourishing virtue and morality, such complete fulfillment of fortune, longevity, health, and tranquility, and such lofty retirement and leisure.
Yet, that which you have not yet given much attention to is nothing other than the Tathāgata’s single great cause and condition.
Now, having again attained realization into the true nature, I venture to offer my congratulations to your honorable household.
At the age of seventy-two, he retired from public service and returned to Sangu. There, he associated with mountain monks and country elders without interruption.
He named his dwelling "Gaozhai" (The High Studio) and inscribed this verse upon it: "The golden girdle has already been laid aside; The message within is but ordinary."
"Those of this time must recognize that the old man of Gaozhai was merely Zhao Sili of Ke Village. He spoke again, saying:

"Be careful not to mistake the final testament left at the end of his life; had it not been for the daily warnings and exhortations of the Master, one would certainly have found no efficacy at such a moment."

He then took his leave of all his relatives and friends. When his son Shan asked about his final affairs, Fan rebuked him with a stern voice. After a short while, he spoke as usual; then, sitting in the full lotus posture, he passed away.
He was seventy-seven years old. His posthumous title was Qingxian (Pure Contributor). Quanshuo lamented him with a verse: "In office, he was a blessing to the state;
In retirement, he became a model for the world. The golden grain has departed from the human realm; The jade tower is now perfected in heaven. The sword of wisdom..."
Without a single flaw; a crystal pitcher, pure to its very depths. The spring breeze flows through the stream-lined path; the solitary moon shines bright upon the clouds. The commentary says:
"The thunderbolt opens at the crown of the head—'Is there? Is there? Call out! 'What is it? What is it? Arise from your own self!"
Zhao Yuedao hit the jackpot; yet, there is still a slight discrepancy. Even so, it cannot be let pass.
A fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes the nostrils of Śakra; a carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow upon being struck with a staff.
The rain poured down like an overturned basin.
Fu Bi (Dharma successor of Chan Master Xiu Yong of Huayan), whose courtesy name was Yanguo, was a native of Henan.
During the Qingli era, he served concurrently as Chancellor alongside Wen Yanbo and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zheng.

The Duke was exhorted by the strategy of Zhao Qingxian. Thereafter, he practiced with diligence day and night. While serving as the military governor of Bozhou, he heard of the flourishing reputation of Xiu Yong’s Dharma assembly and went there to resolve his doubts.
Upon seeing Xiu Yong ascend the seat, [the Duke] observed him gazing like an elephant king; after the master had circled the hall, the Duke attained a slight realization.
He then adopted the etiquette of a disciple and requested to become a member of the inner circle. As soon as Xiu Yong saw him, he said: "Your Excellency has already..."
As he entered, Fu Bi was still outside. Upon hearing this, sweat poured down his back; he immediately attained great enlightenment. He soon sent a verse to Yuanzhao Ben, saying:
"Upon one glance at Master Yong, my realization entered deeply; through these causes and conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Old Teacher.
Though a thousand miles of mountains and rivers separate us, I face his spiritual light and wondrous voice as if before my eyes. He then welcomed Yong to the provincial seat to consult with him.

Regarding the mental factors (*citta-dharma*), in a later letter responding to Yang Yong, he wrote: "When I encountered the Master, it was like recovering something that had been lost since beginningless time.
Once this is recognized, one must certainly pull oneself out of the ocean of birth and death; this is no ordinary kindness.

Though one exerts every ounce of strength and cuts through the path, one cannot escape it. I constantly reflect on how the ancient patriarchs, at the very beginning, were established in their own [nature]..."
The Master resided there for twenty or thirty years, or at the very least, for several decades.
Attending upon him day and night, he heard the Way and the Dharma, and only then did he attain a thorough understanding from top to bottom. He then reflected:
"Twice I received the Master’s grace, and together we spent two months seeking instruction. Had I been more clever than others, how much more effort could I have applied? If..."
It was not that the Upādhyāya skillfully devised expedients or exerted himself to extract and reveal [the truth]; how else could one have seen its limits? He further sent a letter to Ben, saying:
"I, Bi, have devoted myself to the Way of the Patriarchs for a long time. I have always regretted not meeting an enlightened person to open my understanding."

I, a humble and ignorant person, was fortunate enough yesterday to guard my brush. My territory borders that of Yingzhou, and I invited Master Yong to visit me so that we might gather together for several months.
Through the power of his compassion and skillful means, he caused me to attain realization. Now that the day for the summer retreat is approaching, on the fourth month...
I have returned to Ying quite abruptly; as for the work of polishing and refining, I have yet to achieve any significant merit.

Old age and illness persist, and my dull faculties find it difficult to enter [the Way]. This is what the ancient master Guling meant when he said: "Unexpectedly, in my old age, I have been able to hear the ultimate teaching and see it."
As for Bi, today he has received the Dharma from Master Yong; however, its ultimate source derives from the Old Monk.
Since the lineage is most authentic and must be maintained, I hope you will further bestow your compassion upon me to accept me as your disciple and grant me your guidance from afar.
To cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it is to be the Pang Yun of Mount Nanyue and the Pei Xiu of Baizhang. Later, he petitioned for Master Yong to be appointed;
when Yong ascended the hall, his words of thanks included: "That was a mistake on one occasion; I too shall follow error with error.
Bei composed a verse in praise, saying: "Ten thousand trees and a thousand flowers desire to flourish, yet the Sleeping Dragon has not yet emerged from the blue seas."
Ming. Auspicious omens appeared as vermilion clouds and colored mists; as before, the Southern Mountain was a single hue of green.
Wen Yanbo, courtesy name Kuānfū, was a native of Jiexiu. He served four successive dynasties, holding the offices of general and minister for over fifty years.
His official rank reached that of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), and he was enfeoffed as Duke of Lùguó. While serving as Governor of Luoyang, he once went to Long’an Temple to observe a fast.
While paying homage to a sacred image, he suddenly saw it break and fall to the ground. Without showing even the slightest reverence, he merely looked at it and departed.
A monk nearby asked, "Why do you not prostrate? Bo said, "Since the image is already broken, with what shall I prostrate?

The monk replied, "It is like the earth of a public road that people dig up to fashion into an image; the wise know it is still road-earth, while ordinary people call it an 'image. This arises only from later conceptualization."

The Official was about to depart. Upon his return, he found that the image had filled the road. The image is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished; the road likewise has no newness or antiquity. Bokwon attained a realization through this.
When Bokwon was serving as the Prefectural Commissioner (Sijang) in Northern Beiping, he was on good terms with Zen Master Jungwon of Tianbasi Temple.
One day, Won came to visit him for a farewell. Bokwon said, "Master, you are old; where will you go now? Won replied, "I am going to enter extinction. Bokwon laughed.
It was said that he spoke with playful ease and personally escorted [the deceased] back home. He conversed with his master and disciples about the profound and stable resonance of the Way;
his talk and laughter were full of flavor, showing him to be no ordinary monk. When someone went to check on him, they found that he had already passed away while seated.

Greatly astonished by this marvel, and as it was then the height of summer, a fragrant breeze brushed against people. After some time, his body was cremated; the color of the smoke was pure white and translucent, and countless *śarīra* relics were recovered. (From the *Bopiqin*)

He went there to observe. Taking the white lapis lazuli bottle bestowed upon him by the Emperor, he placed it before the seat and made this vow: "The Buddha-Dharma is truly efficacious; I pray that śarīra will fill my bottle.
As soon as he finished speaking, smoke descended from the sky and entered the bottle. When the smoke vanished, the śarīra were inside exactly as he had wished.
From then on, Bo redoubled his efforts in his devotion to the Way, regretting only that he had come to know it so late, and focused his mind single-mindedly on Amitābha.
The Buddha would burn incense in the morning and sit in meditation at night, never for a moment being lax. He would frequently make this vow:
"May I always be diligent and energetically cultivate all virtues; may I realize the essence of the mind and extensively deliver all sentient beings.

Thereupon, together with Dharma Master Jingyan, he gathered one hundred thousand people for a Pure Land assembly. The Layman Ruru offered this verse in praise: "I know your courage and resolve are great."

Like a celestial being, he vowed to establish one hundred thousand karmic connections in the Western Quarter. He did not seek a livelihood for his own body alone; rather, he urged everyone together onto the ferry at the riverbank.
When his life came to an end, he passed away peacefully while reciting the Buddha’s name. His lifespan was ninety-two years.
Ouyang Xiu, courtesy name Yongshu, was a native of Luling. Originally he did not believe in Buddhism.

In the sixth year of the Jiayou era, he served as an Acting State Councilor and concurrently acted as the editor for the translation of Buddhist scriptures. Having ascended to one of the two highest offices of state, he frequently suffered from illness.

He once dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where ten men, wearing ceremonial caps and robes, were seated in a circle. One man said, "Acting State Councilor, how have you come to this? You ought to return home at once. Xiu then departed.
After walking a few paces toward the gate, he went again to ask them, "Are you not followers of the Śākya clan? Are you not what are called the Ten Kings? They replied, "Indeed.

He then asked, "When worldly people provide meals for the Sangha and commission the production of sutras, is there truly any benefit? They said, "How could there not be? Upon waking, his illness was completely cured.
From that time on, he first gave rise to faith in the Dharma. While residing in Luoyang, he traveled to Mount Song, where he dismissed his attendants and servants and let his mind roam freely.
Xiu went to a temple where tall bamboos filled the courtyard and the scenery was fresh and beautiful. While resting within the hall, an elderly monk nearby was reading a sutra with composure.

Xiu asked, "What sutra are you reciting? He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. Xiu said, "In the past, eminent monks at the moment of death and rebirth were mostly able to cast off their bodies with laughter and ease.
What path leads to such a state? He replied, "It is the power of meditative concentration and wisdom. Furthermore—
Question: "Why is it now so desolate and devoid [of practitioners]? Answer: "In the past, people were settled in meditative concentration and wisdom at every thought-moment;

how could they have been distracted at the moment of death? Nowadays, people are distracted at every thought-moment; how could they attain concentration and wisdom at the moment of death? Xiu Da sighed in deep admiration.

Later, he retired from office with the title of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince. While residing in Yingzhou, because the Governor of Ying was extremely devoted to the virtuous achievements of Chan Master Xiu Yong, he [Xiu Da] then made full preparations [to honor him].

When Sengyong arrived at the banquet, Xu hurriedly asked him, "What is the teaching of the Buddha? Sengyong then engaged in a profound discussion, pointing toward the wondrous and expounding upon the subtle.
He moved with ease through the capital of the Huazang Dharma-realm and composed himself within the luminous pearls of the Indra’s Net.
Xu stood in awe and said, "I never knew that the Buddhist scriptures were so wondrous as this. When he was about to die, he summoned [Sengyong].
He earnestly admonished his sons and younger brothers, saying: "In my life, I was renowned for my literary works and strove to disparage the Buddhists.

Now that I am decrepit and worn out, I have suddenly heard these profound doctrines; it is only now that I shall study them—what a fate! Alas! You must all exert yourselves and avoid falling into such regret later.

Thereupon, he abandoned wine and meat, put away sounds and sights, and sat in silent meditation with a heart extinguished of worldly desire. He ordered an old soldier to go near the temple to borrow some flowers.
He was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* when he reached the eighth fascicle; he then sat upright and passed away.
Fan Zhen, whose courtesy name was Jingren, served successively as Hanlin Academician. Someone once asked him, "Why do you not believe in Buddhism?
Fan Zhen replied, "Must you wait for me to join my palms and prostrate myself before you can say I believe? One day, Huang Tingjian visited him.
Zhèn sat facing him all day long, maintaining an upright posture and never once looking back, nor did he show any sign of weariness.
Zhèn said, "For twenty years, not a single thought has ever arisen in my breast; for two or three years, I have hardly read any books."
"If there are no guests, you sit alone all day long and do not sleep until the second watch of the night; even when your children shout and clamor within mere paces of you, you do not hear them.
Jiān said, "You, sir, are truly a master practitioner of Buddhism."
Sima Guang, styled Junshi, was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Wengu. Initially, he did not favor Chan Buddhism.

However, after Fan Zhongyan [the "Rich Fan"] inquired about the Dharma with Yuanzhao, Sima suddenly attained a point of realization. Fan Zhen, regarding this as a mockery of Sima, said: "How could I say that there is no Chan in the world?
It is simply that what we Confucians have heard is such that there is no need to abandon our own tradition to follow their scriptures. Later, because of Zhen’s discussion...

[Zhao] Mengfu realized the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). He then composed a poem in jest, saying: "There is no need for celestial maidens to scatter; you have already understood how to stir the meditative mind.

Zhao Zhen did not accept this. [Mengfu] again teased him, saying: "I, this lowly son, attained realization long ago; you, Jingren, have now fallen back into delusion. He further said: "Once the shore is reached, what need is there for a raft?

To wield a hoe, one does not need gold. Let the floating clouds come and go as they will; the bright moon remains in the heart of heaven. This was the sixth of his "Verses on Resolving Meditation" (*Jieshan liu*).
The verse says: Anger is like a blazing fire; greed and desire are like sharp blades. To be perpetually sorrowful throughout the day—this is called the Avīci Hell.

Yan Hui found peace in a humble alley; Mencius nurtured the "vast and courageous" spirit (*haoran*). Regarding wealth and honor as floating clouds—this is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

Filial piety and fraternal respect penetrate the divine intelligences; loyalty and trustworthiness prevail among the barbarians. Accumulating goodness brings down a hundred blessings—this is called "Acting."

Regarding cause and effect: their words serve as teachers for a hundred generations, and their conduct serves as the law for all under heaven. As time passes, these cannot be obscured; this is called the indestructible body.
It is the peaceful dwelling of the benevolent and the straight path of the righteous. When practiced with sincerity and over a long duration, it is called the Treasury of Radiance.
Through the Way and righteousness one cultivates the self, and through merit one benefits the myriad things. Thus becoming a worthy one or a great sage, this is called a Buddha.

The Bodhisattva Shao Yong, styled Yaofu, was a native of Fanyang. He resided in Luoyang for forty years, living in contentment with poverty and delighting in the Way. In winter he used no stove, and in summer he used no fan;
for several years at night he did not even go to his mat. He had a poem on studying Buddhism which says: "Eating to satiety and wearing fine clothes..."
Time passes easily; as the days grow long, what can one do with sorrow? In my prime, I sought fame and turned to Confucius; in my old age, fearing death, I draw near to Śākyamuni.
In vain I wish to sever worldly ties, yet they become ever heavier; I strive to eliminate illness, yet it returns in greater measure.
The vast expanse of the Yangtze River is as smooth as a roll of silk, yet alas, though there is no wind, waves arise once more.
Lu Gongchu, courtesy name Huishu, served as Chancellor alongside Sima Guang. Initially, Guang did not favor Buddhism. Gongchu exhorted him, saying:

"The Buddhist teachings on the mind and its operations are concise and essential. If one extracts their most vital points and understands them, they generally consist of rectifying the mind and taking 'no-thought' as the fundamental principle.
It does not necessarily require one to practice every detail or become a person outside the secular world. Guang agreed with this. One day, the Emperor...
He asked with composure about the way of governance, eventually reaching the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi. Sengzhao wrote in his inquiry: "Did Yao and Shun know this Way?
The Emperor replied, "How could Yao and Shun not have known it? Sengzhao said, "Yao and Shun knew this, yet they regarded only the knowledge of men and the settling of the people as urgent."

This is why he was like Yao and Shun. When the silk wadding was placed over his mouth, although his descendants filled the space before him and his relatives and friends arrived in great numbers, he did not speak at all of matters concerning his own body or worldly affairs.

The eulogy says: When the Duke of Zhongfu (Fan Zhongyan) reflected upon the ancient venerable masters, he observed that they served their own teachers for twenty or thirty years before finally attaining a thorough mastery from top to bottom.
He lamented his own lack of sufficient time for seeking instruction. How could this be the act of one who is empty-headed and arrogant, mistaking brass for gold?
It is what is meant by "thoroughly investigating the ultimate principle, taking awakening as the standard," dwelling thus throughout one's life.
He is surely one such person who trains himself while still on the stage of learning. As the ancient masters said: "One must advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole;
the ten directions of the world are one's entire body. Regarding Master Zheng, I cannot help but feel a lingering sense of admiration.

Furthermore, the eulogy states: Wen Lugong, Ouyang Yongshu, Fan Jingren, Sima Junshi, Shao Yaofu, and Lü Huishu were all illustrious figures in the historical records who stirred the world as eminent men of talent.
Yet, upon examining their lives, there was none among them who did not penetrate the principles of Buddhism, being no different from accomplished masters or Chan practitioners.
Although Ouyang Yongshu initially strove to reject it, he ultimately attained awakening.
Furthermore, how could he be compared to those of shallow roots?
Pan Xingsi (dharma heir of Chan Master Huinang of Huanglong).
Pan Xingsi, courtesy name Yanzhi, was a native of Nanzhou. He initially served as the magistrate of Dehua County. His fellow countyman Xu Jian first...

He went to pay his respects to the Governor of Jiangzhou, Cheng Si. When he arrived to see him, Cheng did not offer him the proper rites; consequently, Cheng Jie returned with his visiting card and ultimately did not take up his official post.
He sought the Way from Huinanyuan and received his seal of approval. He once said, "I am a recluse of this pure age," and thus styled himself the Layman Qingyi (Pure Recluse).
At that time, the Dharma-way of Huanglong was flourishing greatly, and students from all quarters were scrambling forward in fear of falling behind.
Later, although he considered himself one who had already undergone extensive training, when he arrived, he was struck with awe and joined the ranks of the disciples.
When asked the reason for this, Nan said: "When a father is strict, his son is filial. Today’s instruction shall serve as tomorrow’s model. It is like the earth:
that which is high is lowered, and that which is hollow is leveled. If he is to ascend to the heights of a thousand fathoms, I too shall go along with him."
"Exhausted, he reaches the depths of the Nine Abysses; I also share in his skill. When one is at their limit, delusions are exhausted and one is naturally liberated.
He further said: "To nurture and foster them in spring and summer is how they are brought to birth;
to frost and snow them in autumn and winter is how they are brought to maturity. How could I wish to remain silent? Nan also once [discussed] the Buddha...
When Nan-ch’uan was questioned by a scholar on the three phrases concerning "the hand," "the donkey’s foot," and "birth conditions," none were able to penetrate his meaning.

The monastic communities of the world came to designate these as the "Three Barriers of Huang-lung. Whenever someone attempted to respond, Nan-ch’uan would simply say, "Namo" (Homage), and sit upright with eyes closed;

no one could fathom his intention. Later, when asked the reason for this, Nan-ch’uan said: "Those who have already passed through the barrier walk straight ahead with arms swinging; how could they know?"
Regarding this, when an official asked his subordinates whether it was permissible [to visit], they replied that he had not yet penetrated the essential gate.

Subsequently, from the Jia-yu era onward, dozens of recommendation petitions were submitted by high-ranking officials, yet he remained firm in his refusal to emerge from seclusion. He lived by East Lake in Yu-zhang, delighting himself with the lute and books.
One day, Yuan of Qian-an came to visit him while he was tuning his lute. Seeing him thus, Yuan said: "Old and aged as you are, you still..."
Holding a thread of inquiry, Shishuo said, "I must also play it so that it resonates. Wenyuan said, "It is not lacking.
Shishuo said, "How many people can truly know this mind?"
The Eulogy says: Juefan’s inscription on the Master’s portrait states: "A treasury of the birthlessness of Vairocana; a vessel of the Way in Zhendan.
He employs his body as a tongue to discourse upon the wondrous meaning, and uses his hands as the earth to uphold the great thousand-fold world system.

His spiritual acumen was no less than that of Pangyun, yet he understood the Chan of letters; his conduct and withdrawal were largely like those of a youth, yet he encountered an era of peace and brilliance."—Shu Wang Qiang.
He sought him but could not prevail; the Divine Emperor (Shenkao) sought him but he did not rise.

This is what all the scholar-officials of the realm have heard together, yet how could you, Master Gong, have been limited to this alone? Alas! These four characters—"how could he have been limited to this?"—clearly paint the portrait of Pan Yanzhi.
Zhang Shangying (Dharma heir of Chan Master Doushuai Congyue).

Zhang Shangying’s courtesy name was Tianjue, and his sobriquet was Wujin Jushi (the Infinite Layman). As a child, he could memorize ten thousand words a day. At the age of nineteen, he traveled to the capital to take the imperial examinations;
on the way, he passed through the home of the Xiang family. One night prior to this, a deity appeared in a dream to the Xiangs and announced, "Tomorrow, you shall receive the Excellency."

Wang Ying arrived. Xiang treated him with particular distinction and subsequently gave him his daughter in marriage. One day, while visiting a monastery, he saw that the Tripitaka scriptures were bound and displayed with great magnificence and beauty.
He sighed in frustration and said, "The books of our Sage Confucius do not even compare to those of the barbarians. Returning home, he sat in his study reciting aloud until the third watch.
Lady Xiang asked, "It is so late at night; why do you not go to sleep? Ying then replied with his previous sentiment, saying, "I am precisely..."
This person was attached to the theory that there is no Buddha. Xiang Shi responded immediately, saying, "If there is no Buddha, what is there to discuss?

You must hold to the theory that there is a Buddha before you can succeed. Ying doubted these words and consequently desisted. Later, he visited a colleague and saw the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* before a Buddha shrine.
He reached out and picked it up to read, and upon arriving at the passage: "This illness is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element," he suddenly—

He sighed and said, "Can the speech of these Hu people also be such as this? He then borrowed the text to read it. Later, when he returned it, the person from the Xiang family asked, "What book are you reading? He replied, "The Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
The man said, "You should read this sūtra thoroughly before composing a 'Treatise on the Non-existence of the Buddha. Zhiying was struck with awe by these words;
thereupon, he placed deep faith in the Buddha Vehicle and devoted himself to the Way of the Patriarchs. In the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, he served as the Transport Commissioner for Jiangxi.

In the west, he first visited Donglin Zong. Zong questioned him regarding his realization, and finding that it accorded with his own, he granted him formal approval (*inka*), saying, "I have a disciple who has attained the Dharma and resides at Yuxi;
you may speak with him. Later, when Fenyang Ying was touring the administrative districts and passed through Fenning, the various Chan masters went out to welcome him;
they first paid their respects to [the master of] Yuxi and finally inquired after Doushuai Congyue. As for Congyue’s character—

He was short and small in stature. Ying had previously heard Gong Dezhuang say that he was intelligent and likable, so he remarked, "I have heard that you, Master, are quick-witted and skilled in literary composition.
Zongyue smiled and said, "The Commissioner has lost one of his eyes. Congyue was the ninth-generation descendant of Linji;
if one were to compare quick wit and literary skill with the Commissioner, it would be like comparing the Commissioner to Congyue when discussing Chan.

Ying silently took note of this. He then went to visit Doushuai. Yue said to the head seat: "When Commissioner Zhang passes by here, I shall strike him deeply and pierce him through with painful words.
If he is willing to turn his head [toward the Way], it would be a great blessing for our school. The head seat said, "The gentlemen of today are accustomed to receiving deference and service;
I fear that if you provoke them, they may become resentful and cause trouble. Yue replied, "Even if it causes them vexation, so be it."
"I have merely retired to my own monastery; there is nothing else. When their conversation reached a late hour, they discussed matters concerning the Chan school.
Yuan Yue said, "Since Donglin has granted you his seal of approval, do you have even the slightest doubt regarding the teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs?"

[The student] said, "I have been reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the机缘 (opportune encounters) of the venerable masters, yet I am left with only doubt regarding Xiangyan’s ‘one-legged verse’ and Deshan’s ‘begging bowl’ story.
Yue said, "Since you harbor doubts about these, everything else is merely intellectual speculation and conceptual understanding;
how could it ever reach the state of great peace and bliss? Furthermore, as for Yantou’s words regarding the 'final phrase'—does it exist, or does it not? [The student] said, "It exists."

There was one. Yue laughed heartily and returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him. For the entire night, Ying could not sleep peacefully; at the fifth watch, he got out of bed and kicked over his urinal.
Suddenly, he had a great realization and was filled with immense joy. He immediately knocked on the door of the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have already caught the thief.

The Master said, "Where does the Buddha-dharma reside? The Master replied, "It resides where one walks, stands, sits, and lies; where one puts on clothes and eats food; where one defecates and urinates;

where there is neither principle nor understanding; and where life and death cannot be grasped. "You, Zizhan, have ten thousand scrolls of books in your breast, and when you take up the brush, not a speck of dust remains.
Yet, having reached this station, you do not know the location of your own life-force. [Life]—one lifetime.
How intelligent! What need is there to become a Buddha of the three periods? One is simply a man of spirit.
If you, Zizhan, can take this upon yourself, you will regard the wealth, honor, and fame of twenty or thirty years as being as worthless as dirt.

Strive forward. Farewell. Farewell. In the Gengchen year, he was reinstated as a Court Gentleman of the Fourth Rank. In the Xinsi year, he crossed the mountain pass to the north and settled in Changzhou.

He requested retirement from office and retired on his current rank. Later, he moved south, carrying with him daily a single scroll of an Amitābha Buddha image, saying, "This is the official passport for Shi’s rebirth in the Western Paradise. At this time, his illness became critical; Weilin of Mount Jing came to see him.
He waited for [Su Shi] and said, "Enduring Brilliance (Duannming), do not forget the Western [Paradise]. Su Shi replied, "The West is certainly not non-existent, but one cannot apply effort here.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. He once inscribed his own reflection, saying: "My mind is like wood whose fire has been extinguished;
my body is like an unmoored boat. If you ask about the achievements of my life, they are Huangzhou, Huizhou, and Qiongzhou."

The commentary states: Master Sūshun (Sōtō) appeared in this world for one occasion, engaging in mutual exhortation with the venerable elders Fuyin (Hōin), Hōsen (Hōsen), and others, to propagate the Buddha-dharma.
Zippo (Shibayama) said: "The old thief Dongpo took literature as his green forest;
he appeared and vanished before peaks and at crossroads, hiding nowhere—not amidst thorns and brambles, nor within ambushes and poisoned arrows—waiting exclusively to kill."
Without blinking an eye, Xingzhen Han struck upon the pivot; blades and arrows were discharged all at once, corpses lay scattered and blood splashed until the azure stream turned crimson.

Tell me now, was he a thief or not? Try to discern and examine this for yourself. If you can discern it, you will surely find that the boulders blocking the road have long since been doused with boiling water and snow.
Furthermore, the eulogy states: An ancient worthy said, "Sū Dongpo was but a layman outside the gate.

If even Master Dongpo’s realization remained outside the gate, how could the Buddha-dharma be easily spoken? Nevertheless, those reading his writings a thousand years later come to know that the Buddha-dharma exists;
it seems that the Master performed the work of a Buddha through his literary art. One may infer that this man, too, was one who had mounted upon his vows.
...and has come. As for those who proceed by virtue of their vows, how could one possibly permit oneself to lightly interject with idle words?
Master Lianchi’s eulogy states: "When Old Quan (Su Shi) sought to dedicate merit for his deceased ancestors, he commissioned six images of Bodhisattvas at Jile Temple.
Furthermore, Ziyou (Su Che), who moved between the Dharma gates, was also very closely associated with him. This was indeed the devotion of the Su family."
The Three Jewels in the mind have long been pure. In the world, there is one who carves a stele for Master Xifang;

some who rely on it have added vulgar colloquialisms, claiming it originated from Su Shi (Slope Master). This is a fabrication. Those with discerning eyes should not discard the genuine along with the false.
The Master further said: "I have heard that the ancient worthies said: 'Among the gentry and officials, those whose brilliance and acuity surpass others mostly come from among the monks.'"
Come! Yet I have often wondered about this: those who are deluded and do not return are nine out of ten;

those who do not fail their past causes are but one out of ten. What is the reason for this? The world of the five turbidities abounds with conditions for regression; even the worthy cannot avoid them.
Thus, Master Jie was reborn as Dongpo (Su Shi), Master Qing was reborn as Prince Zeng (Zeng Gong), and Master Zhe...
The Master’s subsequent incarnation indulged in wealth and status and suffered much anxiety and pain.
Now, while Dongpo was most intimately connected to the Dharma, even Master Zeng did not [attain it]; how much more so is the delusion of that Elder’s subsequent incarnation!
This is why the realized masters of past and present exhort people to abandon the five turbidities and seek the Pure Land. Thus, Liu Yiji—
From the common people down to these gentlemen, have they not already gained much?

Huang Tingjian (Dharma heir of Chan Master Zuxin of Huanglong), the Grand Historian Huang Tingjian, styled Luzu and surnamed Shangu, possessed the karmic habituation of Prajñā from past lives; thus, although he held a high official post, he remained detached.
It was so. Moving in and out of the Chan school, he had not yet found his direction. He delighted in composing flowery verses, which people vied with one another to transmit.
Once he visited Yuan Tong Xiu, who scolded him, saying, "A man of great stature—would you willingly apply the mastery of your brush and ink to such things?
At that time, Xiu was instructing Li Bashi on the matter of painting horses; Jian laughed and said, "Will you now place me within the belly of a horse as well? Xiu...

He said, "By using such seductive language, you have stirred the lustful hearts of the people of the world; it is not merely that they will end up in the bellies of horses, but I fear they will be reborn in the hells.

Sengjian was struck with awe and repented, apologizing for his transgression. From then on, he ceased writing and devoted himself solely to the Way with tireless diligence, composing the *Pranidhāna* (Vow) Text.
He strictly observed the precepts against alcohol and sexual indulgence, limiting his daily intake to morning congee and a single midday meal.

During the Yuanyou era, while observing the mourning period for his family, he stayed at Huanglong Mountain and attended upon the Patriarch Huichang Xin. He requested instruction on the direct and swift path.
Huichang said, "As for what Confucius said—'Have I been concealing anything from you, my disciples? I have concealed nothing from you'—how do you usually explain this, Master Historian?"
Jian opened his mouth and said, "It is not so! It is not so! While he was thus in a state of distress, a man arrived at the hall and asked, "Who sent you here?
The man replied, "The scholar Dailin Ye. He asked again, "Do you have a letter? He replied, "I do. He asked again, "Where is the letter?
The man immediately reached behind him, pulled back his collar, and presented the letter to the Hall Master. The Hall Master said, "The student..."

When the Way reaches such a person’s field, it is truly appropriate. Jian had a look of deep shame on his face. One day, while attending the hall and walking through the mountains, the rock-orchids were in full bloom.
The Hall Master asked, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *mugicha*? He replied, "I do. The Hall Master said, "Is there anything I have hidden from you?"
Erjian joyfully accepted and understood this. He immediately bowed and said, "Master, you possess such a compassionate and earnest heart.
Xuedou Tang laughed and said, "I simply wish for you to reach home. At that time, he was together with Xuedou Tang’s eminent disciples: Sishi Wuxin, Lingyuan, and Weiqing.
Their affinity for one another beyond the mundane world became increasingly profound over time. He went to visit Yunyan’s Xinfeng and entered the room with the assembly.
Upon seeing him, Xinfeng opened his eyes wide and asked, "The new abbot is dead; you, scholar, are dead. Once burned into two heaps of ash, where will you meet?"
Jian remained silent. Xinyue said, "What you have attained under Huitang has not yet truly settled.

Later, while serving as an official in Qian-nan, his practice grew even more powerful within a state of non-thinking, and he suddenly clarified the meaning of what Sishi had asked. He sent a letter in reply, saying:

"In the past, I was fortunate enough to receive your bitter-mouthed reminders, yet for a long time I remained like one in a drunken dream, with things appearing only as a blur amidst shifting shadows."
Because the doubt had not been fully exhausted and the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) remained unsevered, he merely retreated, looking back at the precipice.

While traveling on the road in Qian-Nan during his period of banishment, he awoke from a midday nap and was suddenly enlightened in a vast, open state. He reflected that throughout his life he had been deceived by how many old monks under heaven;
only the Master Sīnmind (Sixin Daoren) refused to comply with him, and this was precisely the greatest act of true concern for his welfare. —Lingyuan.

He sent this verse: "In the past, we faced one another yet were separated by a thousand li; Now, though ten thousand miles apart, we are more intimate than ever. In our silent solitude, the flavor of our sustenance is shared as simple gruel;
In our joyful conversation, the harmony between host and guest is perfect. Within the room, who can be permitted to question the transformed woman? Within the eyes, do not seek for the pupils.
There is no place in the east, west, south, or north where it can be hidden; The golden-colored *dhūta* practitioner smiles with ever-fresh radiance."
Jianhe said: "The stonemason comes to chisel the dust from the tip of the nose; the handless man arrives and the axe finally meets its mark.

The white ox and the tabby cat—its mind is the Buddha. Dragon eyes and tiger eyes—the host within the guest. Carrying his own flask, he goes to buy village wine; putting on his robe, he returns as the host.
Ten thousand miles apart, they always face each other; within the room of Dead Heart (Sixin), there is freshness. The Hall.

He entered into *parinirvāṇa*. Jia composed an inscription for his stupa and further lamented him with a verse, saying: "The sea wind blows down Mount Laṅkā; The Chan practitioners of the four seas gaze upon it with fixed eyes.
A single tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered; Along with the mist, they rest upon the jade balustrade. He once exhorted Hu Shaoji in a letter, saying:
"In your public pursuit of the Way of Learning (*gongxue*), have you gained much benefit? As for the method of treating illness, you must be profoundly [attentive]."
Seek it! When the joy of dhyāna illuminates and shatters the root of birth and death, then anxiety, fear, lust, and anger will have no place to set foot.

Once the disease is rootless, how can its branches and leaves cause harm? The Elder Cong of Touzi and the Elder Yan of Haihui—whose conduct was not inferior to that of the ancients—are both worthy of close association as they are exceptionally sublime.
To learn false speech and flowery rhetoric from those who are merely scholars of literary composition only increases [delusion].

This is the seed of ignorance. Even the Venerable Cong delighted in receiving men of high intelligence and noble status. Upon opening a scroll for discussion, he would immediately pierce through the nostrils of all the Confucian scholars.
Once one has grasped the essential purport of the principles, looking back at the books previously read, the realm of understanding becomes vast and open;
the six directions are unobstructed, and it saves one’s mental and physical energy to an extreme degree. Nevertheless, a seeker of the Way must apply themselves with sincere earnestness.
I am deeply moved. What the ancients called "if one does not apply oneself with precision, one will not attain the truth" is no empty statement.
When Minister Han Zonggu once sent a letter to Huìtáng, he asked: "In the past, I heard that you, Master, attained awakening and were thereafter free from all doubt.
Yet, since beginningless time, the habitual tendencies of affliction have not been suddenly exhausted; what should be done about this? Huìtáng—
I replied: "I respectfully acknowledge the instructions conveyed by the Secretariat. Regarding the awakening of the past, my mind is vast and free of doubt.
However, since beginningless time, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of affliction have not yet been suddenly exhausted.

Yet, if one holds that there is no dharma remaining outside the mind, one does not know what these afflictive habitual tendencies are that one wishes to exhaust. To give rise to such a thought is, on the contrary, to mistake a thief for one's own son."
From the beginning until now, all that has been spoken as words is merely the administration of medicine according to the illness.

Even if there were afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are treated solely by means of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; these are all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and provisional teachings for the purpose of guidance.
If there were fixed habitual tendencies that could be treated, it would imply that there are phenomena existing outside the mind that could be exhausted—like the shell of a sacred tortoise.
Dragging its tail along the path, it brushes away traces only for more traces to arise; this may be called "using the mind to employ the mind," and it reveals that one's illness is deepening.

If you can clearly realize that there is no dharma outside the mind and no mind outside dharmas, then since both mind and dharmas are non-existent, whom would you further wish to instruct in their sudden exhaustion?
Whenever Peng Qizi, the Governor of Jiuyang, met with venerable elders, he would invariably ask: "When practitioners pass away, they often have much freedom.
Is there a definitive principle that can be heard regarding this? There were many who spoke falsely in response, which Peng Qizi would privately laugh at.

In his later years, while staying by the Pen River, he invited Huitang to his provincial residence. As they conversed leisurely about the Way from morning until evening, [Huitang] asked, "At the moment of death, do you truly have some final instructions?
He replied, "I do. [The Governor] said, "I wish to hear their explanation. He replied, "I shall explain them when you are on the verge of death.
The Governor’s capacity for realization was suddenly awakened; he rose to his feet and said, "This matter must indeed come from a Master like you. Hong Juefan sighed in admiration.
Appreciating his words, [Baizhang] composed a verse, saying: "Ma Zu has a companion, so he comes; When Peng Gong dies, he speaks at once.
A louse bites a person while they sleep; Reaching out with his hand, he catches a flea."
King Zhengyan asked Sixin Wuxin, "I have heard that birth occurs through the conjunction of three conditions.

I have also heard that one dies and is immediately reborn. Why, then, is there such a thing as being 'reborn by seizing a womb'? Wuxin replied, "Suppose you, Zhengyan, were appointed as a Commissioner of Transport.

Wherever you reside, you would immediately occupy that position. Would you still have doubts about this? Zhengyan said, "I would have no doubts. Wuxin said, "Then why do you doubt this [other matter]? King Zhengyan was thus enlightened.
He attained understanding upon hearing these words.
Zhu Shiying of Xianmu asked Zhenjing Kewen about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma. Kewen replied in a letter, saying: "I have received your letter concerning the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is supremely wondrous and non-dual; however, until one reaches this wondrous state, there will inevitably be mutual differences."
Whether long or short, if one reaches the sublime, then the person who awakens to the mind knows their own mind as it truly is: ultimately and fundamentally a Buddha.
They are truly sovereign, truly at peace, truly liberated, and truly pure. In daily life, they employ only their own mind;
as the transformations of their own mind, they grasp what they need and use it without questioning right or wrong. To deliberate with the thinking mind—

Measuring it is already not [the truth]. Nor does one intend with the mind. Each and every thing is genuine; each and every thing is luminous and wondrous. Each and every thing is like a lotus flower that is unsullied by water.
Therefore, by deluding one's own mind, one becomes a sentient being; by awakening to one's own mind, one becomes a Buddha.
Thus, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, and Buddhas are themselves sentient beings. It is only due to delusion and awakening that there is "this" and "that. As for those who study now...
Most do not believe in their own minds, do not awaken to their own minds, and fail to attain the luminous and wondrous enjoyment of their own minds.

They fail to attain the peace, bliss, and liberation of their own minds. Outside of the mind, they falsely conceive of Zen paths, falsely establish what is extraordinary, and falsely give rise to grasping and rejecting.

Even if they practice, they fall into the realms of externalist paths, the two vehicles, or the cessation-views of meditative stillness. After reading the letter, Ying attained realization and subsequently awakened.
Fanjian arrived at Linchuan and became close friends with Daoying. Shortly thereafter, the Elder of Shanglan arrived and said to Daoying, "I have heard that Juefan is skilled only in poetry;
as for Chan, even his master would be mistaken, let alone his disciple. Daoying laughed and said, "Can you, Master, put him to the test? The Elder of Shanglan replied, "Yes.
After one day had passed, they traveled together to Shushan and ate at an inn. The Elder of Shanglan—

He drew on the desk with his hand and said to Daohong, "On the covers of the sutra scrolls, the character 'mi' (rice) must be inscribed. What is its meaning? Daohong immediately drew a circle and added a horizontal stroke across it, saying, "This is its meaning.

Shanglan was struck dumb with astonishment. Daohong then composed a verse for him, which says: A circle is drawn, And a stroke is added across it; The meaning is perfectly clear. Why do you ask again? If you wish to know the truth, Look at the rice grain.
Because it cannot be formed by characters, it is not "eight. The Dharmakāya is fast asleep, without obstruction; the patch-robed monk faces it directly yet does not know its name.

Before a hundred people, he cannot be called forth. Shanglan returned and related this to Ying, who clapped his hands and said, "Who would have thought that even a 'poetry-monk' could understand the meaning of characters?"
The Great Officer Wang of Wei State left behind his name; having grown weary of the world due to the death of his wife, he went to study under Xiang, who was then serving as the Qingman of Yuanfeng.
Upon hearing the Master’s words, Wang realized his true home. One day, Qingman said to him, "You are the Lu Xuan of our time. Wang immediately covered his ears.
Thereafter, he returned to the south of Mount Tan and dwelt in a thatched hut for three years. He once sang: "Within the mountains of Tan, how long is the day!
On the ridges of green pines, the realm of white clouds. Chanting birds and crying monkeys form my place of practice.
With hair unbound, I gather ferns and sing again with laughter; Let people call me a madman, a man of the wild."
The Eulogy says: Huang Shan谷 (Shanwu) guarded the precepts as if guarding a bright pearl; he investigated Chan as if facing an iron wall.

He served his teachers and friends no less than he would serve his own father and elder brother; he exhorted his like-minded companions no less than he would exhort his own children and younger siblings.
Manifesting in the body of a lay official to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom—a man such as this may truly be said to be without shame.
Furthermore, the encomium says: Han Zonggu, Peng Qizi, Wang Zhengyan, and Zhu Shiying each have their own point of entry.
But tell me: when the Magistrate of Weizhou, Wang, covered his ears, was there speech, or was there no speech?
Wu Xun (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huanglong Zuxin).
Wu Xun, courtesy name Dufu, was a native of Xingyuan Prefecture who served as a legal officer (*faco*) in Yuzhang.

At that time, the regional commander Wang Shao welcomed Huaitang into the city and consulted him regarding the essentials of his realization. Xun also went to visit Huaitang, saying: "Throughout your life, you have studied and mastered the teachings..."
He recalled his extensive learning, yet he could not ask his parents for even a single word from before he was born.
Stunned and at a loss for an answer, he spent day and night reflecting on these words. Suddenly, he knew it for himself, yet the kōan had not yet been resolved.

By chance, while reading the biography of Deng Yinfeng, he saw that when the master passed away, he sat upright and inverted, and his robes remained clinging to his body without falling off. He was suddenly struck by doubt, wondering: "How did he pass away?"

The difference between these two cases is truly unfathomable, yet the robe also conforms to this. Why? [Dongshan] went to ask Tangshan about it. Tangshan said, "Now that you are standing in attendance, is this conforming or is it contrary?
[Dongshan] said, "It is conforming. [Tangshan] said, "Do you still have doubts? [Dongshan] said, "I have no doubts. [Tangshan] said, "Since you yourself have no doubts..."
"Why do you harbor doubts about that? Trust my words, and you shall be enlightened. He then presented three verses, saying: "No gates within, no byways on four sides;
Students toil in vain, busy grasping at shadows. Take heed: the moon of the old garden for a thousand ages— Through the night it remains as it was, never hidden.
"I am an old disciple of the Layman of Mount Lu; I have captured the Master’s true essence with perfect intimacy. To gather up the entire earth..."
Having formed an eye, it turns and surges forth in a manner quite distinct and new. *Du!* This worldly fellow of great knowledge has gnawed through all the public cases of past and present;
yet, amidst a heap of scattered refuse, he suddenly picks up a dung-ball from a dung beetle. Clearly, it is not worth a single cent.
"Ten thousand taels of gold would not buy it. He casually picks it up and shows it to others, simply because it is difficult to watch a ball roll on a tray.
(Ei! Dongshan replied with a verse: "Finding fire in water is rare in this world; Looking at it makes one suspect something extraordinary.
From of old, there were no masters or disciples; Now, however, the Old Barbarian is permitted to know. After Dongshan had departed, Xuedou sent him another verse: "The Sea..."
The mountain gate is perilously steep, cutting off all traces of passage; having trodden through the firm barrier, one’s faith is already established.
There exists a foundation for peace and stability of its own, regardless of whether one is from the south, north, west, or east.
Wang Shao (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Zuxin of Huidang).

Scholar Wang Shao, courtesy name Zichun, served as the military governor of Xisai. Considering his own karmic burden from acts of killing to be heavy, he prayed for purification and requested that Foyin Liaoyuan preach the Dharma.
As Liaoyuan offered incense at Shanglan Monastery, he said: "This incense is for those who kill people without blinking an eye."
"The General has attained Buddhahood on the spot. The assembly of great laymen praised this as excellent, and Shao’s mind was also at ease.

When he went out to serve as the Prefect of Hongzhou, he invited Huitang to inquire about the Way; they reached a silent accord, and Shao subsequently composed a verse on seizing the essential point, saying:
"By day I forgot to eat, by night I forgot to sleep, Holding the dragon pearl, I wished to ascend to heaven. Yet now I have cast it all down within my own body— Four [lines missing]."
The ridgepole and the rafters are perfectly round. [He] presents it to the Hall.
The Master, seeing its depth, approves. The collective eulogy says: After Wu De-fu picked up a dung ball from a dung beetle, it was not worth a single coin;
Wang Zi-chun, however, let go of it within his own person. At that moment, where was the "Pearl of the Dragon"? One must empty the mind to resolve this case of injustice.
He struck each of them three times with a painful blow of his staff. Now tell me: was this a reward for them, or was it a punishment?
Guo Xiangzheng (Dharma heir of Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan).
Guo Xiangzheng, style name Gongfu, was born when his mother dreamed of Li Bai. In the fourth year of the Huangyou era, Shouduan resided at Gui...

During the Zong era, Zheng served as the Assistant Magistrate of Xingzi. He went to seek the Dharma from [Master] Xin. Later, when Fandu resided at Chengtian and subsequently moved to Yuantong, Zheng was serving as the Magistrate of Dehua;
their correspondence and visits became even more frequent. When Fandu moved to Baiyun Haihui, Zheng was then in charge of Dangtu.
He went to visit Baizhang Duan and said, "Is the ox pure? Duan replied, "It is pure. Duan rebuked him with a stern voice, and Zheng, unaware, stood there with his hands joined in reverence.
Duan said, "Pure! Pure! It was at this point that Nanquan and Dayue were no different from this. Thereupon, he beat the drum and ascended the seat, saying:
"When the ox comes into the mountains, it has enough water and enough grass; when the ox leaves the mountains, it bumps into things to the east and to the west. Last night..."
While on my pillow, I composed this mountain verse to thank the great scholar Gongfu, an old friend from twenty years ago at Mount Lu.
In response to his diligent request to visit me from afar today amidst the white clouds, I shall hereafter clearly present this to all quarters.
I intend to strip away the flesh-bound sweat-shirt of every monk with nostrils throughout the world; do not say I did not warn you. Thus he said: *Shangda*.
"Ren Qiu Yi Ji transformed three thousand seventy scholars. You, a minor student, have eight or nine disciples. By practicing benevolence, one may know propriety. I was deeply perplexed by this.
Later, hearing a child reciting it, I suddenly attained realization. I wrote to report this to Master Duan, who replied with a verse:
"To hide oneself, there is no need to tuck in the head; To conceal one's traces, why must one withdraw the feet? The golden crow stirs at midnight."
"O Heavenly One! The Jade Hare could not catch him. During the Yuanyou era, he went to Nanchan Monastery in Quzhou to visit Master Quan Wanjuan and requested that the master ascend the seat.
As he stepped forward to offer incense, he said: "A withered tree by the sea, once taken into hand, becomes incense; now it is burned within the incense burner."
To pass straight through the nostrils of the Tathāgata Xiangji and perform such a great feat, one must address the assembly; only then can it be accomplished.
The Elder of Yunju had a seamless monk’s robe to bestow upon Nan Chan. If the Chan Master could wear it, it would be neither too long nor too short:
to step forward, all Buddhas would protect his station; to retreat, the waves of the sea would become still. Today, he lets out a groan.
There were six kinds of earth tremors. He then called out, "Does the great assembly understand this thoroughly?

When there is spirit, one adds to that spirit; where there is no elegance, one creates elegance. Yuanquan said, "We have been mutually obstructing each other. Zheng said, "By whom was this brought about?
At the beginning of the Chongning era, he went to Wuzu to request the Dharma. As Yan ascended the seat, Zheng stepped forward to offer incense, saying, "This single portion of incense..."
I burn incense within this burner to make offerings to my Dharma brother, the Zen Master of our Hall.

I prostrate myself and pray that, upon the seat of the vast and expansive truth, you will split open the gateway of your face and manifest the physical likeness of our late Master for all people to behold. Why is it that they are unable to capture his true form?
We met long ago by the side of White Cloud Rock; things of those days and today are not the same. The night is still and the water cold, so the fish do not bite;
a single burner of incense drifts away from White Lotus Peak. Yan said, "Namo Satvatāprabhāya. Thus it is, thus it is.
How many times have I gazed upon the yellow plum blossoms on the White Cloud Brook as they bloom amidst the snow? Not thus."
It is not so. Tender willows hang down golden threads; one must simply respond to the moment.
Have you not seen how Layman Pang asked Master Mazu, "Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas?

The Master said, "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single gulp, and then I shall tell you. O Great Assembly! To suck up all the water of the West River in a single gulp—ten thousand...
A fathom-deep abyss, exhausted to its very bottom; the footbridge is not Zhaozhou’s bridge. How can bright moon and clear wind compare?
Having again requested Yuan to ascend the seat at Yunju, he held up the incense and said: "How early we have met on this ground of awakening!"
"The stinking fowl-sleeve has now been cast off. If you wish to recognize the single mysterious phrase of Yunju, take care:
the donkey in the back garden is eating grass. He summoned the assembly and said, "This single offering of incense rises to heaven and scorches the earth!
Yuan said, "Today he does not wear it," and was immediately slapped by the Master, who then said, "Thank you for coming from a thousand li away to visit me, sir."
While conversing about the bamboo path on Mount Dongshan, [Yunmen] deeply lent him a dragon to ride out of the cave. "If you encounter a drought, it shall provide rain.
He threw down his staff and descended from his seat. As Yuan was bowing up, he asked, "Have you caught the dragon? Yunmen replied, "It is already here."
Wenyuan asked, "How do you ride? Zheng shook his hands as if dancing and walked away. Wenyuan clapped his hands and said, "Only this fellow has some merit.
Zhengyin Qingshan authored the *Zuoyin'an Shi* (Poems of the Drunken Reciter Hermitage) in thirty fascicles.
Titled *The Collected Works of Green Mountain*.
The eulogy says: "The shadowless tree, the seamless stupa—from where can they be depicted?
(Zhou Dunyi [disciple of the Chan Master Foyin Liaoyuan]).
Zhou Dunyi, courtesy name Maoshu, was a native of Chongling. Initially, he went to see Huitang Xin and inquired about the meaning of the "special transmission outside the teachings.
Xin instructed him, saying: "It is enough simply to attend to matters within your own house. Confucius said, 'If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening.
Ultimately, what constitutes that Way by which one may die in the evening? Yanzi did not change his countenance..."
Joy. What is it that you find joy in? Simply remain within this ultimate state; after a long time, there will naturally come a point of accord.
Furthermore, he consulted Chan Master Donglin Zong, who said: "Our Buddha taught that the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is precisely the true, the non-deceptive, and the sincere.

How great! 'The Great Origin (*qianyuan'), from which all things receive their beginning. It is by means of this real principle that the Way of Heaven undergoes transformation, so that each attains its own correctness."
Life and nature are precisely this true principle. The Way of Heaven, Earth, and the sages consists solely in utmost sincerity.
One must apply oneself to practical cultivation on the path until, all at once, there is a sudden and expansive awakening. One must not merely rely on understanding through words.

Furthermore, I have previously discussed with you in general terms the nature and principle-dharmadhātu, as well as the phenomenon-dharmadhātu, up to the point where principle and phenomena intersect.

Chè attained a clear and solitary realization. He subsequently composed the *Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Tàijí túshuō*), every word of which originated from the oral instructions of Donglin.

Later, while traveling to Mount Lu, he was delighted by its secluded beauty and built a dwelling there. At that time, Foyin Liaoyuan was residing at Luanxi; Changyi visited him, and they discussed the Way together.
Yi asked: "The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: 'That which is called nature is the mandate of Heaven; following nature is called the Way. As for the Chan school..."

Yangshan asked, "What is meant by 'no-mind is the Way'? Yunyan replied, "If you have doubts, seek another teacher. Yangshan said, "Seeking another is not impossible; but ultimately, what constitutes the Way? Yunyan replied, "The green mountains fill the eyes; look as you please. At these words, Yangshan attained sudden enlightenment. One day, seeing weeds growing before his window, he remarked, "This is exactly like my own state of mind. He then presented a verse to Yunyan, saying: "The weeds grow before the window, And I am sitting here alone. I do not know whose house this is, But it is certainly not mine. Yunyan approved, saying, "This is indeed the Way. Yangshan then prostrated himself. Later, when Yangshan was about to depart, Yunyan asked him, "Where are you going? Yangshan replied, "I am going to see Mazu. Yunyan said, "Mazu’s Dharma is not yet mature. You should go to Baizhang instead. Yangshan went to Baizhang and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Baizhang struck him with his staff and said, "Go wash your bowl! Yangshan was enlightened at that moment. He returned to Yunyan and told him what had happened. Yunyan said, "Baizhang’s staff has a handle on its end. Yangshan then bowed. When Yangshan later visited Huangbo, he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Huangbo struck him three times with his staff. Yangshan was again enlightened. He returned to Yunyan and related this. Yunyan said, "Huangbo’s staff has no handle on its end. Yangshan then bowed once more. This is recorded in the *Recorded Sayings of Yangshan*.

It is said that Yangshan’s realization was like a flash of lightning striking a mountain—sudden and total. His verse captures the essence of this experience: the ordinary weeds before the window are seen as the very manifestation of the Way, beyond the duality of self and other. This is the "no-mind" that Yunyan pointed toward. It is not a state of blank emptiness, but a vivid, unmediated presence where the mundane and the sacred are one. As the verse concludes, the seeker realizes that the "house" of awakening is everywhere, and there is no longer any distinction between the master and the disciple, or between the seeker and the sought. This is the ultimate expression of the "Way" as realized through the "no-mind" of Yangshan.
"Originally there was no delusion in the past, and now there is no awakening. When mind and object merge, the hidden depths open wide.

Grass grows deep outside the window, and pines stand by the path; all day long they leave one never tired of looking. He then invited Yuan to serve as the presiding master of the Green Pine Society, emulating the precedent of the White Lotus Society.
Zhiyi once sighed, saying: "This wondrous mind of mine was truly inspired by Huanglong and brought to full illumination by Fo [Yuan]."

Seal. Yet the principles of the *I Ching* are vast and penetrating; had it not been for Donglin’s [Zhang Zai] opening up what was obscured and sweeping away what hindered them, there would have been no way for them to be polished clear.
When the inner and outer were made transparently clear, Zhou Dunyi subsequently propagated and illuminated the Way and its Learning. Scholars called him Master Lianxi.
Cheng Hao, courtesy name Bochun, was a native of Luoyang. He passed the jinshi examination during the reign of Emperor Shenzong and took the study of the Way as his primary responsibility.
The world honored him as Master Mingdao. He once said: "Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the manifestation of radiance, at first I could not fathom its meaning.

Recently, however, upon examining the *Huayan he lun* (Compendium on the Avatamsaka), I have come to understand it clearly. To respond to conditions and shatter delusions is what is termed 'the light that dissolves the defilements of the mind.'"
Liberation is called "clarity" (*prabhā*); this is merely a metaphor for the luminosity of one's own mind.

Being able to transform and guide others, its light illuminates infinite worlds—all of which reside solely within the clarity of the sage’s single mind. For this reason, at the beginning of all sutras, the single matter of emitting light is first mentioned.
Whenever I see Buddhist disciples reading Buddhist scriptures with such dignity and solemnity, I say to those students: [this is the power of that inner light].
He said, "In general, when reading scriptures, one must necessarily act in this manner. Those who read books nowadays have already exhausted their vigor through indolence;
how can they maintain their mastery? One day, while passing by Dinglin Temple, I happened to see a group of monks entering the hall and moving about."
The ceremonial deportment as they paced was majestic; every sitting and rising conformed strictly to the pure regulations.
He then sighed, saying, "The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein. Hou Shiyu asked him about the passage from Mencius: "One must have a task, but not fixate on it;
do not forget it, and do not assist its growth. Hao cited a Chan (Zen) saying in response: "The mind does not exist, yet the task is not non-existent. Hou Shiyu should [have understood this].

Below, there was a provincial governor. He asked again about the similarities and differences between Confucianism and Buddhism. Hao replied, "In the place where you originally came from, are there still Confucians and Buddhists?
Hao’s younger brother, Cheng Yi—the Master of Yichuan—was once asked, "How does the Buddha speak of the matter of birth and death? Yi replied, "It is like bubbles on the water.
He was asked again, "Is the Buddha's teaching on the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) acceptable? Yi replied, "This matter is said to exist."
All these [questions] are difficult; one must attain realization through self-inspection. The Sage resolved it all in a single phrase, saying: "If you do not know life, how can you know death?
Youze, styled Dingfu, was an official serving as Censor-in-Chief. He studied under the two Cheng brothers and once sent a letter to Kaifu Ning.

The Chan Master asked: "The Confucianists adhere to the Five Constant Virtues, desiring that each fulfill its respective role. The Buddhists claim that the world is illusory and vain, seeking to lead people to transcend the ordinary and unite with the Dao.
Why is it that their essential aims differ and their applications diverge? Ning replied: "People are submerged in the dust of emotions and the net of craving;
they contemplate by day and dream by night, without a single moment's rest. One must exert force to sever these bonds and withdraw the dissipated mind. [Death...]

Only through such birth can one emerge. If one merely summarizes the similarities and differences, setting them forth clearly within the boundaries of their respective domains, then my practice is inwardly perfumed by affection while being outwardly stained by the Way;

how could this lead to creation? How could it lead to reversal? If its constancy is such that the mind naturally attunes itself and the Way naturally harmonizes, otherwise it is difficult to settle the matter through mere words and debate. Again, he asked: "In the creation of the Way, there must be an essential method."
Fafang said, "The Way does not reside in speaking or demonstrating; speaking and demonstrating are merely skillful means (*upāya*).
One must rely on oneself to know where to return. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not compatible with you. Lü Juren wrote a letter to ask Fanzhu, saying:
"Since Dingfu followed the teachings of the two Chengs and subsequently traveled among various Chan masters, [the relationship between] Confucianism and Buddhism..."
"There must be no obstruction between the two schools. May I ask why they differ?
Zu replied, "What is taught in the Buddhist scriptures has not been deeply examined even by the world's Confucian scholars. In years past, I once heard Yi-chuan say:
'That which I attack are the traces. But from where do these traces emerge? One must personally reach this state before one can discern their identity.'"
This is different. Many predecessors have never read Buddhist scriptures; therefore, they disparage them in such a manner.
Yet the very points with which they seek to refute Buddhism are precisely those that the Buddhist scriptures themselves do not accept.
Xie Liangze, courtesy name Xian Dao, was a native of Shangcai. Together with You Zu, Yang Shi, and Lü Dalin, he was among the disciples of the Two Chengs and was known as one of the Four Masters.
When asked how to apply effort in the pursuit of benevolence (*ren*), Liangze replied: "One can also achieve it by working on the aspects of *zēngzǐ*—his countenance, appearance, and speech.
Regarding "speech" (*cíqì*), it is similar to what the Buddha referred to as *vāg-vijñapti* (verbal manifestation).
"It flows forth from within the heart. Nowadays, when people utter a single 'ye' (a greeting), it does not emerge from the heart;

this is precisely a lack of benevolence (*ren*). It is a failure to recognize pain and itching. At that time, Lü Dazhong did not fully comprehend the character for benevolence. Zuo said, "The people of the world speak of benevolence..."
If you merely cling to "love," how can you perceive "benevolence" (*ren*)? It is simply like applying effort; such effort approaches the power of benevolence.
What does the practice of benevolence have to do with love? Zhong Qili stood up and said, "Your explanation of the character for 'benevolence' is exactly like a venerable master discussing Chan."

Yang Shi, styled Zhongli, studied under the two Cheng brothers and inherited their transmission of the teachings of the Yellow River and Luo River. He was posthumously titled Master Guishan. He once remarked:
"When Wei Sheng Gao begged for vinegar to give to others, Confucius considered it improper. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states that 'the straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment.
When it comes to this point, there is truly no difference between the principles of Confucianism and Buddhism. Yang Shi was a friend of the Chan Master Donglin Zong.

"Excellent. Zong said, "Although your study of Chan is lofty, you have yet to attain anything regarding Confucianism and Daoism. Zong continued, "As for the essential points of Confucianism and Daoism, you remember some fragments.
But tell me, when it is said that 'the gentleman finds self-satisfaction in whatever he enters,' what is it that he attains? At this, [Zhaozhou] remained silent.
Once, while discussing the chapter on "Form and Color as the Nature of Heaven," Zong remarked, "This is identical to the Buddhist concept of form-emptiness (*rūpa-śūnyatā*)."
