How does this discourse differ from that? One day he visited the home of Jian Qilu. When Qilu asked about the *Yi* (the Book of Changes), [Zhang] took a piece of paper and drew a circle upon it, saying, "This is precisely the *Yi*.
He also composed a quatrain with Chen Yingzhong, which says: "If one knows the *Yi* exists before the lines are drawn, only then does one truly know the *Yi*.
If one seeks the profound within the calendar, I fear it is not yet profound. With white hair as disheveled as this, what have I accomplished? The bookworm merely exhausts itself in vain."
From the *Laoqing bian*: It is also said: "Filling every pool, advancing daily—when will it ever cease? Only upon reaching the sea can the myriad streams find rest.
I fear that Daomadao’s madness has not yet ceased; sitting in stillness, he still races about, craving his own reflection in the mirror."
The eulogy states: "Zanxi (Zhang Zai) opened the transmission of the Yi and Luo schools; yet if one examines its origins, they truly derive from Foyin (Zhaozhou).
Huanglong’s pointing out the core of the *Taiji tu* (Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate) was also obtained from Donglin.

As for the two Cheng brothers, there were none among teacher and disciple who did not seek verification within the Chan school. Thus, what has the Buddha-dharma ever done to harm Confucianism, that the Confucians would bear to act [as they have]?"
"Is this not like the 'go' spear brought into the inner chamber? Excellent indeed! Master I-chuan’s words say: 'That which I attack are the traces.
Yet from where do these traces emerge? If one understands this, one may discuss with them the unified principle of the ultimate purport of Confucianism and Buddhism."
Dai Daochun (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Lingyuan Weiqing).

Dai Daochun, whose courtesy name was Fuzhong, served as the Vice Director of the Imperial Household. One day, after consulting with and receiving instruction from Lingyuan Weiqing, he attained realization and presented this verse:
"At the source of the profound and dark void, where the total mechanism is complete, A single flower of mind reveals the pattern of the seal. I know how many..."
In a previous life, he had made offerings [to the Buddha]. From time to time, he would smile, causing clouds of fragrance to stir.
Gao Shize (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Fuyong Daokai):
Gao Shize, courtesy name Zhongyi, style name Wugong, served as a Regional Commander (Jiedushi) and governed Wenzhou. He visited Fuyong Dao...
Kai. One day, he suddenly attained the subtle and profound mystery. He presented this verse: "Letting go at the precipice, I move freely in all directions;

The great earth and empty space are naturally level and plain. Illuminating the ravines and shining upon the cliffs without borrowing the moon— At the head of my hermitage, there is another screen of light."
The combined eulogy states: The mind-flower seals the text; empty space is level and vast. Are Dongshan and Linji one or two?
Chen Guan (Dharma heir of Chan Master Linyuan Weiqing):
Chen Guan, courtesy name Yingzhong, style name Liaoweng, also known as the Huayan Layman. He was upright and incorruptible in his service at court.

He possessed the wind and spirit of the ancients. He devoted his attention to the inner scriptures and their discourses, yet he alone excelled in the study of Chan, though he had not yet attained great illumination.

Regarding the causes and conditions of the Chan school, he mostly relied on intellectual interpretation; he was particularly fond of the Recorded Sayings of Master Nan, which he annotated exhaustively.
Only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the "Rubbing the Back of the Clay Man" commentary remained unannotated. He once said to others: "There must certainly be a source for these."
However, there was no one who knew this. As the proverb says: "Before the face of a person of great wisdom, there is a three-foot darkness. This is indeed not false.

Later, he went to visit Lingyuan Weiqing, persisting in his reliance on what he had heard and seen in order to seek understanding. Weiqing asked, "Why do you take your own interpretations as the fundamental principle?

He replied, "I have happened upon a resonance with the jade-like clarity [of the teachings]. Thereupon, he attained awakening and sent a verse to Weiqing, saying: "In the study hall, sitting motionless, the myriad complexities come to rest."
The sun is warm, the breeze gentle, and the vegetation lush. Who recognizes the great matter at the end of two thousand years? It resides right now within the very eyes.
Liu Anshi, whose courtesy name was Qizhi and style name Yuancheng, studied under Sima Guang. He once said: "The old gentleman..."
He was profoundly versed in the Buddha-dharma, yet he simply did not speak of it. He once said: "The words of Confucius and the Buddha are like the beginning and the end of one another.
Confucius spoke of 'having no arbitrary conceptions, no compulsions, no fixations, and no self'; the Buddha spoke of 'no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
Their words follow such a sequence that they seem as if uttered by a single person; it is only that Confucius..."
The Three Bonds and Five Constants constitute the Way; thus, the teaching that "form is emptiness and emptiness is form" subtly opens its beginning, allowing people to realize it for themselves.

The mind of Confucius is the mind of the Buddha. If there were no Three Bonds and Five Constants in the world, there would be chaos and disorder, and humanity would be left with nothing but the sound of their own dying breaths—would this be the mind of the Buddha? Therefore, the minds of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism are all one.
First, the methods employed at the gate and in the courtyard differ. He once said to his disciple Ma Yongqing:
"The single character 'Chan' (meditation) also possesses this principle within the Six Classics. However, since the Buddha-dharma had declined, everyone clung to external forms and appearances.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly to the human mind, asserting that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. Those of superior capacity and keen intelligence mostly took delight in this teaching. Thus...
The Way of Chan flourished greatly. Had he not come, the Buddha-dharma would have perished long ago.

Although my relocation to the south was during a time when I derived strength from the most urgent matters of our Confucian tradition, it cannot be said that I did not derive strength from this matter as well.
Is there any worldly affair greater than life and death? Yet this matter alone is of one single flavor; it concerns nothing other than life and death.
With such a perspective, one regards nobility and meanness, as well as misfortune and fortune, with lightness. Furthermore, he once took the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and showed it to Yongqing, saying:
"The Great Being Avalokiteśvara perfumes his hearing until it becomes pure hearing; the six sense-faculties are dissolved and return to being identical with sound-hearing.
This can cause sentient beings, when facing imminent harm, to find that their weapons are like slicing through water or blowing upon light—their nature remains unshakable."

It is like cutting through water or blowing across light; the nature of water and fire remains unshaken. Similarly, even when encountering harm, one's own nature remains profoundly still—this is the power of Avalokiteśvara’s fearlessness.
It is further said: "When the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of hearing and seeing turn back into themselves, one leaves behind all sensory dust and delusions.
This enables sentient beings so that they cannot be bound by fetters, shackles, or manacles. Thus it is called "Attaining Freedom from Obstruction."
Regarding the power of fearlessness: shackles and chains cannot cause harm. My friend, you may use this principle to instruct others, so that future generations do not come to slander the Buddha.
The Eulogy says: Liaoweng, Liaoweng!
You took intellectual understanding as your primary tenet. Had it not been for Lingyuan’s piercing revelation, you would have spent your entire life wandering in madness.
The "Head in the Mirror.
Furthermore, Li Bingshan’s *Mingdao ji* states: Liu Yuancheng said that Sima Guang was extremely proficient in Buddhist principles, yet he simply did not speak of them.
The reason for this was that he wished to preserve the status of Confucius. I, however, maintain that the Buddhist scriptures...
As for those subtle, profound, and hidden marvels that harmonize perfectly with the secular classics, it is only the Confucian scholars of the world who can bring them forth.

Rather than keeping them secret and remaining silent, it would be better to exert every effort to elucidate them from their original source of unity, so that all under heaven and throughout all ages may know that within the Six Classics there is Chan, and that our Sage has already been the Buddha. As for this...
"Is the territory of Confucius not also vast? This argument by Bing Shan is the most sublime; no one has been able to equal it.
Su Che (the Dharma heir of Chan Master Shun of Hongzhou):
Su Che, courtesy name Ziyou, style name Yingbin. He held successive offices including Hanlin Academician and Vice President of the Department of State Affairs. Foyin...

While staying at Mount Jinshan, Ché composed a verse and offered it, saying: "Coarse sand is offered to the Buddha, and the Buddha joyfully accepts; Strange rocks are presented to the Sangha, and the Sangha does not disdain them.
I have come from afar empty-handed—do you still require more? There is nothing further with which to add. Yin replied: "Empty hands bring it forth, yet it is difficult to let go;
The Three Sages and Ten Saints gather their heads to gaze upon it. Only such an offering as this can be truly enjoyed. [He added: "Wood..."
Even the "mare and the clay ox" were pleased. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, Zhe was exiled to Gaoyang. There he met Huangbo Quan at Chengsi Temple.
Quan gazed at him intently and said, "You are serene and wise. If you devote yourself to the school of the patriarchs, why should you fear that you will not accomplish this Way?"
Zhe took note of this and subsequently practiced seated meditation. He repeatedly sought resolution from Quan, but found no accord. Later, he learned that Cui Cong resided at Shousheng Temple;
Zhe went there to inquire about this matter. Cong did not answer. Zhe questioned him again, whereupon Cong said slowly, "Yuanzhao never spoke of the Way to others;
I, too, have nothing with which to speak to you. At this, Zhe attained the meaning beyond words. He once also consulted [him further].
Xinfa was with Master Shun of Hongzhou. Shun showed him the karmic conditions of "pinching the nose. At that moment, Zhe attained great enlightenment and presented a verse, saying:
"In middle age I heard the Way and discerned right from wrong; By chance I met the old master, Shun. Pinching the nose, I directly entered the true countenance;
Shaking my head, I will not accept other tongs or hammers. Withered cane and tattered robes—what business do you have? White wine and green..."
"Who am I? On the eastern veranda, the waning moon rises; a cup of ambrosia, as smooth as molasses. The commentary says:
"The sound of the stream and the color of the mountains, white wine and green salt—it is difficult to say who is the elder brother and who is the younger."
Hu An-guo (a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Shangfeng Xiù).
Hu An-guo, courtesy name Kanghou, was a native of Chong’an. He passed the jinshi examination during the Shaosheng era and served successively as a Reminder (Gishizhong).

From his youth, he possessed a disposition inclined toward transcending the mundane. He studied with great diligence and practiced with vigor, taking the sages as his model. After long training under Shang...

Feng Xiu attained the meaning beyond words. During the Chongning era, while traveling to Yaoshan, he encountered a Chan practitioner who cited the story of Nanquan killing the cat and asked Anguo about it.
Anguo replied with a verse: "In hand, he holds the pivot of life and death, encompassing heaven and earth; His arrangements, whether expansive or restrictive, depend on the moment.
The jade hall’s rabbit and horse are not dragon-elephants; In his grand function, majestic and imposing, they know nothing at all. Furthermore:
A letter sent from Fengzhou says: "Mount Zhurong resembles the heavens of Ducheng; the ten thousand ages of rivers and mountains are before one's eyes.
One must believe that Sīxin has never truly died; last night the autumn moon was once again full. Feng Dangshi, in his later years, took a fond interest in Buddhism.
He once sent a letter to An-guo saying: "The songs and dances of Bingzhou are exquisite and beautiful; I have closed my eyes and not looked at them for days."
"To discuss Chan is considered superior. An Guo said, "If it is as you argue, you have not yet grasped the principle of Chan.
To close one's eyes and refuse to look is already one kōan."
The Eulogy says: As the master within the realm of consciousness, he received the transmission outside the teachings. His death-mind did not die; his state of peace remained ever-abiding.
Fan Chong (Dharma heir of Chan Master Yantong Min). Fan Chong, courtesy name Qiantu, also known as Zhixu.
Having served in the Han-yuan (Imperial Academy), he was appointed to govern Yuzhang. On his way there, he passed by Yantong and went to pay his respects to Min.
After the tea was finished, the Chan Master said, "In what meritorious karma did I engage in past lives that I have now been born into this class of purple-robed officials?
I feel quite far removed from this matter. Min called out, "Director of the Imperial Library! Chong responded with an assent. Min said, "How could there be any distance?
Chong leaped up in joy and said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. Min replied, "It is four stages' journey from here to Hongdu. Chong stood still for a moment, lost in thought.
Min said, "If you see it, you have already seen it; if you attempt to think about it, you are immediately mistaken.
Chong was suddenly enlightened.

When the Imperial Commissioner Wu Juhou returned to Zhongling with his insignia of office, he went to visit Min and said, "I was on my way to the provincial examinations when I passed through Zhao..."
At the state barrier, Min asked the former resident, Elder Ne, about the matter of passing through the barrier. Ne said, "Just go and serve as an official.
More than fifty years have passed since then. Min asked, "Have you attained clear understanding?

Ne replied, "I have passed through this eight times, always keeping this thought in mind, yet I am still not entirely free and easy. Min handed him a fan and said, "Please use this fan. Wu then waved it.
Xuefeng Fanchan held up a fan. Xuanmi said, "Is there anything here that is not refreshing? Wuzhuo suddenly attained realization and said, "I ask for the final word.
Xuanmi waved the fan twice. Wuzhuo said, "Intimate! Intimate! Xuanmi said, "The tongue of a barbarian extends three thousand miles."
The Imperial Censor Peng Rulin had personally transcribed the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra as an offering to Min. Min picked it up and said, "This is the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra;
which one is the Censor's sūtra? Peng replied, "This was written by me with my own hand. Min said, "What you have written are merely characters; which one is [the sūtra]?"
Regarding this sutra, Lin said, "It cannot be avoided. [The other] asked, "Is it that one manifests in the body of a government official to preach the Dharma?
Lin said, "Everyone has their share. [The other] said, "Do not slander the sutra. [Lin] asked, "How is it so? Min held up the sutra and showed it to him.
Lin clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "Ka! Min said, "You say again that it is 'not to be attained'. Lin prostrated himself.
Grand Councilor Lu Hang was with Min by the brazier; Hang asked, "There is no need to laboriously bring up the karmic conditions of various masters; let us go directly..."
"Cut off a single phrase; I beg the Master to point it out. Min responded with a stern voice and a gesture, saying, "Look at the fire!

Heng hurriedly pulled back his robe and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He thanked him, saying, "Clearly, the Buddha-dharma is not so much as this. Min shouted, "Put it down! Heng replied, "Yes, yes."
Du Xiang, the Left Minister, asked Cuiyan Min: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; how can one arrive at it?
Min said, "The whole body enters the mass of fire. Du Xiang asked, "Ultimately, how does one understand it? Min said, "Go straight on."
Fengxiang hesitated. Min said, "Would you like another cup of tea? Fengxiang replied, "There is no need. Min asked, "Why do you not understand anything?
Fengxiang attained the essential meaning and said, "I see now that it was originally far too near. Min said, "A hundred thousand and eight thousand [miles].
Fengxiang then composed a verse: "The inconceivable is a great mass of fire; going thus, one does not leave this very place. Min said, "Ei! You still have this..."
Xiang said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. Min said, "Go right away like this; the cauldron is cast of iron.
Xiang bowed his head in thanks.
The collective eulogy says: "A pity that five red-tailed carp were pickled to death inside the *yuantong* (Universal Penetration) pickle jar.

Xu Fu (a Dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin), the State Councilor Xu Fu, styled Shichuan and titled Donghu Jushi (East Lake Layman), would frequently attend his father, Dragon Diagram Official Xu Xi, on visits to [the patriarchs].

Fachang and Lingyuan engaged in philosophical discourse all day long, yet Fuxian listened to them with an air of indifference. Only after Fachang passed away did Fuxian regard him with awe during their casual conversation;
it was then that he first developed deep faith in this Way. Later, while observing the mourning period for his father, he felt that there was nothing by which he could repay his debt of gratitude.
Wangji requested Master Yuanzhixiao to preach the Dharma. After Yuanzhixiao had ascended the seat and finished the question-and-answer session, he said:
"Good sirs, it is like Longtu reading ten thousand scrolls of books; it is like water being passed from one vessel to another, not a single drop left behind.
But tell me, where does this habitually reside? Now, after consciousness has been relinquished, where does this one who possessed those ten thousand scrolls of books go?"
"Where should it be placed? When Fu heard this, he felt a sudden sense of liberation and said, "I have no further regrets.
Yuan descended from his seat and asked, "Scholar, what did you just see that you speak thus?
Fu replied, "If there were anything seen, I would be failing the Master. Yuan said, "In that case, I am not your equal. Fu replied, "The Master is..."
"What is the movement of the mind? Yuan laughed heartily. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, he served as a Ministerial Secretary (Shangshu Waibang).

Together with fellow officials of like mind, he hung his alms bowl in Zemo Hall at Tianning Temple and applied himself diligently to the study of Yuanwu Keqin. Yuanwu also rejoiced in his transcendent realization.
One day, [Yuan] went to the office of the Record Keeper and pointed to Yuanwu’s crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), saying, "The feet of this old fellow..."
Fuyou was still standing with his feet not touching the ground. Wuzu turned his face toward him and said, "How could the turtle ever have escaped from the jar?
Fuyou looked down and said, "I am glad that this old man’s feet are now planted on the ground. Wuzu said, "Do not slander him. Fuyou then withdrew and departed.
The Eulogy says: Xū Shīchuān realized the essential meaning under Língyuán, yet he still had his alms bowl hanging at Yuánwù’s gate;
his feet had not yet truly touched the ground.
Zhào Lìjīn (a dharma successor of Cíqín Chánshī).
The Marquis of the Commandery, Zhao Lingjin, styled Biaozhi and surnamed Chaoran, was initially appointed to Nan’gang, where he frequently associated with Chan monks.

He occasionally converted his official hall into a chamber for Moke (Wang Wei). It happened that Yuanwu was residing at Oufu; Lingjin went there to seek instruction and joyfully submitted himself to his guidance.
Yuanwu did not grant him any concessions, so Lingjin earnestly entreated him, saying: "Regarding this matter, one must desire to attain it; it requires nothing less than..."
It is only upon dying once that one attains this; it is a matter of profound, silent realization. He once wrote a brief account himself, saying: "My house was poor and met with robbery;
who knew that nothing remained? The empty room was unoccupied; how many times did the thieves come and beat it? Having realized this, he entrusted me with the instruction to provide protection.
He went to pay his respects to Daohui. Upon hearing of his arrival, Daohui ordered the drum to be beaten to summon him into the room.

As Jinxiong approached with incense in his sleeves, Daohui said, "The story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl—how do you understand it? Jinxiong replied, "What kind of bowl are you looking for? and swept his sleeves, walking out.
Daohui rose and grabbed him by the collar, saying, "The ancients attained enlightenment right here; why have you not attained it? Just as Jinxiong was about to respond, Daohui struck him.

He said, "What bowl are you going to seek? Jinqian replied, "Only then can this old fellow begin to attain awakening. He once presented a dharma discourse, saying: "When Caoshan took his leave of Wuben, he asked, 'Where are you going?
[Wuben] said, 'I am going to the place of non-change. [Caoshan] asked, 'In a place of non-alteration, how could there be going?
[Wuben] said, 'Going itself does not alter. Unless one’s feet tread upon the solid ground, how could one ever penetrate through to the bottom?"
It is thus. How could it be measured by the mechanisms of language or the workings of thought?

It is because one has trodden the path to its deepest extremity, reaching a state where there is no longer any leakage, that one cannot be confined within the net of conceptualization. Those who study the Way should resolve their will to transcend the physical form.
Unifying birth and death, blending past and present, and severing coming and going—one must necessarily reach for the higher stream and attain mastery.
One must penetrate the profound and mysterious gateway of ultimate truth and reality to settle one's own self, becoming stripped bare, pure, and stainless.

Without even a hair’s breadth of conceptual thought falling into worldly conditions, one’s mind should directly become like withered wood or rotten stumps, like a great dead man without the slightest breath; in every moment of mind, there is nothing.
Know that every thought-moment is non-abiding; even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not alter it.

Thus, one can cause flowers to bloom upon withered wood, manifesting great potential and giving rise to great function, mobilizing compassion and pity. This is the function of no-effort and the action of no-activity;
how could it fall into the categories of gain and loss, right and wrong? To allow even a single hair’s breadth of attachment is to encounter resistance within the realm of birth and death.

If one has not yet crossed over oneself, how can one deliver others? The Great Being Vimalakīrti did not dwell in the Golden Grain Heaven, but resided in wine shops and brothels to perform the great Buddha-work of liberation. Layman Pang was a response-body of the stage of succession;
he did not dwell in Tuṣita Heaven, but cast aside precious jewels to weave bamboo sieves by the Han River and engage in the dynamic exchange of giving and taking with the Great Master. This passage—
From the highest literary forms down, none are otherwise; one must necessarily exercise "a drop of water and a drop of frost," regardless of whether one is in the court or the countryside.
Through tempering and refining, like Cao Shan, Mañjuśrī (Mojie), and Old Pang, one may then not let fall one’s compassionate vows—is this not indeed fitting?
As for all other worldly entanglements in the human realm, how could such dust and grime be worth keeping in one’s breast?
The eulogy says: "With a mind empty, I dare ask: how can one transcend? Since it is an empty room, there is no person; whom would you call a thief?
When the thief comes seeking to strike, who is it again?"
Li Mīxùn (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Kèqín).

Li Mīxùn was a Court Gentleman (Shìláng) and styled himself the Lay Practitioner Pǔxiàn. In his youth, he studied with such speed that he could read five lines of text simultaneously. At the age of eighteen, he passed the provincial examination;
subsequently, he attained the jinshi degree in the capital and rapidly ascended through high and important offices. By the age of twenty-eight, he served as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū).

Sharen went to attend Yuanwu. One day, returning from his morning court duties, he reached Tianjin Bridge when his horse bolted. Suddenly, he attained realization, and sweat poured from his entire body.

He went straight to Tianning Monastery; just as he arrived, Yuanwu happened to be coming out the gate. Seeing him from afar, Yuanwu called out, "Layman, congratulations! Your great matter is now finished.
Sharen replied with a stern voice, "Why are you seeing double, Master? Yuanwu gave a shout, and Sharen also shouted.
Thereupon, his spiritual acumen was swift and sharp; whenever he engaged in dialogue regarding awakening, he never yielded when the moment was right.

When he was appointed to the Ministry of Personnel, still in the prime of his life, he suddenly requested to resign from his salary and rank to return to Lianjiang in Min. There he built a hermitage to enjoy himself. One day, he manifested a slight ailment.
Having finished bathing in hot water, he sat cross-legged and composed this verse: "In vain have I spoken of Mupohu since ancient times; today it is clearly revealed.
Space has toppled Mount Sumeru—what need is there to speak of the path beyond? He then threw down his brush and passed away.
The commentary says: To see a horse leap and attain realization is not that the Master’s eyes are dim; rather, it is the Minister’s eyes that are dim.
Even if one were to topple Mount Sumeru, it would still be like gold dust in the eye.
Zhang Jun (the Dharma heir of Chan Master Kegin):

Zhang Wei Gong Jun, courtesy name De-yuan, was the father of Nanxuan. He served as the Right Vice President of the Council of State and concurrently presided over the Secretariat for Military Affairs.
He once inquired about the Way from Yuanwu, who said: "Yantou said, 'To reject external objects is superior; to pursue external objects is inferior.'"
"If one can turn swiftly upon objects, all things will stand downwind. He further showed a verse, saying:
"Gathering back the light and withdrawing the colors, trust in the true nature; every affair is perfectly accomplished, every object is new. If there is a mind within, there are still objects;

how then could one move a step out through the thoroughfare? Xun bowed in submission and offered a verse, saying: "The single transmission outside the teachings is the pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Originally..."
Coming, there is neither awakening nor delusion; when drifting clouds have dispersed, the blue sky remains. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. The eulogy states:
Master Guoyi said, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something generals or ministers can accomplish.
Zhang De-yuan served as both general and minister, yet he also heard the teaching of the Single Transmission. This is no small matter for a great man.
"What is that? Nevertheless, as for this one point that transcends all, have you ever even dreamed of it?
Feng Jie (Chan Master Qingyuan Foyan, successor to Chan Master Qingyuan).
Feng Jie, courtesy name Jichuan, was a native of Suining. In his prime, he traveled extensively to study under various masters before finally relying on Foyan Yuan. One day, together with...
As Yan was walking through the Dharma Hall, he happened upon a youth hurrying across the courtyard. The youth chanted: "Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed.
Yan patted the youth on the back and said, "Excellent! Thereupon, the youth attained realization. In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, Yan was appointed as a Grand Secretary.
It happened that Dahui was about to ascend the hall at Mingqing Temple; when Dahui descended from the seat, Yan pulled him aside and said, "Every time you speak to the scholar-officials..."
The Master said, "Previously you said, 'I will certainly never become such a creature. Why then have you failed today?
Huì replied, "The entire earth is this Venerable Gǎo; where do you see him? As Jí was about to respond, Huì struck him with his palm and said, "It is I who have brought this upon myself.
At that moment, the assembly turned pale with alarm. Jí laughed loudly and said, "The Elder and I..."

The Buddhist Dharma was thus encountered. After a month had passed, [Hui] specifically requested alms and sat for the summer retreat. Jingshan inscribed his quarters with the name "The Unmoving Pavilion. One day, Hui ascended the seat and raised the following case:
Yaoshan asked Shitou, "I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.
However, I have heard that in the South there is the direct pointing to the human mind, whereby one sees one's nature and attains Buddhahood; this I truly do not yet understand. I humbly hope—"
The Compassionate One gave him instruction, saying: "To say 'it is so' is not permissible; to say 'it is not so' is not permissible;
to say 'it is both so and not so' is entirely not permissible. What will you do? Shanshan was at a loss for a response. The Master said:
"Your karmic affinity does not lie here. You should go to Jiangxi to see the Great Master Ma. When Shanshan arrived at Mazu’s place, he asked the same question as before. Mazu said: "There is."
At times, Master Yaoshan taught him by raising his eyebrows and blinking; at other times, he did not teach him by raising his eyebrows and blinking.

At times, that which was taught by raising the eyebrows and blinking was correct; at other times, that which was taught by raising the eyebrows and blinking was incorrect. Thereupon, Shanshan attained great enlightenment.
After Huì had finished his verse, Jí went with him to the Abbot’s quarters and said, “I have understood the kōan that the Master just presented.
The Master asked, “How do you understand it? Jí replied, “It is not so; *sulu svāhā*. It is not not-so; *sili svāhā*. It is neither so nor not-so; *sulu*.”
*Svāhā*. The Seal of Wisdom is expressed in verse as follows: The Sanskrit and the Chinese are unified into one. "Alas!

Worldly person, having attained this samādhi, you shall later come to know it. Later, he served as the Prefect of Qiongzhou; wherever he went, he remained in tranquil seclusion without weariness. He once composed a verse of self-praise:
"In the intervals between public duties, I delight in sitting in meditation; rarely have I ever let my side touch the bed. Although I appear in this world..."

The minister’s countenance remained serene; his fame as a venerable elder spread throughout the four seas. In the autumn of the twenty-third year, he informed his close acquaintances in advance that he would pass away on the third day of the tenth month.
On that day, he ordered a high seat to be set up in the rear hall and received visitors as he had done in his usual manner.

Around the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he descended the steps and gazed toward the palace. With solemn prostrations, he requested that the Commissioner of the Canal Administration take charge of the affairs of Qiong.

Donning his monastic robes and stepping onto the high seat, he exhorted the officials, clergy, and laity: "Each of you should turn toward the Way, support the teachings, and raise the banner of the Dharma.
The Commissioner of the Canal Administration entreated him, saying: "The Administrator’s coming and going are as free as this; why not leave behind a verse to commemorate what we have rarely heard?"
Jie opened his eyes wide, sought out a brush, and wrote: "The third day of the first month, the eleventh; the middle ninth, the seventh of the last—these are the words of the old man.

When the turtle’s eyes turn red, [the time has come]. Having finished writing, he took up his staff, rested it upon his knee, and passed away. Jie had once served as the abbot of famous monasteries since the Jianyan era.
Many of the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*) were destroyed by warfare; [the Emperor] provided stipends to have them reprinted, totaling one hundred twenty-eight collections.
There is a verse that says: "I am afflicted by the habit of craving; I regard wealth as equal to empty space. I make no calculations for descendants, nor do I seek the pleasures of sound and color."
The monthly stipend I receive shall be used solely to redeem these Buddhist scriptures, so that all who read them may enter the state of Nirvana without remainder.
Even the Buddhas of antiquity abandoned their entire bodies for the sake of a half-verse; therefore, I do not begrudge my wealth in order to reveal the path to those wandering in delusion.
I ask those who cherish wealth: though they spend their days calculating every *zhi* and *zhu*, when the day of impermanence suddenly arrives, can they truly escape birth and death?
The commentary says: Feng Jichuan’s "Immovable Pavilion" is like a thousand-fathom snow-capped peak and a ten-thousand-fathom cold pool.
*Ei!* (A cry of realization). From what source did Foyan obtain this meager livelihood? He has utterly ruined the old man of Jing Mountain.
The *Wangsheng ji* (Anthology on Rebirth) states: When Feng Jie first sought the Way in the Zen forests, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism in his later years.

He composed the *Xifang wen* (Text for the Western Paradise) and the *Mítuó chanyi* (Repentance Ritual for Amitābha). Initially serving as the military governor of Lunan, he led both monastics and laypeople in holding "mindfulness assemblies" (*xièniàn huì*) dedicated to the Original Teacher of the Lotus Pond [Amitābha].
The eulogy says: According to the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), the Master first studied under Longmen Yuan and subsequently under Miaoxi. Each...
There was one who attained realization; at the time of his death, he set a specific date, ascended the seat, took up his staff, pressed it against his knees, and passed away.
His mastery and magnificence were truly like those of the great patriarchs of the Zen school. Yet, he never spoke of rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Why is this? It is simply because the authors of these works differ in the principles they establish as their primary gates, each following what they themselves value most.

Since those who emphasize the direct pointing to the human mind ought naturally to focus exclusively on clarifying the ground of the mind while omitting the Pure Land—as is the case with Huaiyu’s *Jintai ji*, Zongmi’s *Zuiji yuanzhao lu*, and the *Lianru biaoming lu*, none of which include such records—it follows that they do so.

This passage specifically points back to the Pure Land. Thus, it details his lifelong practice of *nien-fo*, his rebirth at the end of his life, and his realization of the nature of mind with sovereign ease.
This is as the saying goes: "Once one has attained the vision of Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
It is analogous to how Yan Hui was categorized among those of "exemplary conduct" (*xing-de*) due to his profound virtue, even though he did not participate in governance.

Regarding this matter: if one values talent above all else, then even Yanzi possessed the capacity of a royal minister yet did not speak of his own virtuous conduct; this too is simply because their respective domains differ.
Those engaged in the practice of pure karma should wish for firm faith and remain free from delusion.

Wang Gu, whose courtesy name was Minzhong, served as a Grand Secretary (Shilang). He had studied under Huanglong Huaitang, Cuiyan, and Yangqi, and further attained realization in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Wang Gu’s ancestors for seven generations had abstained from killing and were fond of releasing captive creatures;

however, upon reaching Wang Gu himself, he personally gave rise to doubts regarding these minor dharmas and said to Xiaofahua: "If one does not kill and does not release, entrust everything to the state of no-mind."
Hualei raised his voice and said, "You are greatly mistaken. How can you interpret this as an understanding of emptiness? Even the pillar standing before us has no mind of its own;

how could several such pillars save even a single suffering sentient being in this world? In ancient times, when [the Master] first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he released one million living beings.
Throughout his life, he was diligent and never ceased counting his prayer beads while reciting the Buddha’s name."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he constantly visualized the Western Pure Land. A monk traveling to the Pure Land in a spiritual journey saw Gu and Ge Fan there.
(Zhang Jiucheng, dharma successor of Chan Master Miaoxi Zonggao.)
Zhang Jiucheng, styled Zishao, was a native of Qiantang. When he was young, his father had books piled up beside him while instructing a guest to take an examination.

Jiucheng set down his scroll, adjusted his robes with reverence, and said, "The refined and the coarse, the fundamental and the derivative, are originally not two different things. Do not say that what is written on paper is insufficient;
much of it involves learning below and attaining above. I dare to take the sages and worthies as my model. The elders were struck with amazement and sighed, saying, "Truly extraordinary!"

He was a youth. At fourteen, he entered the local school (*junxiang*). He would remain shut in his room all day long; whether the cold made the glue crack or the heat melted the gold, he never crossed the threshold of his door.
Neighboring students peered through cracks and saw him sitting upright with knees drawn up, facing a large stack of volumes as if conversing with the divine.
They were all struck with awe and came to revere him as their teacher. Later, he traveled to the capital to study under Yang Shi of Gui Shan.
Nevertheless, his heart yearned for renowned scholars such as Yang Wengong and Lü Weizhong, whose refined and subtle accomplishments all originated from the study of Chan.
Thereupon, he went to visit Baoyin Chuming to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way. Chuming said, "In this matter, one must simply not abandon it moment by moment.
After a long time of pure cultivation, when the proper season arrives, realization will naturally occur. He then cited Zhao...
Regarding the "Pine Tree" kōan from the State (Zhou): Cheng was instructed to reflect upon it constantly. After a long time, he had no realization.
He took his leave to visit Chan Master Qingcheng of Shanquan. Cheng asked, "Is it not true that everyone has their share [of this matter], and that each person attains full perfection?
Qing replied, "Indeed. Cheng said, "Why is it that I have no point of entry? Qing took out a rosary from his sleeve and showed it to him, asking, "Whose is this? Cheng looked down.
Yang Wudui said, "If it is yours, then take it. As soon as one engages in thought, it is no longer yours. Cheng was struck with awe.
Not long after, while staying at the residence of the Su family, he went to the latrine one night.

While reflecting on the words, "The heart of compassion is the sprout of benevolence," he suddenly heard the croaking of frogs. He attained a sudden and profound realization, and unconsciously exclaimed: "It is like this..."

"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? [The Master replied,] "The cypress tree in the courtyard. [Huangbo] suddenly burst into laughter; sweat poured down his body. He composed a verse, saying:
"A single frog croaking on a moonlit spring night— It shatters heaven and earth, making all one family.

At such a moment as this, who can understand? Only Xuansha knows the ache in his feet at the mountain pass. In the early years of the Xiangxing era, he passed the imperial examination as the top graduate (Zhuangyuan) and was granted office.

He served as the Acting Assistant Administrator of the Army Garrison of the Eastern Command and was subsequently promoted to Court Historian. Not long after, he was appointed Junior Minister of the Imperial Clan Registry concurrently serving as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.

Following the resignation of Chancellor Zhao Ding, Cheng submitted a second petition to request his own departure from office. In the autumn of the year Ding-si (1167), Dahui Zonggao was preaching the Dharma at Mount Jing;
Cheng read his *Essentials of Discourse* and sighed, saying, "I now know there are those who uphold the School of the Patriarchs; it is my regret that I did not meet him sooner."

He then went to pay his respects. One day, he asked about the meaning of "investigating things" (*gewu*). Wuxian said, "You only know there is 'investigating things,' but you do not know there is 'things being investigated' (*wuge*).
Upon hearing this, Cheng suddenly grasped the subtle essence of the teaching. He inscribed these words on the wall: "Zishao investigates things; Miaoxi [Wuxian] has things investigated.
If you wish to recognize the single thread, it is two times five hundred. From that time on, he engaged in inquiry and practice, and attained the Dharma for himself.

He was titled the Layman Wugou (Stainless). In the year of Xinyou, while providing a meal for the monastic community at Mount Jing, Dahui Zonggao remarked that Wugou’s Chan was like a divine-arm archer’s bow.
He then spoke this verse: “A single shot from the divine-arm bow Pierces through a thousand layers of armor. Pick it up carefully and look at it— What is it but a pair of stinking leather shoes?
Qi Hui suspected that this was a critique of him and ordered an official of the Censorate to lodge a formal accusation. Zonggao subsequently issued a warrant in pursuit.
He was sentenced to Hengzhou and subsequently demoted to Nan'an Commandery. Once settled in exile, he continued his discourse on the sutras as usual;

his hands never ceased turning over the pages, and after many years, the traces of his footsteps remained clearly marked upon the courtyard stones. In the spring of the Bingzi year, by imperial decree, he was appointed to guard Yongjia, and Daogong was also released and returned home.

They met at Gan River, where they stayed for some time in cordial conversation. Traveling eastward together by boat, they engaged in a profound discussion regarding the essential tenets of the school, never once mentioning past events.
Cheng had previously ordered his nephew, Yu Xian, to pay respects to Baoguang. Xian said, "I have never bowed before monks. Cheng said, "You should simply inquire of him.

Xian then took up the three phrases beginning with "That which Heaven mandates is called nature" (*ming-tian wei xing*) and questioned Baoguang. Baoguang replied, "Ordinary people do not know [this]."
"The destiny of one's natal year and the primary life-force are falling away; furthermore, you wish to drag good people into a fire pit.
How can you fail to break through the very first point regarding the sages and worthies? Xian said, "Can my teacher break through for the sages and worthies?
Gao replied, "'That which Heaven mandates is called nature'—this is the pure Dharma-body. 'To follow nature is called the Way'—this is the perfect and complete retribution-body."
"The body is the Way; practicing the Way is what is called 'teaching. This is precisely the manifestation of the thousand, hundred, and ten billion transformation bodies.
Cheng said, "The Imperial Decree has been fulfilled. What words can you offer for my prostration? In the year Wuyin (1298), Xutang Gaofeng again took charge of Mount Jing.

Cheng said, "Whenever I am in a dream, I invariably recite the *Analects* and the *Mencius*. Why is this? Gaofeng cited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Because of stillness and tranquility, the Tathāgatas of the worlds of the ten directions..."
The mind manifests therein, like a reflection in a mirror. Cheng said, "One cannot hear this treatise unless one has a master.
Afterward, Cheng established the six perfections of the mind and made no plans for his descendants. Consequently, he took the *Avataṃsaka* as his spiritual friend and provided two meals daily;
he used these to feed the monastic community. He also once made offerings to the sixteen great devas, and all the tea cups used for these offerings were...
It transformed into milk. He spoke in verse: "I prostrate to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha of the ten directions; I prostrate to all the devas who protect the Dharma.
I now make offerings to the Triple Gem and the devas, As small as a drop in the ocean or a single hair on a cow.

What wondrous artifice could possibly move them? Let me borrow the power of consciousness to explain it for you: My mind is no different from that of the Buddhas and devas. When even a single speck of dust arises..."
Separated by the barriers of the earth, yet when the dust of delusion is cleared away, awareness becomes perfectly pure. For this reason, the Buddhas and devas descend to appear before us.

When I wish to make offerings to the Buddha, the Buddha immediately manifests; when I wish to make offerings to the devas, the devas likewise manifest. If a son of the Buddha should give rise to doubt, let him ask:
"From where does this milk come? Doubt is itself the dust, and the dust is itself doubt; it is ultimately not like the state of the Buddhas and devas. I, now...
I shall sweep away your doubts for you, like hot water poured on snow or fire melting ice. If you now harbor even the slightest suspicion or delusion, the hawk has already flown off to Silla.
He once composed a verse on Huanglong’s Three Barriers, saying: "What is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
If all the monks in the world were without mouths, Even if you were to suddenly leap up and walk away, You would still be running inside a ghost cave. (One cannot avoid this [taboo]). I...
What are his feet like? They are like a donkey’s feet. Furthermore, he has been stuck by sticky glue. He turns over and flies straight up to Tuṣita Heaven;
already he has encountered that rat poison (and cannot spit it out). Every person has their own place of karmic affinity.
Beneath the Iron Ring Mountains for many thousands of years, the three calamities reach as far as the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. This donkey still remains right there (having exerted great effort).
The commentary states: "Wondrous Joy" refers to the "Stainless Chan," which is like the Shenbi bow. When the Shenbi bow is fired once, it penetrates through a thousand layers of armor.
It is also said: "The Old Master Wugou cannot be deceived by even a single point. Yet, upon examining his time, his seeking of the Way was truly arduous.
He first studied under Baoyin, then again under Shanquan; finally, at a moonlit night when frogs were croaking, he attained sudden enlightenment.
To have attained awakening is still not enough. To overturn the table and snatch away the fire tongs is still not enough.

Only when one has investigated things until they are thoroughly understood (*wùgé*) and grasped the subtle meaning—attaining mastery over both the Buddha and the demon within the painted image—is there finally a point of self-acceptance through discernment.
It is said that the final great matter was accomplished at the end of nine years of practice under the Elder of Jingshan. Therefore, it is said: "Not entering..."
Staggering waves; it is difficult to encounter a fish that suits one's wishes.
Li Bing (a dharma heir of Chan Master Zonggao). Li Bing, courtesy name Hanlao, was a native of Rencheng.
During the Chongning era, he served as an Academician of the Hanlin Academy. Later, he was appointed as a Vice President of the Council of State.

Regarding administrative affairs: Bing had devoted his heart to the ancestral way for many years. Hearing that Dahui Zonggao was vigorously refuting "silent illumination" as a deviant form of Chan, he felt both doubt and indignation.
He went to listen to Huiguan, arriving just as Huiguan was addressing the assembly. Huiguan raised the story of Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” and delivered this verse:
“The cypress tree in the courtyard— Today I raise it once again To break through Zhaozhou’s barrier. Suddenly...
He searched for words. He ventured to ask the assembly: "Since you have all broken through Zhaozhou’s barrier, why do you specifically search for words?
After a long silence, he said: "At first I thought only of the length of the thatch; only after burning it did I realize the ground was uneven. Suddenly, Bing attained realization and said to Hui:
"Had it not been for the Master’s later words, I would have nearly missed it. After their parting, he sent a letter to inquire about his doubts and seek resolution.

He said, "I recently visited the Hall of the Counting-Sticks and received your blows that shattered my ignorance and stagnation. Suddenly, I attained a realization. Looking back, I see that my faculties and consciousness have been dull and obtuse;

all the learning and understanding of my life have fallen into mere emotional views. Every taking up and every discarding was like walking through a thicket of brambles in tattered rags—only to become further entangled.
Now, with a single laugh, my doubts are instantly released. My joy and gratitude are immeasurable; it would not have been possible without the Great Master."
"You have shown such profound compassion in your detailed instructions. How could I have reached such a state? Hui replied in his letter:

"Since you arrived in the city, you have been dressing, eating, embracing your children, and playing with your grandchildren; everything remains as it was before. Having cast off all feelings of attachment and stagnation, you likewise harbor no thoughts of seeking the extraordinary.
Even your long-standing habitual obstructions have become somewhat lighter. Upon reading these words three times over, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. This...

This is indeed the verification of studying the Buddha. Were it not for a person of extraordinary capacity who, within a single smile, brings a hundred matters to completion and a thousand tasks to resolution, one could not know that our own house possesses this ineffable, wondrous excellence.

If it were otherwise, the two dharma-gates of "doubt" and "anger" would remain unbroken until the end of the future; even if the vast void were made the entrance to Yunmen’s gate, and the grasses and trees...
Even tiles and stones all emit radiance; though one may attempt to assist in explaining the underlying principle, there is nothing that can be done.

Only then will one believe that this matter of causal conditions cannot be transmitted and cannot be learned; it must be personally realized and personally awakened to, personally accepted and personally stilled, before one finally reaches the end.
"Your Excellency has now, with a single laugh, suddenly lost all that was gained. What more is there to say? Furthermore, it is said: 'This matter is extremely difficult;

one must give rise to a sense of shame before it can be attained. Often those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom obtain it without expending effort, whereupon they develop a sense of complacency and cease to practice.
They are frequently snatched away by the phenomena of the present moment and fail to act as their own masters."
It is attained. Yet, as days pass and months deepen, one becomes deluded and fails to return to the Way.

One’s power cannot overcome the force of karma; Māra seizes the opportunity, and one is surely taken into his grasp. Even at the moment of death, one will find no strength. Remember my words from the other day:

in principle, there is sudden awakening, and through that awakening, all is simultaneously dissolved. In practice, however, things are not suddenly eliminated; they are exhausted only through gradual stages. Whether walking or staying...
Whether sitting or reclining, you must by no means forget this. As for the various other distinct sayings of the ancients, they should neither be regarded as real nor as unreal.
After a long time of steady practice, you will naturally and silently accord with your own fundamental mind;
there is no need to seek anything else that is superior or extraordinary. Bing also wrote again in a letter, saying: "Recently, I have received your kind reply, which is complete..."

He fully grasped the profound purport. There were three instances where Bing personally verified this: first, regarding matters, whether adverse or favorable, he responded spontaneously according to conditions without retaining them within his breast;
second, his long-standing habitual tendencies were so thick that they did not require deliberate expulsion, yet they naturally became light and subtle;

third, regarding ancient kōans which he had previously found utterly bewildering, he suddenly attained glimpses of realization from time to time—this was not something he could have been unaware of himself. Hui then replied: "I do not know what has happened since the past few days."
Are you relaxed and expansive according to conditions, and free and sovereign as you wish? Within the four modes of deportment, are you not overcome by worldly defilements?

In the two states of waking and sleeping, have you attained the single suchness? In your former dwelling, are there no more restless activities? Regarding the mind of birth and death, does it no longer continue in succession?
Merely exhausting ordinary sentiments, there is no separate "saintly understanding. Since you broke into a smile, your true eye has been opened wide.
All traces of conceptualization are suddenly forgotten. Whether one has gained strength or not is like a person drinking water: the coldness or warmth is known by oneself.

Nevertheless, in the midst of daily life, you should follow what the Old Man of Yellow Face taught: strip away the fundamental nature, eliminate the auxiliary causes, and contravene the manifest karma.
This is the man who has finished with affairs; it is the true expedient within the absence of expedients, and the true [realization] within the absence of cultivation or verification.
Cultivation and realization constitute the true taking and discarding within the state of no-taking and no-discarding. Later, when his illness was nearing its end, he sent a verse to Miguang, saying:
"In years past, I once crossed the ferry at the ford of adversity; I deeply relied upon the power of the Dharma to serve Yunmen.

Now that my spirit and faculties have somewhat returned, I intend to repay my teacher for his unrequited kindness. Miguang replied: "Sitting steadily upon the huchang chair, you have already reached the ford. Why..."
Returning to the place of origin, he sought the Gate of Non-duality; when the eight sufferings arose, his entire body was fully manifest. Who knows who can repay such profound kindness?
Bing received the response and passed away after finishing the reading.

The commentary says: With a single laugh, all that could be attained is instantly lost. Where, then, is there any "right nature" to be hollowed out, any auxiliary causes to be eliminated, or any present karma to be contravened?
The old man of Wondrous Joy (Miaoxi) merely busies himself helping others climb over the wall, unaware that beneath his own heels the mud is several zhang deep.
Wu Weiming (Dharma-heir of Chan Master Zonggao). Wu Weiming, courtesy name Yuanshao, was a native of Shaowu.
Having studied under Zhenxie for a long time, he attained the *svatantra-samādhi* (the samādhi of self-mastery) as his ultimate realization.

He once wrote a postscript to the "Brahmacarya" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, stating that he had achieved a point of awakening and entry into the meaning of this chapter. Dahui... [text continues]
Seeing him, he laughed and said, "This man has realized nothing more than a state devoid of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). He has already had his face branded by a false teacher.
Yunmen, if he were to see him, would surely exert all his strength to save him. Ming then went to Changle and entered the room with the assembly.
Huì said, "What you have realized is what Yongjia called 'vast emptiness that negates cause and effect'—a chaotic mess."
This is utterly reckless and will only invite calamity. You have thus cited a passage from the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* as a mistaken scriptural proof, saying:
"If one relies on this citation to claim that the absence of pure conduct is itself true pure conduct, then one slanders the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and shall enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Furthermore, today there are various heterodox teachings everywhere, each claiming for themselves to have attained the Unsurpassed Way, deceiving the barbarians.
To deceive the Han people! You recklessly fabricate interpretations regarding the circumstances of the ancients' entry into the Way.
Furthermore, there is another class who act as petty peddlers at the seats of masters; having caught a single word or half-sentence, they use it to seduce the ignorant masses. Linji said:

"There is a certain class of blind shaven-headed soldiers who take the meaning from the scriptures and, through deliberation, compose phrases and meanings; they are like those who take up a lump of excrement."
The son held it in his mouth and then spat it out to give to someone else. Mingwen’s mind was filled with doubt.

That evening, he entered the room, and Huì raised the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature to question him. Just as he was about to answer, Huì struck him. He then remained there to seek instruction.
One day, Huì said: "There is no need to display your skills; you must simply break through with a sudden 'spit' and cut off with a sharp 'snap,' only then can you match the Living."
If one merely displays such clever maneuvers, there will be an end to them. He then took his leave. While traveling along the Yanping road, he suddenly attained realization.
He wrote several verses in succession to send to Huì, all of which were things he had heard within the [master’s] room. One said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not an object.
My whole body is a single string of golden chain-bones. Zhaozhou personally saw Old Nanquan; he could explain it."
Radishes grow in Zhenzhou. Hui-zheng’s verse says: "A single string of golden-locked bones throughout the entire body, fit to serve as a model for gods and humans.
If you wish to recognize Linji’s little page-boy, he is none other than the white-handed thief of those bygone days."
Wu Qian, courtesy name Yifu and style name Lizhai, served as Chancellor during the reign of Emperor Lizong. He attained realization through the practice of Chan.
He once composed a preface to *Dahui’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye*, which states: "This matter extends through antiquity and the present, pervading heaven and earth.
Whether viewed from the front or the side, straight or across, opened or closed, bright or dark—there is nothing that does not see, yet there is nothing that is seen."
Nor is there a non-viewing. There is nothing to be viewed. I speak directly and dare to say: to say that correctness is itself departure; to say that the Dharma is itself dust;

to say that the eye is itself a boring tool; to say that the treasury is itself a blockage—therefore, these four words must be cast away into the great ocean before one can avoid bearing the cangue and shackles, and being caught within the snare of others. Even so, for those of initial capacity and dull faculties, it is likewise.
If you wish to attain even one or half [of the truth], you must speak in a mixture of barbarian and Chinese tongues. Looking here and looking there, some traces of light will begin to appear.

At this moment, it is precisely right to risk your life and cast away your body, charging straight ahead with a single spear like a rat entering a cow's horn, crowding against the wall and pressing against the partition.

There was nowhere else to go. In the midst of this intense confusion and distress, suddenly his head split open and his forehead cracked; sweat flowed from his entire body, and he attained a state of rest.

Only then did he realize that the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, the Heavenly-eye, and the Buddha-eye are nothing but a single pair of ordinary eyes. At this point, it is said that the work of a student of the Way is finished. Yet, this is not yet the case for Old Man Lüzhai, who immediately spoke a verse: No place to go, In the midst of bewilderment and distress, Suddenly the head splits and the forehead cracks, Sweat flows from the whole body, And a moment of rest is found. Then one knows that the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, the Heavenly-eye, and the Buddha-eye Are but a single pair of ordinary eyes.
Reaching this point, it is said that the task of the student is complete. But even so, it is not yet the end for Old Man Lüzhai. Thus he spoke a verse:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Later, having been slandered and exiled by Jia Sidao, he stayed at the Jiedai Temple in Fengting, Xunzhou, and said to the monks:
Formerly, Mañjuśrī said to the World-Honored One: "When I first entered the inconceivable samādhi, I bound my mind to a single object.

As for what is called binding the mind to a single object, it is like the contemplation of the sun, the contemplation of the moon, the tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the white mark on the bridge of the nose, and so forth."
Although the matter is shallow and mundane, its principle is truly profound and subtle. As Zhaozhou said: "In my twelve periods of the day, I do nothing but eat porridge and rice;
only during the two periods [of eating] do I employ a distracted mind. When Guishan asked Lan'an, "What tasks do you perform during your twelve periods of the day?"
An said, "Herding an ox. Mian asked, "How do you herd it? An replied, "Once it enters the grass, I pull it back by the nose.

These are all methods of binding the mind to a single object. Subsequently, the venerable masters further devised clever expedients, instructing students to contemplate a "head-word" (huatou), such as "The dog has Buddha-nature," "Three pounds of flax," "A dried-up dung pellet," or "Canton Cloth."
The "Shan" (shirt) and the "juniper trees before the courtyard"—these are all points where the path of logic is blocked. They are taught for people to contemplate at random.
First, by looking again and again, and doubting over and over, one must never let go throughout the twelve periods of the day.
Suddenly, when the nostrils flare open with a single burst, that is precisely where the person establishes their own body and life. All of this involves binding the mind to a single object.
This is evidence of his realization. Having attained great mastery within the Dharma-gate, while he was in Xunzhou, he foreknew the day of his death and told people, "I am about to depart;
there will surely be thunder and rain tonight. It happened exactly as he said. He composed a poem and passed away while sitting upright.
Lu Zhengji held the rank of Scholar of the Xianmu Academy. He attended Chan Master Ren of Changlu and asked, "Who is the person who hides a pearl within their robes?
Ren stood up and shook out his clothes, saying, "There is not a single thing. Lu responded with repeated agreement. Ren presented him with this verse:
"You have now arrived intimately at Changlu; Shaking out your garments, there is nothing at all. From now on, should you encounter someone who asks,"
He merely remarked, "The wind is fierce and the waves are rough. He replied with this verse: "A needle meeting a grommet—our affinity was established long ago.
For a thousand years I have stood alone; the snow-filled courtyard is cold. If a practitioner asks about the path ahead, Reaching Chang'an ten thousand li away is not difficult.
Ren approved of it.
Zhang Zi, styled Yuezhai, served as a Scholar of the Secretariat (Zhizhigeshi). Upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained enlightenment to the Way. His verse says:
"A single strike of the bell blocks the faculty of hearing; From the side of this lump of flesh, the thief is driven out. If someone asks what school I understand, The god Śūnyatā’s face is black."
Lu Benzhong, whose courtesy name was Jurén, served as a Court Reader (Shìdú). He once sent a letter inquiring about the essential points of Dahui’s Chan teachings.

Dahui replied in a letter, saying: "A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. If the doubt regarding the *huatou* is shattered, then a thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts will all be shattered at once.
If you persistently ask others, 'How are the Buddha's words? and 'How are the Patriarchs' words?'—what can the elder masters of various quarters do for you?"
As for what this means: "For eternal kalpas there will be no time of awakening. Yet, within this very state, there is naturally a moment of realization.
Lu You, whose courtesy name was Wuguang and who styled himself Fangong, served as a Court Attendant (Dazhizhi). He once asked Chan Master Songyuan Yue:
"May I hear about the learning transmitted through the mind? Yue replied, "Since it is transmitted through the mind, how could it be obtained from hearing?

You, having attained understanding, presented this verse: "How many times have I driven my carriage into the imperial capital? Whenever I met a monk, my eyes were equally clear and bright. Only today do I realize the uniqueness of the Chan school:
To speak of existence and discuss emptiness, one must listen with the eye."
You Mao, courtesy name Yanzhi, was a native of Liangxi. He passed the jinshi examination during the Shaoxing era.

Having heard of the world-transcending Dharma of the Śākya clan, he went to see Chan Master Guizong, intending to plan a life of seclusion. Zhu Yuanhui sent him a poem which said: "Do not hasten, sir, to flee to Chan."
Having concluded these verses on the local sites, [Zhang] Mao was appointed as the Governor of Taizhou. When Emperor Xiaozong stood at the palace balcony, he personally sent for him, asking:
"What are the most excellent sights of Southern Tai? Mao replied: "Tàipíng Hongfú (Great Peace and Abundant Blessings) and Guòqīng Wànnián (Guoqing for Ten Thousand Years). The Emperor said:

"I have heard that the Stone Bridge Yingzhēn (Yingzhen of the Stone Bridge) is a man of great strength who occasionally appears. With what method would you deal with him? Mao clenched his fist and said: "Your servant..."
There was a precious sword of the Vajra King; [the Emperor] was delighted and bestowed upon him the four characters "Shu Su Chu Lao Ren" (The Elder Who Fulfills His Initial Vow).

Upon arriving at the prefecture, he governed the people with benevolence and love. He rose to the rank of Minister of the Ministry of Rites and was posthumously honored with the title Wenjian (Wenjian).
Ye Shi, whose courtesy name was Zezheng and sobriquet was Shuixin, held the office of Palace Counselor for the Imperial Library (Baomu Xueshi).

He once remarked that while Buddhist scriptures contain many contradictory points, there are also not few instances of consistency. He went to inquire of Shiyan Lian, who said: "The Buddha takes precept, concentration, and wisdom as his fundamental principles."
When the mind does not engage with external conditions, the flowing water and blooming flowers, the soaring kites and leaping fish, are all the true nature of the self.

The essential point lies in illuminating all manifold differences as one; when phenomena and principle are fused into a single whole, through long practice over years and months, the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness will naturally seal the original mind.
If you can withdraw your gaze and turn your hearing inward, you will find that outside the mind there is originally no other thing. There is no need to inquire into many categories or details.
The opposite is also true; it is precisely through this that one knows where to return.
Chen Guiqian, who served as State Councillor for the Bureau of Military Affairs, replied in a letter concerning Chan to Zhen Xishan, stating in brief:

"Regarding your question as to whether one should contemplate the 'critical phrase' (huatou): I say that when a single thought is unborn, the whole body is the Buddha. Where else could there be a critical phrase?"

It is solely because one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the sensory dust that thought after thought arises and perishes. The skillful means of the Buddhas and Patriarchs cause one to chew upon words that have no meaning or flavor;
yet, one must thoroughly perceive the natural radiance of one’s own original ground before it can be considered ultimate.
Although this is inherently possessed by every person, it is merely shrouded by deluded thoughts. Unless one undergoes intense refinement through practice, it will never become clear and pure.
The Commentary says: A single string of golden locks and bones—viewed with the correct eye, they are but lumps of excrement.
As for Wu Lizhai, Lü Juren, Lü Zhengji, Zhang Yuezhai, Lu Fangweng, You Yanzhi, Ye Shuixin, and Chen Guiqian—all of them moved freely between Confucianism and Buddhism.
Why was it that after the Song dynasty there were so many who manifested themselves to preach the Dharma?
Liu Yanxiu (Dharma successor of Chan Master Zonggao).
Liu Ziyu, courtesy name Yanxiu, was appointed as Prefect of Yongjia and went to seek the Way from Dahui.
Dahui said, "When a monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, 'No. Just look at it like this. Later, Ziyu...
He revealed the truth upon the cypress tree. The verse says: Zhaozhou’s Cypress Tree is quite senseless;

To seek it within the objective realm is also most difficult. At every turn, green willows are fit to tie a horse; Before every door, one passes through to Chang’an. Hui once replied in a letter, saying:
The old Pang said, "The mind is like the environment; It is neither real nor unreal, Neither existent nor non-existent. He did not care whether there was [existence] or not.

Do not be constrained by this. It is not that sages and worthies have already finished their business; if an ordinary person can truly become an "ordinary person who has finished their business," then what are Śākyamuni and Bodhidharma but lumps of clay?

And what are the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings but the rattling sound of a hot bowl? Since you have attained self-confidence and are free from doubt within this gate, this is no small matter. You must...
To let go of what is raw to cultivate what is ripe, and to let go of what is ripe to cultivate what is raw—only then does one begin to correspond even slightly with this matter.
It often happens that gentlemen find a moment of sudden awakening amidst unfavorable circumstances, yet lose it entirely amidst favorable ones.
You must know this: even while in favorable circumstances, you must constantly apply the perspective of unfavorable ones.
Maintain this timing within your mindfulness; you must never allow it to be forgotten for even a moment. If you secure the root, do not worry about the branches;
if you know how to become a Buddha, do not worry that the Buddha will not understand your words. This one point is easy to attain but difficult to maintain; you must never treat it with negligence.
You must ensure that the beginning is upright so the end is upright, expanding and extending this principle. Only then may you apply what remains from your own cultivation to all things.
Huang Yanjie (Dharma heir of Chan Master Zonggao).
Huang Yanjie, styled Jiefu and nicknamed Miaode, had his doubts suddenly severed beneath Dahui’s single shout. Dahui bestowed his robe upon him.
He once raised the story of Shoushan’s bamboo cane; when he reached the point where Ye County stepped forward and seized it, he snapped it in two.
He threw it down the steps and asked, "What is this? Shanshan said, "A blind fellow. [The Master] said, "When Miaode reaches this point, he is utterly incapable of anything;

he can only remember what he has learned. He then recalled a quatrain he had once composed on wax plum blossoms: "About to chew the wax at the branch tip, Startled by the fragrance, yet resembling orchid.
Deep within the snows of the village ahead, Do not mistake them for mountain plums."
The collective eulogy says: Liu Ziyu ties his horse to the green willows; Huang Jiefu gazes upon the plum blossoms on the deep-snowed ridge.
Zhaozhou’s story of the cypress tree and Shoushan’s story of the bamboo cane—let us set aside this entire bundle for a later day.
Once Xinkong has woken from his drowsiness, we shall deliberate upon it again.
Qian Duandi (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Jingyuan).
Qian Duandi, courtesy name Chuhe, styled Songchuang, served as a State Councilor. He once studied under Huguo Jingyuan and clarified his own fundamental matter.
Later, he reached the ultimate depth regarding every aspect of the essential purport of the Chan school. In the winter of the丙申 (Bingshen) year of the Chunxi era, Jiantang...
Jingui returned to stay at Pingtian, where he subsequently established a close relationship with him. In the autumn of the Dingyou year, [Zhaoqing] manifested slight illness.

He wrote a letter summoning Jingui, along with the abbots of Guoqing and Ruiyan, containing words of parting. When Jingui and two Chan masters arrived at his bedside, he rose from his prostrations and sat cross-legged, speaking and laughing.
After some time, he said joyfully: "The floating world is illusory; fundamentally, there is no coming or going. The four great elements..."
The five aggregates must ultimately come to an end. Even though Buddhas and Patriarchs possess great majestic power and virtue, they cannot escape this one point.
Among all the elder monks and spiritual friends throughout the world, is there anyone who can leap over it?
It is because earth, water, fire, and wind combine through causes and conditions to meet for a brief moment; one must not mistakenly take them to be one's own.
A great man is vast and unconfined. When he acts, he must hold fast; wherever he stands, it is all true.

Like setting sails with the wind, whether going up or down the stream, one may utilize the occasion for a feast to offer praise and celebration. Whether departing or remaining is entirely at his own will.
This is the single path of Great Liberation and the gate to Nirvana opened by the sages of antiquity—the originally pure and quiescent realm, the Unconditioned Greatness.
"This is the Way. Now that I am thus, am I not joyful? The external conditions of worldly toil have been swept away all at once. I am grateful for the visit of you, masters of the various mountains;
may you all grant me your witness. I humbly entreat you to take care of yourselves. Setting down his brush, he looked at the assembly and said, "It is better for me to sit and depart."
"It would be better to lie down before departing. Ji said, "If you, Excellency, are simply leaving, why concern yourself with sitting or lying down?
Li smiled and said, "Dharma-brother, you should cherish yourself for the sake of the ancestral path," whereupon he closed his eyes and passed away.
Qian Xiangzu (Dharma heir of Chan Master Jingyuan).
Qian Xiangzu, courtesy name Gongxiang, style name Zhian, was a native of Qiantang. He visited Huguo Jingyuan, who said to him:

"If you wish to investigate this matter, you must reach the point where both mind and dharmas are forgotten. As long as attachment to dharmas is not forgotten, even if you accord with the principle, it is not yet awakening."
The Patriarch said, "As soon as it involves the lips and tongue, one falls into conceptual thought; how can this be? Yuan said, "It is fundamentally without sores; do not wound it.
The Patriarch was suddenly enlightened and attained realization. While guarding Jinling, he made the true practice of the Pure Land his daily contemplation.
He frequently established ten reception centers throughout the local districts, all of which were named after the Pure Land and Sukhāvatī. He also founded Zhizan (Cessation Monastery).

The High Monk’s Quarters (*Gaosengliao*). This was a place for inviting monks to discuss the Way. Since the Left Prime Minister had retired from office, he had increasingly advanced in his pure practices (*śukla-karman*).
In the second month of the fourth year of the Jiading era, he fell slightly ill and wrote a verse, saying: “The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land;

Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, not even a speck of dust remains. My mind is pure and transcends that realm; Today I know from afar that a single blossom has opened. There was a monk... [text fragment ends]
When those who came to inquire after his illness asked him, the Master said, "I do not crave life nor do I fear death. I shall not be reborn as a deva, nor shall I become a human;
I seek only birth in the Pure Land. Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Later, someone dreamed that from the midst of the sky it was said:
"Prime Minister Qian has already been born in the Lotus Palace of the Western Paradise as the Bodhisattva Ciji."
The commentary says: Both Master Liangqian and Master Yuan were eminent disciples of the Dharma gate.

One resigned from his ministerial post to cultivate the practice of Pure Land, drawing near to the World-Honored One of Ultimate Bliss; the other, at the time of his passing, summoned Jiandang and entrusted him with the great matter of the Zen school before departing with a smile.
Now tell me, are these two elders the same or different? *Pah!* Be careful not to mistake them.
Pan Lianggui (Dharma heir of Chan Master Shouxun).
Pan Lianggui, courtesy name Yirong, was a native of Jinhua. He held the official rank of Longtu. At the age of forty, he turned his mind toward the ancestral gate.

Wherever he went, he hung up his alms bowl and joined the assembly to seek instruction. Later, he relied upon Fudeng Shouxun; after a long time, however, he did not achieve resonance with him. Consequently, he complained, saying:

Lianggui said, "I simply wish to know what it is like at the moment of death. Xun replied, "This is a fine envelope; let us keep it for future use. If we do not settle this matter now, it will be improper.
Suddenly, if it is replaced by another envelope, there will be no way to rectify it in the end.
