He then asked about the story of Nanquan cutting up the cat: "I have contemplated this for a very long time, yet I still have not fully penetrated it. I beg you, Master, to harmonize it for me."
Shang said, "Have compassion. Xun replied, "You only know how to manage other people's cats; you do not realize that you have lost your own dog.

At these words, Gui was as if awakened from a drunken stupor. Xun spoke again, saying, "It is no easy matter for you to have made this one step forward, yet you must further understand that there is a stage beyond this before you can truly succeed. Nowadays, when scholars and officials speak of Chan or the Way, they merely—"
To rely on and cling to doctrinal principles is, for the most part, merely a superficial pleasure—like buying oil-cakes with money;
once eaten, one is no longer hungry, while regarding everything else as a deception is truly laughable. I value only this "yes, yes."
The commentary says: Nanquan’s cat and Zhaozhou’s dog—one has many aspects, yet the two are no different.
Since Master Pan understands his own dog, how could he alone fail to understand another’s cat? What is another’s cat?
When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; take it home in a bottomless basket.
Zeng Kai (dharma heir of Chan Master Huiyuan).
His courtesy name was Tianyou. He had long studied under the gates of Yuanwu and Dahui. In the *xinwei* year of the Shaoxing era, Fohai Huiyuan was appointed to Guangxiao Temple in Quzhou;
Zeng Kai and Zhao Lingjin went together to visit him. Zeng Kai asked: "What is goodness?"
Zhishen said, "Lanterns and pillars; cats and dogs. Mendi asked, "Why is it that praise brings joy while disparagement causes affliction?
Zhishen said, "Minister, have you ever met a true teacher (Sanskrit: *kalyāṇamitra*)? Mendi replied, "I have been seeking instruction for thirty years;
why do you say I have not seen one? Zhishen said, "See him in the place of joy; see him in the place of affliction. As Mendi was about to speak, Zhishen [continued].
As Huikong was about to respond, Yuan said, "The one who opens his mouth is not you. Huikong was left bewildered. Yuan called out to him, "Where have you gone, Minister?

At this, Huikong suddenly attained realization and nodded his head, speaking this verse: "The Great Way is originally perfect and complete; Why do people create distinctions? If you wish to know the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own face."
"Alas, blind donkey! A veritable pest in the monastic groves. With a single sound that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism has been leaked. If someone asks further, 'What is the meaning?
he picks up his whisk and slices them across the mouth. Yuan said, "He too only manages to get one peg."
Ge Tan (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huiyuan).
Ge Tan’s courtesy name was Qianwen, and his style name was Xinzhai. Having achieved high honors in the civil service examinations during his youth, he set his aspirations upon the Chan school.

He first visited Wuan Quan, who instructed him to investigate the saying, "This very mind is Buddha. After a long time without attaining realization, he requested, "Master, what expedient means can you provide to enable me to enter?"
"I have attained entry. Quan said, "The layman is far too insatiable. Subsequently, Huiyuan came to reside at Jianchi, and Tan followed him there to study.

Tan then recounted the words Quan had shown him and requested that they be expounded for the sake of the assembly. He asked Huiyuan to elaborate upon them, saying: [The text continues with Huiyuan's response.]
"Mind itself is Buddha"—his eyebrows trail the ground. "Neither mind nor Buddha"—his two eyes are crossed. "In a butterfly’s dream, home is ten thousand *li* away;
on the branch of the *subing* tree, the moon is at the third watch. After staying for ten days, he returned. One day, [Dongshan] raised the phrase:

"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. [Zhaozhou] suddenly attained realization and spoke this verse: "Not mind, not Buddha, nor yet a thing; The moon shines upon the waters of the West River."
Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the mountain rises abruptly; within the shadows of the radiant sun, it turns its body upside down. A wild fox leaps into the den of the golden-haired lion.
"I fully approve," he said, and immediately sent a letter and a verse to present to Yuan. Yuan replied: "This matter cannot be conveyed by paper or ink.
Since you, Layman, have been able to surpass me, you shall surely hear what is to be heard. He then returned to Huqiu. Yuan went out to meet him and said, "As for dwelling..."
When Layman Jianchu saw this, he stopped and said, "This may enter the realm of the Buddha, but it has not yet reached the realm of Māra. Layman Tan bowed;
Yuan assumed a solemn expression and said, "Why do you not say that the golden-haired lion leaps into the den of the wild fox? At this, Tan attained sudden realization.

In the sixth year of the Chunxi era, while serving as Prefect of Linchuan, he was stricken by a slight illness in the eighth month. He asked for his brush and wrote in large characters: "Beating [the drum] within the great ocean..."
The drum sounded; from atop Mount Sumeru, he heard the bell. The karmic mirror suddenly shattered, and he leaped forth into the void.
Summoning his subordinates, he said: "Life and death are like day and night; there is nothing strange about them. If one speaks in terms of the Way, how could there be birth and death?
To interpret them as birth and death is to be far removed from the Way. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
The commentary states: Zeng Tianyou studied under the father and son of Yuanwu for a long time;
Ge Xinzhai studied under Master Wuan for a long time, yet both lost their sense of smell beneath the assembly of Fohai. To know the essential point, look south while facing north.
Mo Jiang (Dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanjing). Mo Jiang was styled Shaohu;
he was a native of Fenning in Yuzhang. While serving as an official in Western Sichuan, he visited Nantang Yuanjing to inquire about the essentials for resolving his mind.
Nantang instructed him to maintain mindfulness of the "good place. Just as he happened to enter the latrine and smelled a foul odor, he suddenly—
He covered his nose with his hand, whereupon he attained realization. He immediately presented this verse: "From of old, my natural grace has loved elegance;
I have often laughed at those who seek it outwardly. Though there be ten thousand variations and a thousand differences, there is nowhere to find it;

it was originally right here on the tip of the nose. Dongshan replied: "When a single dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are complete; with its wondrous function pervading all directions, what more is there to seek? A green serpent emerges from its scabbard."
The demonic armies were subdued. The blue-eyed barbarian monk smiled and nodded his head.
Regarding Wang Xiao (the Dharma heir of Master Yuanjing Chan):
Wang Xiao of the Longtu [Academy], whose courtesy name was Guanfù, attained awakening upon hearing the sound of the *kaizheng* board at Liuzhao Temple. He then questioned Nan...
The Abbot said, "I have a certain point of view, yet as soon as I am questioned by someone, I find myself unable to speak.
I wonder where my fault lies. The Abbot replied, "Your fault lies in having a certain point of view. The Abbot then asked, "When did you arrive at your post?
Xiao replied, "On the fourth day of the eighth month last year. The Abbot said, "How long has it been since you left the provincial administration office? Xiao replied, "Last month."
On the second day, the Master said, "Why is it said that one cannot open one's mouth? At this, Xiao attained awakening.
He offered this praise: "These two worldly fellows: one has his ailment in his nostrils; the other has his ailment on his tongue."
With just this single medicine of Nantang, one can ensure that both shall have their original countenances restored.
Have you not heard it said that this medicine can both kill people and bring them back to life?
Zhang Shi (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Daoyan).
Zhang Shi, courtesy name Jingfu, served repeatedly as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel. He once sought instruction from Daoyan, asking:
"If one sees it immediately upon seeing, any deliberation is already an error; what then? Daoyan said: "You still ask while not knowing. Zhang Shi said: "Precisely..."

"Know that there are times when it is like this. Yan said, "Hearing sounds and seeing forms is exactly as usual. Lü Xi was suddenly enlightened and composed a verse, saying: "Hearing sounds and seeing forms is exactly as usual;
If one examines them thoroughly, the principle of the refined and the coarse naturally manifests. It is like the void containing the azure expanse;
There has never been so much as a single hair’s breadth of excess. Yan approved of this. Later, when his illness reached its final stage, he remained in meditative composure.

The old man requested instruction. Lü Xi said, "To cast off the private desires of human nature is like the molting of a cicada; to harmonize with the subtle wonder of the principle of Heaven is like the thawing of spring.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. Throughout his life, Xi had devoted himself deeply to the Classics and Histories, always holding the ancient sages and worthies as his own standard.
His writings include commentaries on the Analects and Mencius, as well as treatises on the Supreme Ultimate (*Tàijí*). Scholars honored him as Master Nánxūn.
The eulogy says: In the azure void, he sheds his skin like a cicada as spring melts away; he dots the eyes of Yan Chuan and stands tall like the pine of Liangxi.
Now tell me: is this the study of Chan, or the study of the sages? Let all people in the world grope for it as they please.
Li Hao (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Tiantong Tanhua). Li Hao was a Minister of the Board of Rites.
His courtesy name was Deyuan, and his style name was Zhengxin. A native of Jianchang, he passed the imperial examinations during the Shaoxing era.

Having previously read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it felt as though he were returning to a familiar home. When Ying’an Tanhua was preaching the Dharma at Mingguo Monastery in Quzhou, Li Hao went to join him.
When Cheng entered the room, Huazhen struck him on the chest and asked, "After you die, Elder Minister, where will you go?

Hao was struck with terror and broke into a sweat. Huazhen shouted at him to leave. Hao withdrew, but within ten days of his retreat, he had mastered the inner sanctum. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Kang, saying:
"The gate has the shop of Sun Bin; The household keeps the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early— Who awakens to this?"

Furthermore, who was it that was deluded? When Yantong saw this, he praised it as excellent. There was also a seller of rouge who had likewise long studied under Yantong and prided himself on his realization.
Haoguan presented him with a verse, saying: "Without applying red powder, one is naturally elegant; Often, practitioners of Chan stop short at this point.
After having penetrated the snares and patterns of past and present, One returns here to receive a punch."
Wu Shisang (The Daoist Wu Shisang of Xianzhou Mountain, Jianning Prefecture;
Dharma heir of Chan Master Daoxian). He frequently used his own spiritual matters to question various Chan masters, including Kaisu Daoxian.
He subsequently retired to tie up a thatched hut to the left of the monastery and served him as an attendant. One night, he suddenly attained awakening and composed a verse.

Xingshan said, "Originally there are no seams or gaps; as soon as one touches it, it shines with brilliance. Since this is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, why need one use it to shoot at sparrows?
Xingshan replied, "When it snaps with a 'tsai' sound, there is true joy and liberation; birth and death, the mundane and the sage—all are utterly submerged."
Beneath the mountains of Xianzhou, he laughs aloud: "I do not辜负 (fail) the heart we pledged long ago.
The collective commentary says: No awakening, no delusion; no seams, no cracks. The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it.
Zhu Xi (Dharma heir of Chan Master Daoxian). His courtesy name was Yuanhui;
his style name was Huian. He was a native of Wuyuan. In his youth, he took no pleasure in studying the conventional examination essays (*shiwen*).

Upon hearing an elder master discuss Chan, which directly pointed to the fundamental mind, he suddenly attained awakening to that single point of luminous, alert awareness. At the age of eighteen, he...
He studied under Liu Pingshan. Pingshan suspected that he was preoccupied with the pursuit of the civil service examinations;

when he searched through his satchel, he found nothing but a single volume of Dahui’s Recorded Sayings. Xī once wrote a letter to Daoqian, saying: "Previously, I received the instructions of Miaoxi [Dahui].
Since then, I have been unable to retain written texts or engage in mental calculations; I will not allow even a hair's breadth of such things to remain in my breast. I shall simply..."
"Whenever you speak of this 'dog' case, I wish for you to constantly remind yourself of it. I pray you will offer a word to alert me to my own shortcomings. Qian replied:

"For twenty years I have been unable to reach the ground of non-doubt. Later, I suddenly realized that if one simply knows what is wrong and rushes forward with courage, it is like cutting through both sides with a single stroke.
One must maintain this single thought-moment; do not deliberate upon the 'dog' case, and do not engage in intellectual analysis."

Do not seek to know or perceive; do not force yourself to take it upon you. Xi attained awakening upon hearing these words. He composed a poem on his practice of dwelling in seclusion and reciting the sutras, which says:
Sitting upright and alone, with nothing to do, I casually open the books of the Śākya clan. For a while, I rest from the tethers of worldly dust; Transcendent, I dwell in harmony with the Way.
The gate is closed, secluded amidst the bamboo grove; Birds sing after the mountain rain has passed. Having realized this dharma of non-action, Body and mind [are at peace].
He remained as composed as ever. He further remarked, "The study of the Buddha and that of our Confucianists are very similar.

For instance, it is said: 'There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally solitary. It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither with the four seasons.
Its falling away is not another thing; its spreading out is not mundane dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Look at this!"
"What kind of insight? He replied, "In the Buddha-dharma there are three gates: Teaching (Jiao), Discipline (Lü), and Meditation (Chan). The Chan school does not rely on written texts;
it seeks directly to recognize the mind and see one's nature. The rules of discipline are extremely strict, allowing no transgression even as small as a hair or a speck of dust.
The Teaching has three branches: the Tiantai Teaching, the Cien Teaching, and the Yanshou Teaching. The Yanshou Teaching is in the South."
There is no transmission [of this]. His learning was close to Chan. The Tiantai teachings consist primarily of rational inquiry and exegesis;
the Ci’en (Xuanzang) teachings likewise consist only of exegesis. If a Confucian can see through the underlying principles and understand them within his own mind, that is the fundamental capacity.
To combine this with the discourses of Chan is what constitutes critical discernment; to combine this with the origins and regulations of the teachings is what constitutes comprehensive mastery.

This is precisely it. Furthermore, when viewed through the lens of the Vinaya, many people nowadays say that being occupied with worldly affairs robs one of their time and hinders their study of the Way.
This is all because they are unable to steer the boat and merely resent the winding of the stream. When encountering wealth and honor, apply your practice upon that wealth and honor;
when encountering poverty and lowliness, apply your practice upon that poverty and lowliness. As the saying goes: "Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of your head..."
Even when concentration and wisdom are perfected and clarified, one still does not lose the delusions and inversions of the myriad worldly affairs;
being addicted to and attached to them, there is not a single thing that is not a theatrical performance—truly, it is not worth setting eyes upon.
Master Ruiyan would daily ask himself, "Is the Lord of the House awake? and would answer himself, "He is awake. Yet, those who study nowadays do not...
It was thus.
Lu Jiuyuan, styled Zijing, was a native of Jinxi. When he was three or four years old, he asked his father, "Where do heaven and earth reach their limits?
His father smiled but did not answer. Thereupon, he reflected deeply until he forgot to sleep or eat. During the Qiandao era, he passed the jinshi examination.
He served as the Prefect of Jingmen Commandery and resided at Mount Xiangshan to teach. His students numbered several hundred, and scholars referred to him as Master Xiangshan.
He once remarked: "Confucius said, 'Attack those who hold heterodox views; such things are harmful. In the present age, this applies to various classes of people."
To designate the teachings of the Buddha and Laozi as heterodox is a misunderstanding; for during the time of Confucius, Buddhism had not yet entered China.

Although there was the doctrine of Laozi, it was not yet prominent. If one were to claim that because his methods did not accord with our own Confucianism he was therefore heterodox, this would not be pointing at the Buddha and Laozi.
One day, the disciple Zhu Jiye said: "Lately, heterodox and deviant doctrines have harmed the Way, causing people..."

He did not know the fundamental abyss. [The other] asked, "How is that so? Yi replied, "It is like those students of the Chan school who all consider [certain things] indispensable, yet also claim that what transcends form (xíng-ér-shàng) harms the Way, thereby causing people not to know the fundamental abyss. He said: [This is why].
My friend, let us speak of it: what exactly is this "fundamental"? And what exactly has harmed you?
You do not know that you yourself are harming [the Way], so how could you know that others are harming it? Bao Xian Dao once said, "Everyone says that Chan is something humans cannot do without;
yet now you, my friend, say it harms the Way. These two views are quite fit to be tied together as one bundle. As for the present...

That which harms the Way is, in fact, these idle words. Furthermore, when Liu Chun-sou was practicing Chan, a friend surnamed Zhou asked him, "For what reason have you abandoned the Way of our Confucianism to practice Chan? Chun-sou replied, "It is like this:
for the followers of Śākyamuni it is a hoe; for the Confucians it is an axe. Although what they hold differs, nevertheless—"
"But these are all the same hand. I now simply wish to clarify this hand by means of that [axe].
Zhou replied, "If it is as Master Chun-sou says, I would rather clarify this hand by means of the axe itself; I do not wish to clarify this hand by means of the hoe.
Yuan said, "Master Chun-sou has indeed used an excellent analogy; Zhou You may also be called one who provides an excellent response. (Xin Kong remarked: "A person has two [hands].")

The hands—bending and extending are within my own power. If I wish to take up the hoe, I take up the hoe; if I wish to take up the axe, I take up the axe. What is the use of seeking to clarify him? What use is there in clarifying him? Now there was a sick man whose two hands were both paralyzed;

though renowned physicians of the age could not cure him, he suddenly encountered an immortal who came wandering through the human world and bestowed upon him a divine elixir, whereby his condition was restored to its former state. Whether moving here or there, he naturally attained clarity. Master Chun was not skilled at providing an analogy; Zhou Yi may also be said to have been unskilled at responding.
Yuan once sat in silence all day long, and when Fumin saw him, he said to him, "What binds you so? Yuan then recited this verse of his own:
It was said: "Swift as a wild goose encountering a favorable wind; powerful as a great fish released into a vast valley.
Zhao Dongshan praised Yuan, saying: "The Confucians say your learning resembles Chan; the Buddhists say my Dharma has nothing like this.

You have transcended them both, alone attaining harmony with the fundamental mind, awaiting the Sage for a hundred generations. His posthumous title was Wen'an. His poetry, prose, and recorded sayings were transmitted to later generations.
Zhen Dexiu, courtesy name Jingyuan, was a native of Pucheng. At the age of four, he received instruction in the classics; upon merely glancing at them, he could recite them from memory.

During the Qingyuan era, he passed the jinshi examinations and served in successive offices until he reached the rank of Vice President of the Board of Civil Office. The world honored him as Master Xishan.

Following the teachings of Zhu Wen Gong as his primary authority, he took it upon himself with great earnestness to uphold the Way of the Classics. He was also profoundly learned in Chan Buddhism and once remarked regarding the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa-sūtra* (Yijiao jing): [text continues]
With upright mind and right mindfulness as the foremost, one should deeply understand that upholding the precepts is the foundation of wisdom.
Regarding the method for restraining the mind, it is like tending cattle or driving horses: do not allow them to run wild. Abandon anger, cease delusion, quiet desire, and diminish seeking.
Thereafter, one proceeds from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, it is said:

"I have read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, wherein Avalokiteśvara declares that 'hearing, contemplation, and cultivation' constitute the foremost method of universal penetration (*pariśuddha-mukha*). It states: 'Initially, within the sphere of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object;

once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise. Thus gradually increasing, what is heard and the act of hearing both come to an end; when hearing is exhausted, [the self-nature of hearing is revealed]."

Abiding thus, that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty. When emptiness and the realization of emptiness reach ultimate perfection, even that which is emptied by emptiness ceases. Once birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before you.

If you can thus uproot a single faculty through this perfect method, then all faculties will be liberated. In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, you will traverse the three levels of emptiness and be no different from the Buddhas.
Furthermore, upon reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* up to the section on the four fruits of arhatship, he then ceased [his recitation].
He sighed and said: "That which the Srotāpanna realizes—is it not what Avalokiteśvara refers to as 'first, within hearing, entering the stream and losing the object'?
Entering the stream is not the existence of some dharma; it is simply not entering the six sense-objects, abiding securely and eternally."
This is what it means to have entered the stream. As for the name *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner), there is in reality no coming and going;
as for the name *anāgāmin* (Non-returner), there is in reality no non-coming. For "going" refers to entering the dust of the world, while "coming" refers to returning to the source.
Although the *sakṛdāgāmin* is able to come, they are not yet able to be without going. The *anāgāmin*, however, does not merely not go, but also...
There is no coming. Upon reaching arhatship, the intention of coming and going is exhausted, and not a single dharma can be apprehended.

Thus, although there are four fruits by name, in reality they are but a single dharma; it is merely that one passes through the three gates of emptiness, resulting in differences of depth and shallowness.

Furthermore, regarding the "Universal Gate" chapter of the Lotus Sutra, I have read this Universal Gate chapter since my youth. Although I have not yet been able to deeply understand its meaning, I have [often]...
I have conjectured this. Formerly, Li Wen, the Duke of Tang, asked Chan Master Yan of Yaoshan, "What is it like when an evil wind blows a boat and drifts it into the land of ghosts?
The Master said, "Li Ao, you little fellow, why do you ask such a thing? Duke Wen was startled, and his anger manifested on his face.
The Master laughed and said, "To give rise to this mind of hatred and anger is itself the black wind blowing the boat and drifting it into the realm of ghosts."
It is a kingdom. Alas! Mount Yaoshan may truly be called one who excels at awakening others. Inferring from this, we know that when profit and desire blaze fiercely, they are a pit of fire;
when greed and attachment lead to drowning, they are a sea of suffering. In a single thought of purity, the blazing flames become a pool;
in a single thought of alertness, the boat reaches the other shore. When calamities and afflictions bind us, wherever we find peace, there is no "I."

In times of fear, may one be like shackles falling away of their own accord; when evil people invade and oppress, or when others act with violence and injustice, may I harbor no anger or envy, remaining like a wild beast fleeing on its own.
Those who read this sutra should contemplate in this way, and thereby know that the Great Being of Potalaka truly acts for the sake of humanity.
This is no idle talk. (The story of the black wind blowing the ship refers to the matter of Yu Di.
The commentary says: Ziyang [Zhang Zai] rejected Buddhism, and people vied with one another to imitate him.

Yet they failed to realize that although Ziyang’s realization was not direct, there was no aspect of his lifelong studies through which he did not secretly penetrate Buddhist principles. Moreover, his initial entry into the Way was originally attained [from a Buddhist source].
Regarding the Chan school, in his later years he even lamented that the Sixth Patriarch was a true sage;

thus, he was not refuting Buddhism itself, but rather refuting those who abandon the Buddha of one's own mind to seek an externalized Buddha with form. Lu Xiangshan’s entire being was permeated by Chan.

Zhen Xishan’s entire work consists of teachings on the Confucian school. Although the three high officials differed in how they manifested their praise for the Buddhist gate—some remaining hidden while others were overt—their utmost effort in honoring and protecting it was one and the same.
Nevertheless, as for that which lies beyond this, they have yet to even dream of it.
The Layman Oxherder (Dharma Heir of Chan Master Wumen Kai).
The layman Yu was a native of ancient Hangzhou. During the Chunyou era of the Song dynasty, he studied under the master Wumen Kai and attained a sudden, great enlightenment.
He once said: "The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean; it all enters through minute streams. It is like a person splitting bamboo: once the first knot is penetrated," [the rest follows effortlessly].
One section [is resolved]; the rest are all cut as easily as slicing through a whetstone, requiring no further effort. Since my childhood, I have harbored this ambition:
to visit renowned masters and engage in "mouth-drums" (debates) with practitioners from all quarters, believing that the Buddha-dharma was nothing more than this, until I finally cast it all aside.
Later, I visited Master Wumen Kaiming, also known as Fuyan Chanshi; whenever he opened his mouth—
He was blocked head-on by Wumen and repeatedly told, "No, no. Withdrawing to reflect on this, he thought, "I have labored for so many years;
how could there not have been moments of joy? I have attained fragmentary insights time and again.
Yet he ultimately could not accept Wumen’s "No, no. Later, upon meeting Chouan, he went to consult him, asking, "What did you receive from Master Wumen?"
[This is] a view. To dare to invert right and wrong before humans and devas—Chou-an said: "While under the seat of Wumen, I had no dharma to obtain and no path to transmit;
I obtained only two characters. I asked: "How do you explain these two characters? He replied: [He spoke the two characters.]
"No, no. Because of this, I have come to know the way in which the Old Man of Wumen treats people:
he never lightly sprinkled even a single drop of foul water upon anyone. Although I am not clever, I was led away by the indictment of Chou-an;

my grievance is not small. Thus, I describe the 'Gate of Right and Wrong,' saying: 'Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood. Turning the light back to reflect within.'"
Utterly obstructed. As soon as you attempt to deliberate, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles. When encountering people, you pass judgment; when meeting things, you praise or disparage them.

You value antiquity and slight the present; you prize what you hear and despise what you see. Let him speculate as he will—while you linger in hesitation, you have not yet awakened from your dream, for the gate of right and wrong remains before you.
How can one penetrate this? Let us look at the question posed by Laywoman Shen of Anji County: "Is there cause and effect? He replied, "There is.

She asked, "If a student of the Way truly has no place of awakening, why does the Master intentionally say it is not so? Is there cause and effect? He replied, "The Buddha-dharma does not conform to human sentiment;
how could there be no cause and effect? Because Baizhang gave a single erroneous response, he fell into the wilds for five hundred lifetimes.
Huguo said, “The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds. Since I have no mind, what use have I for all dharmas?

The Master said, “How many phrases are there regarding this ‘is’ and ‘is not’? Huguo said, “There are four phrases. The Master asked, “What are the forms of these four phrases? Huguo raised his staff and said: “*. (A single word of affirmation.)
The first phrase—being both existent and non-existent—is untenable. The second phrase—being neither existent nor non-existent—is likewise untenable.
The third phrase—being both existent and non-existent—is untenable. The fourth phrase—being neither existent nor non-existent—is also untenable.

"If one can depart from these four propositions, only then will one see the natural splendor of the original ground. [The student] asked: "Can I depart from them? [The Master] said: "You cannot depart.

[The student] asked: "Everyone has their share; why can I not depart? [The Master] said: "When the hen marries, she flies with the cock; when the dog marries, it follows the master. [The student] asked:
"What is the natural splendor of the original ground? [The Master] said: "The crescent moon shines over how many prefectures? How many?

[The Master asked: "How many people are joyful, and how many are sorrowful? [The monk] said: "I do not ask about this kind of scenery. [The Master] said: "Then I ask about that original local scenery. [The monk] said:
"It is that which has no marks of male or female. [The Master] said: "Since it has no marks of male or female, what concern for right or wrong could there be? [The monk] said: "..."
"Is there something further beyond this? He replied, "There is. [The Master asked,] "What is this matter that is further beyond? He replied, "A horse-leech clings to the leg of a heron;
when you ascend to heaven, I shall ascend to heaven as well."

Wang Rixiu, whose courtesy name was Xuchu and sobriquet Longshu Jushi, was upright, serene, simple, and refined. He had read extensively through the classics and histories, yet one day he cast them aside, saying, "These are all merely habitual practices;
they are not the ultimate Dharma. I shall instead seek my return to the Western Land. From then on, he applied himself with diligence to the recitation of the Buddha's name.
At the age of sixty, he wore plain clothes and subsisted on vegetarian food, performing a thousand prostrations daily and retiring only at midnight.

He composed a text titled *Exhorting the World through the Visualization of the Pure Land*. Three days before his passing, he took leave of all his relatives and acquaintances, saying, "After this, we shall not meet again.
On the appointed day, after finishing his reading, he performed his usual devotions and recitations; suddenly, in a forceful voice, he called out, "Amitābha Buddha!
and proclaimed, "The Buddha has come to welcome me! He stood upright and passed away, as motionless as a planted tree. A person from the region dreamed of two...
The one who was led westward by a woman in blue robes has since been served and honored by every household as the Master Padmasambhava. The praise says:
Longshu’s exhortation to aspire toward the Western Paradise is most fervent; his earnestness did not stop at mere words, but he truly practiced what he preached.
As for the extraordinary and marvelous events at the moment of his death, they have shone brightly through the ages. Alas! Is this not the testimony of a sage of the Pure Land?
"Is this one who enters the marketplace with hands hanging down?
[The Master] praised him, saying: "How profound! The difficulty of Zen practice does not lie in the eloquence of speech, but in the awakening of the mind.
Formerly, when Xiangyan studied under Guishan, he could answer ten questions for every one asked, and a hundred for every ten; yet Guishan did not approve. One day, Guishan..."
The Master said, "I do not ask about your lifelong studies or intellectual understanding; bring me a single phrase regarding that fundamental matter before you were even born from the womb.

Yanguan was at a loss and had no reply. Later, upon gaining awakening while striking a bamboo stalk, he bowed toward the mountain from afar and said, "The Master’s great compassion exceeds that of my own parents. Had he explained it to me at that time, how could there have been the events of today?"

The Cowherd Layman (Niu-tou Jushi) spent his entire life beating the drum of his mouth with various masters; yet when he encountered Wumen, the moment the latter opened his mouth, [Niu-tou] declared it was not so.
Later, upon meeting Chuanxiu (Chou-an), he finally attained the Dharma-gate of sovereign freedom in a flash of realization.
Is this present "drumming of the mouth" not itself the seal of right and wrong? Is it the awakening of the mind? *Ei!* There is a thorn in the soft mud.
Furthermore, the eulogy says: "Right and wrong are like a thousand waves competing to rise; the Pure Land text is a single expanse across the clear sky.
Now tell me, are these two the same or different? If you say they are the same, it is a vague and superficial Buddha-nature, a muddled and indistinct True Suchness.
If you say they are different, it is like Xu Liu carrying a board, each seeing only one side. It cannot be thus, nor can it not be thus."
Neither "thus" nor "not thus"—neither is acceptable. Ultimately, how is it? Look at the footnote beneath this.
Song Lian (Dharma-heir of Chan Master Qianyan Yuanzhang). Song Lian was a native of Jinhua.
His mother dreamed of a strange monk who came with a handwritten copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and said to her: "I..."
It was then that Yongming requested a room for Yanshou, wishing to complete this volume there. Upon awakening, [Yanshou] was immediately born; consequently, he was named Shou (Longevity).
Later, his name was changed to Lan, with the courtesy name Jinglan, and he took the pen-name Wuxiang Jushi (The Non-Form Layman). At six years of age, he could memorize over two thousand words daily;
at nine, he was able to compose poetry. He entered Mount Qingluo and read through the Tripitaka three times. He once went to visit Qianyan.
Yuán Cháng’s speech was like rolling thunder. Lán wished to humble him and engaged him in debate; after several thousand words, they failed to reach an agreement, and Yuán Cháng withdrew.
Two years later, Lán visited Yuán Cháng again. Yuán Cháng asked, "I have heard that you have read through the entire Tripitaka; is this true? Lán replied, "It is so.
Yuán Cháng asked, "Did you read it with your ears, or did you observe it with your eyes? Lán replied, "I observed it with my eyes. Yuán Cháng said, "If one uses the eyes..."
"As for one who is able to contemplate this—whom do you mean? Zeng Lang raised his eyebrows toward him. Thereupon, they looked at each other and laughed. Changchu replied in a letter to Lang:
"The other day I received you for one night in the mountains; today a letter has arrived reporting that [you have said] such and such."
Upon reading this once, Wuming could not help but laugh. "What is there to laugh at? [The interlocutor asked]. "I laugh at Jing-lan sitting in a well and observing the sky," [Wuming replied].
"It is like a poor man who picks up tin and tells others he intends to sell it as silver; he simply does not recognize the value of the goods himself.
While it is unacceptable to teach others not to recognize the value of goods, why is that so? Because Jing-lan has long been amidst the clamor of worldly toil..."
Within the realm of form, one has rolled about until the stage of "rotting bones" is fully matured; one calculates and deliberates through words and language, dallying with cleverness.
Because of this abundance of karmic consciousness, when suddenly hearing our teaching of "letting go," one thinks it can serve as a practice for stillness and enable transcendence of birth and death.
For a moment, a thought of weary detachment arises, but upon turning back, one sees that there is no thinking.
When there is no place for words or measures, one mistakenly identifies this as the Dharma-body. It is like a multi-faceted crystal window, or like Mount Sumeru;
it cannot be expressed through speech. This is merely a temporary crossroads—how can you revile it?
